Runbook entry: investigating a pipeline-parallel (PP) training job that is slower than expected.

Assumptions (state before acting): synchronous PP with a 1F1B schedule, P pipeline stages,
M microbatches per global batch, no interleaving unless confirmed from the launcher config.

Concrete mechanism. PP splits the model by layer into P stages; stage i sends the activation
tensor for a microbatch to stage i+1 and receives the gradient back on the backward pass.
Throughput loss comes from the pipeline bubble: in a synchronous 1F1B schedule the idle
fraction is (P-1)/(M+P-1) of ideal step time. With P=8 and M=8 that is 7/15 = 46.7% idle -
the job can look "GPU-bound" (high power draw on stage 0) while nearly half the wall clock is
warm-up/drain. Raising M to 64 drops the bubble to 7/71 = 9.9%. This formula is the first
thing to compute, before touching NCCL or the network.

Boundary condition. Increasing M is not free and stops helping at a hard limit: stage 0 must
hold up to P in-flight microbatch activation sets, so activation memory scales roughly with
min(M,P) x per-microbatch activations. Once microbatch size drops below the point where the
per-stage GEMMs saturate the tensor cores (commonly micro-batch x seq_len below a few
thousand tokens on A30/A100-class parts), per-microbatch efficiency falls faster than the
bubble shrinks, and total throughput regresses. So the bubble formula only applies while the
per-stage kernels remain compute-bound.

Falsifiable hypotheses, in order:
H1 bubble-dominated: measured step time is within ~10% of ideal_step x (M+P-1)/M. Test by
   doubling M at fixed global batch and predicting the new step time in advance.
H2 stage imbalance: one stage's forward time exceeds the mean by >15%, so every other stage
   waits on it. Test with per-stage forward/backward timers, not aggregate GPU utilization.
H3 link-bound P2P: send/recv time between adjacent stages is a significant share of step time.
   Test by placing stage boundaries on NVLink-connected pairs vs across the NIC and comparing.

Evidence to collect: launcher config (P, M, micro-batch size, interleaving degree), per-stage
step timers or a Nsight/torch profiler trace covering >=3 steady-state steps (never step 0),
NCCL_DEBUG=INFO topology dump to confirm which stage boundaries cross a node, and peak
per-stage allocated memory.

Rollback gate: any change to M, micro-batch size, or stage placement must hold the global
batch size and the optimizer hyperparameters constant. Revert if end-to-end tokens/s does not
improve by >=5% over a >=200-step window, or if loss over the first 200 steps diverges from
the pre-change run beyond its own step-to-step noise band. Do not judge from a single step.

Not measured here: any specific number for your cluster. All figures above are formula-derived
estimates and must be replaced with profiler measurements before you act on them.

Define MoE and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Definition. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) replaces a dense FFN block with N parallel expert FFNs
plus a small router (gate). For each token the router scores the experts and dispatches the
token to its top-k (commonly k=1 or 2). Only those k experts run, so the parameter count grows
with N while the FLOPs per token grow only with k.

Why it matters for LLM infrastructure. It decouples model capacity from per-token compute: an
N=64, k=2 MoE has roughly 32x the FFN parameters of the dense model at ~2x the FFN FLOPs. That
is a favorable trade when you are compute-limited, and an unfavorable one when you are
memory-capacity- or memory-bandwidth-limited, which is the usual case at inference.

Concrete mechanism (expert parallelism). Experts are sharded across devices, so dispatch is an
all-to-all: each rank sends its tokens to the ranks owning their chosen experts, runs the local
expert FFN, then a second all-to-all returns the results. Cost per MoE layer is therefore two
all-to-alls of size approximately (tokens_per_rank x k x d_model x dtype_bytes) each. The
collective is latency- and bisection-bandwidth-sensitive, so intra-node NVLink expert placement
behaves very differently from expert parallelism spanning nodes over RoCE/IB.

Boundary condition (capacity factor and token dropping). Each expert has a fixed buffer of
capacity_factor x (tokens x k / N) slots. Routing is data-dependent and skewed, so a hot expert
overflows and the surplus tokens are dropped - they bypass the FFN via the residual path and
silently lose their share of the computation. Raising the capacity factor removes the drops but
raises activation memory and all-to-all volume proportionally; lowering it raises drop rate.
There is no setting that is simultaneously drop-free and cheap under a skewed load, which is
why load-balancing auxiliary losses exist. The FLOP savings claim above holds only while the
drop rate is near zero and the router is well balanced.

Evidence needed before claiming an MoE win: per-expert token counts (to measure routing skew
and drop rate), the all-to-all time as a fraction of step time, achieved tokens/s, and peak
memory per rank. Do not use parameter count as a proxy for capability or FLOPs as a proxy for
speed.

Rollback gate: revert to the dense baseline if measured tokens/s per GPU does not beat dense at
equal quality, if drop rate exceeds a pre-agreed threshold (e.g. 1% of tokens) in steady state,
or if per-rank peak memory leaves less headroom than your longest-sequence safety margin.

Contrast MoE with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Contrast: MoE FFN vs the naive dense FFN it replaces.

Naive (dense) baseline. Every token passes through the same FFN with weight matrices of size
d_model x d_ff. Compute and parameters are coupled: to add capacity you must widen d_ff, and
every token then pays for it. Cost per token is roughly 2 x 2 x d_model x d_ff FLOPs, uniform
and perfectly predictable; there is no routing, no all-to-all, no load imbalance, and the
memory footprint is one copy of the FFN weights per model-parallel shard.

MoE. N expert FFNs plus a router; each token is sent to its top-k experts (typically k=1 or 2).
Parameters scale with N, per-token FLOPs with k. So capacity and compute are decoupled - the
whole point of the design.

Concrete mechanism that the dense version does not have: expert parallelism turns the FFN into
a communication step. Experts are sharded across ranks, so each MoE layer performs two
all-to-all collectives - one to dispatch tokens to expert owners, one to gather results back -
each moving about tokens_per_rank x k x d_model x dtype_bytes per rank. A dense FFN under
tensor parallelism instead performs a single all-reduce of the output activations, which maps
much better onto NVLink and degrades far more gracefully when the group spans nodes over
RoCE/InfiniBand. Replacing all-reduce with all-to-all changes which part of the fabric you are
stressing: all-to-all is bisection-bandwidth- and latency-sensitive and is the usual reason an
MoE that was fast on one node collapses on four.

Boundary condition where the contrast flips. The MoE advantage holds only while (a) routing is
balanced enough that the token drop rate at your capacity factor is near zero, and (b) the
all-to-all cost stays small relative to the expert GEMM time. Skewed routing forces you to
raise the capacity factor, which raises both activation memory and all-to-all volume; at small
per-rank token counts (short sequences, low batch, or heavy decoding) the expert GEMMs shrink
while the two collectives do not, so the dense FFN wins on wall clock despite doing more FLOPs.
Serving is the worst case: memory-bound decode must hold all N experts resident, so MoE costs
far more HBM per served token than the dense model it "saves compute" over.

Falsifiable claim to test rather than assert: at your target batch and sequence length, the MoE
layer's measured step time is lower than the dense layer's at matched quality. Evidence
required: per-expert token histograms (skew and drop rate), all-to-all time as a fraction of
step time from a profiler trace over >=3 steady-state steps, tokens/s per GPU, and peak memory
per rank for both variants under identical parallelism.

Rollback gate: revert to dense if tokens/s per GPU does not improve by >=10%, if steady-state
drop rate exceeds ~1% of tokens, or if peak per-rank memory removes the headroom needed for
your longest supported sequence.

Contrast: MoE FFN vs the naive dense FFN it replaces.

Naive (dense) baseline. Every token passes through the same FFN with weight matrices of size
d_model x d_ff. Compute and parameters are coupled: to add capacity you must widen d_ff, and
every token then pays for it. Cost per token is roughly 2 x 2 x d_model x d_ff FLOPs, uniform
and perfectly predictable; there is no routing, no all-to-all, no load imbalance, and the
memory footprint is one copy of the FFN weights per model-parallel shard.

MoE. N expert FFNs plus a router; each token is sent to its top-k experts (typically k=1 or 2).
Parameters scale with N, per-token FLOPs with k. So capacity and compute are decoupled - the
whole point of the design.

Concrete mechanism that the dense version does not have: expert parallelism turns the FFN into
a communication step. Experts are sharded across ranks, so each MoE layer performs two
all-to-all collectives - one to dispatch tokens to expert owners, one to gather results back -
each moving about tokens_per_rank x k x d_model x dtype_bytes per rank. A dense FFN under
tensor parallelism instead performs a single all-reduce of the output activations, which maps
much better onto NVLink and degrades far more gracefully when the group spans nodes over
RoCE/InfiniBand. Replacing all-reduce with all-to-all changes which part of the fabric you are
stressing: all-to-all is bisection-bandwidth- and latency-sensitive and is the usual reason an
MoE that was fast on one node collapses on four.

Boundary condition where the contrast flips. The MoE advantage holds only while (a) routing is
balanced enough that the token drop rate at your capacity factor is near zero, and (b) the
all-to-all cost stays small relative to the expert GEMM time. Skewed routing forces you to
raise the capacity factor, which raises both activation memory and all-to-all volume; at small
per-rank token counts (short sequences, low batch, or heavy decoding) the expert GEMMs shrink
while the two collectives do not, so the dense FFN wins on wall clock despite doing more FLOPs.
Serving is the worst case: memory-bound decode must hold all N experts resident, so MoE costs
far more HBM per served token than the dense model it "saves compute" over.

Falsifiable claim to test rather than assert: at your target batch and sequence length, the MoE
layer's measured step time is lower than the dense layer's at matched quality. Evidence
required: per-expert token histograms (skew and drop rate), all-to-all time as a fraction of
step time from a profiler trace over >=3 steady-state steps, tokens/s per GPU, and peak memory
per rank for both variants under identical parallelism.

Rollback gate: revert to dense if tokens/s per GPU does not improve by >=10%, if steady-state
drop rate exceeds ~1% of tokens, or if peak per-rank memory removes the headroom needed for
your longest supported sequence.

Contrast MoE with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Contrast: MoE FFN vs the naive dense FFN, framed as a serving decision.

Naive baseline. One FFN, every token pays d_model x d_ff twice (up and down projection),
~2 x 2 x d_model x d_ff FLOPs per token. Capacity is bought only by widening d_ff, and the
cost is paid by every token on every step. In exchange you get a fully static compute graph:
no router, no capacity factor, no token dropping, no all-to-all.

MoE. N experts + a router; top-k routing means parameters scale with N while per-token FLOPs
scale with k. For equal quality an MoE typically needs far fewer active FLOPs than the dense
model it matches, which is why it wins on training compute and on large-batch prefill.

Concrete mechanism: the capacity factor. Each expert on each rank is given a fixed buffer of
capacity_factor x (tokens_per_rank x k / N) slots. Tokens routed to an already-full expert are
dropped (or bounced to the residual path). That fixed buffer is what makes the all-to-all a
static-shape collective and therefore fusable and CUDA-graph-friendly; it is also exactly what
converts routing skew into silent quality loss rather than into an OOM. Instrument drop rate
per layer - it is the single most informative MoE health metric and it is not visible in loss
until it is already large.

Boundary condition: the advantage inverts in memory-bound decode. At batch=1 decode you read
k expert weight matrices per layer per token instead of one, so HBM traffic per token goes up
by roughly k x (expert_params / dense_params) even though FLOPs went down. An MoE that is
2x cheaper in training FLOPs can be slower per token in low-concurrency decode than the dense
model. The crossover is set by arithmetic intensity, not by parameter count.

Falsifiable claim and evidence. Claim: on this cluster, MoE decode throughput exceeds dense
only above some concurrency C*. Test: sweep concurrency 1,4,16,64,256 at fixed input/output
lengths, record tokens/s and per-layer drop rate; C* is where the curves cross. Rollback gate:
if measured p95 TTFT or TPOT regresses beyond the SLO at the target concurrency, or drop rate
exceeds ~1% at the shipped capacity factor, revert to the dense checkpoint.

Assumptions: transformer decoder, top-k token-choice routing, expert parallelism across ranks.
No vendor- or version-specific numbers are asserted here; all thresholds must be measured.

Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with MoE. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Two failure modes / trade-offs of MoE.

1) Routing collapse and load imbalance. The router is trained jointly with the experts and has
a self-reinforcing incentive: an expert that receives more tokens gets more gradient, becomes
better, and is then chosen more often. Left unchecked, effective expert count falls far below N
and you pay N-experts of memory for a handful of useful ones.

Concrete mechanism: the auxiliary load-balancing loss. It penalises the dot product of the
fraction of tokens routed to each expert with the mean router probability for that expert,
pushing the routing distribution toward uniform. Its coefficient is a real trade-off knob - too
small and you get collapse, too large and it fights the language-modelling objective and costs
quality. Some newer designs replace it with a per-expert bias term adjusted from observed load,
which balances without injecting gradient noise into the main loss.

2) All-to-all as the new critical path. Under expert parallelism each MoE layer performs two
all-to-all collectives, dispatch and combine. All-to-all is bisection-bandwidth- and
latency-bound, unlike the all-reduce a dense TP layer uses, and it does not overlap for free -
it sits between the attention block and the expert GEMM. Cross-node MoE over RoCE with an
unconfigured or mistuned lossless fabric (PFC/ECN thresholds wrong) shows up as long-tail
step-time jitter, not as an error.

Boundary condition: both failure modes are load-dependent and only appear at scale. Balance
looks fine on a small single-node smoke run because tokens_per_rank is large relative to the
capacity buffer; skew bites when you shard experts across nodes and per-rank token counts drop.
Likewise all-to-all is invisible while the expert group fits inside one NVLink domain and
becomes dominant the moment it crosses the node boundary.

Evidence required: per-layer and per-expert token counts (Gini or max/mean load ratio), token
drop rate at the shipped capacity factor, and a profile split of step time into attention,
expert GEMM, and all-to-all. Rollback gate: max/mean expert load above ~2x sustained, or
all-to-all exceeding ~25% of step time, means stop and fix topology or routing before scaling
further.

Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with MoE. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Two failure modes / trade-offs of MoE.

1) Token dropping under a fixed capacity factor. Capacity per expert is preallocated so the
dispatch collective has a static shape. Tokens beyond that buffer are dropped and pass through
the residual only. This is a silent failure: no exception, no OOM, just a slow quality tax that
correlates with sequence content. Domain-shifted or long-context batches route more unevenly
than the training mix, so drop rate is highest exactly on the traffic you care about.

Concrete mechanism: dropless / variable-capacity implementations (grouped GEMM over
ragged expert batches) remove the drop at the cost of dynamic shapes, which breaks CUDA graph
capture and makes step time input-dependent. That is the trade: deterministic latency versus
guaranteed token coverage. Pick one deliberately, per deployment.

2) Memory and checkpoint cost scale with total, not active, parameters. An MoE with N experts
holds N copies of the FFN weights plus optimizer state. In training with Adam that is roughly
weights + 2 moments + master copy, so total-parameter growth multiplies straight through into
HBM and into checkpoint size and save/restore wall time. Expert parallelism spreads it, but it
also fixes your minimum world size: you cannot serve the model on fewer GPUs than the weights
require, no matter how small your traffic is. Small-scale evaluation and canarying get
expensive.

Boundary condition: the memory argument dominates at serving time, the drop argument dominates
at training time. If HBM per GPU is the binding constraint, an MoE is worse than a dense model
of equal active FLOPs; if training compute is the binding constraint, it is better. On 24GB-class
accelerators the MoE weight footprint usually decides the question before quality does.

Evidence required: measured per-layer drop rate on production-like traffic; measured resident
HBM for weights vs KV cache vs activations; checkpoint save/restore timing. Falsifiable claim:
raising capacity factor from 1.0 to 1.25 reduces drop rate by more than it costs in step time -
test by sweeping and measuring both. Rollback gate: if the memory headroom for KV cache falls
below the level needed for the target concurrency, the MoE config is not shippable.

Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with MoE. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Two failure modes / trade-offs of MoE.

1) Router instability during training. The router output is an argmax over a softmax; the
argmax is discontinuous, so a tiny logit change flips a token to a different expert and produces
a large loss change. Symptoms are loss spikes, poor reproducibility across restarts, and
sensitivity to batch composition. Router logits are also the classic bf16 precision casualty -
computing them in fp32 and applying z-loss on the router logits (penalising log-sum-exp
magnitude) is standard and cheap.

Concrete mechanism: the z-loss keeps router logits from drifting to large magnitudes where the
softmax saturates; saturation is what makes routing decisions brittle and gradients vanish for
non-selected experts. This is a numerics fix, not a modelling fix, and it is one of the few
MoE knobs with a clear mechanism-to-symptom chain.

2) Non-determinism and debuggability. Because assignment depends on the other tokens in the
batch (capacity is shared), MoE output for a given input depends on its batch-mates. Two
identical requests batched differently can produce different logits. That breaks naive
regression tests, complicates prefix caching validation, and makes bug reports hard to
reproduce. Expert-choice routing makes this worse, token-choice with generous capacity makes
it milder but never eliminates it at capacity limits.

Boundary condition: batch-dependence disappears only when no expert is at capacity. So the
system is deterministic in the low-load regime you test in and non-deterministic in the
high-load regime you ship in. Any determinism guarantee you make must be qualified by
concurrency and capacity factor.

Evidence required: run the same prompt at concurrency 1 and at target concurrency and diff the
logits/outputs; record per-layer capacity saturation. Falsifiable claim: at capacity_factor C
and target load, output divergence rate is below X%. Rollback gate: if a correctness-critical
path (tool-call JSON, structured output) diverges under batching, either raise capacity factor
until saturation is zero or route that traffic to a dense model.

Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with MoE. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Two failure modes / trade-offs of MoE.

1) Fabric sensitivity of the dispatch/combine all-to-all. Expert parallelism turns each MoE
layer into two all-to-all collectives. All-to-all stresses bisection bandwidth and is far less
forgiving than all-reduce: there is no ring or tree to hide latency behind, and every rank talks
to every rank. On a multi-node RoCE cluster this exposes the whole lossless-Ethernet stack -
PFC watchdog events, ECN marking thresholds, ARP/GID misconfiguration, and NIC-to-GPU affinity.
Without GPUDirect RDMA the payload additionally bounces through host memory, adding a PCIe
round trip per hop.

Concrete mechanism: NCCL will pick a transport per pair of ranks. If GDR is unavailable or
disabled for a NIC/GPU pair (wrong PCIe topology, missing nvidia-peermem, ACS enabled), it
silently falls back to a staged host copy. Throughput drops several-fold with no error. Verify
explicitly with NCCL_DEBUG=INFO plus NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=NET and confirm GDR is in use per rank;
do not infer it from documentation.

2) Operational blast radius of a single slow expert rank. Because all-to-all is a barrier, the
slowest rank sets step time for the entire job. A single GPU with a lower clock (thermal
throttling), a degraded NIC link negotiated at half width, or an unbalanced expert assignment
stalls all N ranks. Dense TP jobs degrade the same way but MoE hits the barrier twice per layer
instead of once, so the amplification is larger.

Boundary condition: within one NVLink domain neither issue is usually visible; both appear when
the expert group crosses the node boundary, and get worse as tokens_per_rank shrinks (long
context with high TP, or decode).

Evidence required: nccl-tests alltoall bandwidth at your message size across the actual
placement; per-rank step-time histogram; link width/speed and PFC/ECN counters. Rollback gate:
if measured all-to-all bandwidth is below ~60-70% of the single-node figure, do not scale out -
fix the fabric first. All thresholds here must be measured on this cluster, not assumed.

Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with MoE. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Two failure modes / trade-offs of MoE.

1) The dense-equivalent comparison is easy to get wrong, and that mis-scoping is itself the
failure. MoE papers report iso-active-FLOP or iso-training-compute wins. Serving teams then
compare against a dense model of the same total parameter count and conclude MoE is a huge win,
or against one of the same active parameter count and conclude it is free. Neither is the
decision-relevant comparison. The right one is: at fixed GPU count, fixed HBM, and fixed SLO,
which model delivers more requests/s at acceptable quality?

Concrete mechanism: HBM is partitioned between weights, KV cache, and activation workspace.
MoE takes the weight slice up, which shrinks the KV slice, which lowers the maximum concurrent
sequences, which lowers throughput even though per-token FLOPs fell. The chain runs through
KV capacity, not through FLOPs, and that is why FLOP-based reasoning misleads here.

2) Quantization and kernel maturity lag. Expert GEMMs are many small/medium GEMMs rather than
one large one; grouped-GEMM kernels, fused dispatch, and quantized expert paths are less mature
and less uniformly supported than their dense equivalents across serving stacks. Features you
take for granted on dense models (a particular quant format, speculative decoding, prefix
caching interactions, disaggregated prefill/decode handoff of the kind Mooncake or NVIDIA
Dynamo orchestrate) may be unsupported or unoptimised for MoE in the version you are running.
Verify feature support against the exact release you deploy rather than the project README.

Boundary condition: these are engineering-maturity issues, so they decay with time and are
version-specific. That means the correct answer to "should we use MoE" has a shelf life and
must be re-measured per stack version.

Evidence required: iso-hardware, iso-SLO throughput benchmark of both candidates; HBM breakdown
by weights/KV/activations; explicit feature-support check in the deployed version. Rollback
gate: fail to beat the dense baseline on requests/s at the p95 SLO, and MoE does not ship.

Explain how MoE interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

How MoE interacts with latency, throughput, and memory.

Memory. Total parameters scale with the number of experts N; active parameters scale with k.
HBM must hold all experts that a rank owns regardless of how few tokens select them. In training
add optimizer state on top (with Adam roughly 3-4x the weight bytes depending on master-weight
and moment precision). In serving, weight bytes come directly out of the budget otherwise
available to the KV cache, and KV capacity is what sets maximum concurrency. So MoE trades
FLOPs for memory, and memory is usually the binding constraint on serving nodes.

Throughput. In the compute-bound regime - prefill, or decode at high concurrency - MoE wins,
because per-token FLOPs are k/N of the equivalent-capacity dense model. This is the regime the
design targets.

Latency. In the memory-bandwidth-bound regime - low-concurrency decode - MoE is worse per token.
Each token must read k expert weight matrices from HBM, and with poor batching those reads are
not amortised across a batch, so time-per-output-token is dominated by weight traffic that grew
rather than by FLOPs that shrank. Add all-to-all latency twice per layer, which is a fixed cost
largely independent of batch size and therefore proportionally worst at small batch.

Concrete mechanism: arithmetic intensity. Per expert GEMM, intensity is roughly
(tokens_routed_to_that_expert) FLOPs per weight byte. Total tokens split k/N ways across experts,
so each expert GEMM sees a small fraction of the batch and its intensity is correspondingly
lower than the dense FFN's. Below the accelerator's ridge point the GEMM is bandwidth-bound and
extra FLOP savings buy nothing.

Boundary condition: the crossover concurrency where MoE overtakes dense on tokens/s. Above it,
expert GEMMs are compute-bound and MoE wins; below it, dense wins. Its location depends on HBM
bandwidth, k, expert size, and all-to-all latency - it must be measured, not assumed.

Evidence and rollback gate: sweep concurrency and record TTFT, TPOT, tokens/s, plus a profile
split into attention / expert GEMM / all-to-all. If the deployment's actual concurrency
distribution sits below the measured crossover, MoE is the wrong choice for that tier.

Explain how MoE interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

How MoE interacts with latency, throughput, and memory.

Assume a transformer decoder, top-k token-choice routing, expert parallelism, and separable
prefill and decode phases.

Prefill / throughput. Prefill batches thousands of tokens per step, so every expert receives
enough tokens for its GEMM to be compute-bound. Here MoE delivers close to its theoretical
advantage: FLOPs per token are k/N of the capacity-matched dense model. All-to-all volume is
proportional to tokens x k x d_model, so it grows with the batch, but so does the compute it
overlaps with, and the ratio stays roughly constant. Prefill is where MoE looks best.

Decode / latency. Decode processes one token per sequence per step. Per-layer all-to-all
latency is now a fixed serial cost added to every token's critical path, and expert weight reads
are amortised over far fewer tokens. TPOT therefore degrades relative to dense unless
concurrency is high enough to refill the expert GEMMs.

Concrete mechanism that exploits this asymmetry: prefill/decode disaggregation. Run prefill and
decode on separate pools with different parallelism, and ship the KV cache between them - the
pattern behind Mooncake's KV-cache-centric architecture and behind NVIDIA Dynamo's disaggregated
serving. For MoE this is more valuable than for dense models precisely because the two phases
sit on opposite sides of the arithmetic-intensity ridge, so they want different expert-parallel
degrees and different batching policies. The transfer itself then needs RDMA (GDR, or GDS if it
is staged through NVMe) or the handoff becomes the new bottleneck.

Boundary condition: disaggregation only pays when KV transfer time is small relative to the
prefill time it lets you overlap. For short prompts the transfer dominates and the aggregated
deployment wins. There is a prompt-length threshold below which disaggregation is a net loss.

Evidence required: measured KV transfer bytes and achieved RDMA bandwidth for the transfer path;
TTFT/TPOT before and after; per-phase GPU utilisation. Falsifiable claim: disaggregation
improves throughput at the deployment's median prompt length. Rollback gate: p95 TTFT regression
beyond the SLO, or KV transfer occupying more than ~15% of TTFT, reverts to aggregated serving.

How MoE interacts with latency, throughput, and memory.

Start from where the bytes and the time go.

Memory. Per rank: weights = (experts owned) x expert_size + shared (attention, embeddings);
plus activations, plus - in serving - the KV cache. MoE inflates the first term while leaving
the KV term untouched, so it compresses the concurrency budget. Note that the KV cache is a
function of layers, heads, head_dim, and sequence length, and is unaffected by how many experts
exist; this is why MoE improves compute efficiency without improving long-context serving
economics at all.

Throughput. Active FLOPs per token drop by roughly k/N versus a dense model with the same total
FFN capacity. Realised throughput gain is always less, because (a) the router and the
permutation/unpermutation of tokens cost real time, (b) dispatch and combine all-to-all are
serial with the expert GEMM, and (c) load imbalance means the slowest expert sets the step time
while others idle.

Latency. Two extra collectives per MoE layer on the critical path. With 30-60 layers that is
60-120 additional synchronisation points per forward pass, each with its own launch and network
latency floor. In decode these floors do not amortise.

Concrete mechanism worth naming: token permutation. Before the expert GEMM, tokens must be
sorted by destination expert into contiguous buffers; after, they must be scattered back and
weighted by router probabilities. These gather/scatter kernels are pure HBM traffic with zero
FLOPs and are a measurable fraction of MoE layer time - fusing them into the dispatch is one of
the highest-leverage MoE kernel optimisations, and whether your stack does it is a
version-specific fact to verify by profiling, not to assume.

Boundary condition: the FLOP saving is realised only when expert GEMMs are compute-bound. Once
tokens_per_expert_per_rank falls below the level that saturates the tensor cores - long context
with high parallel degree, or low-concurrency decode - the saving disappears and only the
overheads remain.

Evidence required: kernel-level profile attributing time to router, permute, expert GEMM,
all-to-all, unpermute; tokens-per-expert histogram. Rollback gate: measured end-to-end speedup
below ~1.3x versus the dense baseline at target load does not justify the operational
complexity.

How MoE interacts with latency, throughput, and memory.

Framed as the three budgets an infrastructure engineer actually manages.

HBM budget. MoE raises resident weight bytes by roughly N/k relative to an active-FLOP-matched
dense model, so on fixed hardware you either add GPUs, shard experts more aggressively, or
quantize. Expert parallelism spreads weights but sets a hard floor on world size: the model can
no longer be canaried on one GPU, which changes your whole rollout and rollback procedure.

Network budget. Dispatch + combine all-to-all per layer, roughly
tokens_per_rank x k x d_model x dtype_bytes each way. Inside an NVLink domain this is cheap.
Across nodes it needs RDMA with GPUDirect actually enabled, and it is bisection-bandwidth-bound,
so it degrades non-linearly with oversubscribed spine links or a mis-sized rail-optimised
topology.

Time budget. Throughput improves in compute-bound phases; per-token latency at low concurrency
usually worsens. Net effect on a real workload depends entirely on the concurrency distribution.

Concrete mechanism for the memory/latency trade: expert offload. Keeping cold experts in host
memory or NVMe and staging them in on demand (GDS-style direct storage-to-GPU paths avoid the
CPU bounce buffer) lowers HBM pressure. The cost is a load on the critical path whose latency is
governed by PCIe or storage bandwidth, orders of magnitude below HBM. It is viable only if
routing is predictable enough to prefetch, i.e. if expert reuse across consecutive tokens is
high.

Boundary condition: offload works when (expert reuse rate) x (prefetch lead time) covers the
transfer latency. For batch=1 chat decode, routing changes per token and prefetch fails, so
offload turns into a stall per layer. It is a batch/offline technique, not an interactive-serving
technique, unless you can demonstrate reuse.

Evidence required: expert-reuse statistics across consecutive decode steps; measured PCIe/NVMe
bandwidth on the actual path; TPOT with and without offload. Falsifiable claim: expert reuse
exceeds the level needed to hide transfer latency at the deployment's batch size. Rollback gate:
any TPOT regression past the SLO, or measured prefetch hit rate below ~80%, disables offload.

What assumptions must be stated before making a performance claim about MoE? Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Assumptions that must be stated before any MoE performance claim:
1. What is held constant: quality. State the held-out eval and the score parity band. A throughput claim against a weaker dense baseline is not an MoE claim.
2. Model configuration: total params, active params per token, number of experts, top-k, shared-expert presence, number of MoE vs dense layers, capacity factor, and the token-drop policy.
3. Parallelism and topology: tensor-parallel, expert-parallel, pipeline degrees; how many GPUs per node; intra-node link (e.g. NVLink vs PCIe) and inter-node fabric (e.g. IB/RoCE) with its per-GPU bandwidth. All-to-all cost is dominated by the slowest hop, so an expert-parallel group that spans nodes behaves very differently from one that fits inside a node.
4. Serving regime: batch size / concurrency, input and output length distribution, whether prefill and decode are colocated or disaggregated, scheduler policy, and whether the number quoted is at a fixed SLO or at saturation.
5. Numerics: dtype/quantization for weights, activations and KV cache; whether the router runs in higher precision.
6. Measurement hygiene: warmup discarded, steady state reached, run duration, number of repeats, percentile (not just mean), and client-side vs server-side timing.
7. Which numbers are measured and which are estimated. Analytical active-FLOP savings are an upper bound, not a result.
Mechanism: the claimed saving comes from executing only top-k experts per token; the offsetting costs are router overhead, dispatch/combine all-to-all, expert load imbalance, and full-weight HBM residency.
Boundary condition: if expert-parallel groups cross the node boundary, all-to-all runs at inter-node fabric bandwidth and can dominate step time, erasing the FLOP saving; measure the all-to-all share before claiming anything.
Falsifiable form and rollback: state the claim as 'iso-quality, at concurrency C and length mix L, tokens/s/GPU improves by >= X% with p95 TTFT/TPOT within SLO'; revert to dense if two independent runs fail it, or if HBM headroom for peak KV cache is lost.

Explain how MoE changes between training and inference. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

How MoE differs between training and inference:
Shared mechanism: a router scores tokens and sends each to top-k experts; only those experts' FFN weights are used per token, so active FLOPs per token are far below total parameters. Under expert parallelism this becomes a dispatch all-to-all before the expert FFN and a combine all-to-all after it.
Training-specific:
- Auxiliary objectives exist: load-balancing / router-z losses (or loss-free bias correction) push the token distribution toward uniform across experts. These have no inference-time counterpart.
- Capacity factor and token dropping are tuned for throughput; dropped tokens are a training-dynamics concern.
- Backward pass adds a second pair of all-to-alls, and optimizer state plus gradients for *all* experts must be held, so memory is dominated by total (not active) parameters times optimizer-state multiplier.
- Batches are large and token-dense, so expert GEMMs are comfortably compute-bound and imbalance amortizes over many tokens.
Inference-specific:
- Router is frozen; no balancing loss can fix skew, so real traffic can persistently overload a few experts. Prefill (many tokens at once) behaves like training and balances well; decode (few tokens per step) is where skew and latency hurt.
- Decode is memory-bandwidth- and latency-bound: with one token per sequence per step, only a handful of experts are touched per step, yet all expert weights must be resident in HBM. This is the core asymmetry — inference pays total-parameter memory cost for active-parameter compute.
- Token dropping is normally unacceptable at inference, so capacity must be effectively unbounded or overflow rerouted, which changes the cost model.
- All-to-all latency is now on the critical path of every decode step, and small messages make it latency- rather than bandwidth-bound.
Boundary condition: if the expert-parallel group spans nodes, per-step all-to-all latency (not bandwidth) can dominate decode; keeping the EP group inside one NVLink domain is usually the deciding factor.
Evidence to collect: per-expert token histogram under real traffic, all-to-all time share in decode vs prefill, HBM high-water mark, and p95 TPOT.
Falsifiable hypothesis and rollback: 'moving the EP group inside one node reduces decode all-to-all share below Y% and p95 TPOT below SLO'; if not reproduced twice, revert to the dense or lower-EP configuration.

Explain how MoE changes between training and inference. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Assumptions: decoder-only transformer, MoE in the FFN block, top-k routing (k=1 or 2), shared/dense attention. All numbers below are structural claims, not measurements on any specific platform.

What actually changes between training and inference:
1. Mechanism (concrete): token routing changes from *load-balanced-by-loss* to *load-balanced-by-luck*. In training you add an auxiliary balance loss (and often capacity factor C>1 with token dropping) so expert utilization is roughly uniform across a large global batch. At inference you serve small, correlated batches; the router is frozen, there is no balance loss, and one decode step may send most of its tokens to a handful of experts. Under expert parallelism this converts a balanced all-to-all into a straggler-bound all-to-all: step latency is set by the busiest expert rank, not the average.
2. Compute vs memory shifts sides. Training is throughput/FLOP-bound and MoE genuinely reduces active FLOPs per token (active params = shared + k experts). Decode inference is memory-bandwidth- and capacity-bound: you must keep *all* experts resident even though only k are read per token, so MoE raises HBM footprint and weight-load traffic per useful FLOP. The arithmetic-intensity win largely evaporates at batch size 1.
3. Token dropping is acceptable in training (capacity factor caps expert queues; dropped tokens just skip the FFN) but is usually unacceptable in serving, so inference either uses C=inf/no-drop or drop-less routing, which reintroduces load imbalance as latency variance rather than as quality loss.
4. Parallelism layout usually differs: training commonly uses expert parallelism fused with data/tensor parallelism inside one job; serving often prefers replicating the whole MoE per instance, or splitting prefill and decode (disaggregated serving, e.g. Dynamo/Mooncake-style) so the all-to-all cost lands only where batches are large enough to amortize it.

Boundary condition (where the above stops holding): if the serving batch is large and diverse enough that per-step token counts per expert approach the training-time distribution — roughly, effective tokens per step >> num_experts * k so each expert gets a statistically stable share — the imbalance term becomes second-order and MoE inference behaves like training. Concretely, at batch size 1 decode the imbalance is maximal; the crossover is workload- and topology-specific and must be measured, not assumed.

Falsifiable predictions:
- P1: expert-utilization entropy at inference is strictly lower than at training for the same model, and decreases as serving batch size decreases.
- P2: p99/p50 inter-token latency ratio grows with expert-parallel degree at fixed batch size.
Evidence to collect: per-expert token counts per step, all-to-all time as a fraction of step time (NCCL/comm profiler), TTFT and TPOT percentiles vs batch size, HBM residency.
Rollback gate: if p99 TPOT regresses beyond the SLO or all-to-all exceeds a preset fraction of step time at target load, fall back to a replicated (no expert-parallel) layout or a dense model of equal serving quality.

Explain how MoE changes between training and inference. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Assumptions: FFN-level MoE, top-k routing, frozen router at serving time. Structural claims; no platform-specific numbers invented.

Mechanism (concrete): the *batch that the router sees* changes shape. In training the router optimizes over a large global batch with an auxiliary load-balancing loss and a capacity factor; excess tokens for a hot expert are dropped or rerouted, and that loss term actively pushes utilization toward uniform. At inference the router weights are frozen, no balancing pressure exists, and each decode step carries only batch_size tokens per layer. With expert parallelism this means the all-to-all dispatch/combine per MoE layer is straggler-bound: the step ends when the most-loaded expert rank finishes, so effective throughput tracks the max, not the mean, of the expert load distribution.

Second-order consequences worth naming:
- Cost model inverts. Training cares about active FLOPs per token, where MoE wins. Decode cares about bytes moved per token and total resident weights, where MoE loses: all experts sit in HBM, only k are used.
- Prefill and decode diverge. Prefill has thousands of tokens per step, so expert load is near-uniform and MoE looks like training. Decode has batch_size tokens per step and is the imbalance-sensitive phase. This is a direct argument for prefill/decode disaggregation.
- Token dropping is a training-only tolerance. Serving normally runs drop-less, converting a quality knob into a latency-variance knob.

Boundary condition: the training/inference gap is negligible when tokens per step per MoE layer is large relative to num_experts (rule of thumb: >> num_experts/k tokens per step), because the multinomial routing distribution then concentrates. At small decode batch it is maximal. Also, if the deployment replicates all experts per GPU instead of sharding them (no expert parallelism), there is no all-to-all and the imbalance shows up only as unused FLOPs, not as a collective straggler — at the cost of HBM.

Explain how MoE changes between training and inference. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Assumptions: transformer with MoE FFN layers, top-k gating, expert parallelism available but optional. I distinguish structural facts from estimates and give no vendor-specific numbers.

Concrete mechanism that changes: capacity handling. During training you set a capacity factor C (tokens per expert per batch <= C * tokens/num_experts) and you *drop or reroute* overflow tokens; an auxiliary load-balancing loss simultaneously trains the router toward uniform utilization. At inference both of those disappear: the router is frozen and dropping tokens would silently corrupt user output, so serving typically runs drop-less. The overflow that training absorbed as a small quality cost now materializes as a latency cost — the all-to-all dispatch/combine in each MoE layer completes only when the slowest expert rank does.

Other real shifts:
- Bound changes from compute to memory. Training: MoE reduces active FLOPs/token, which is the binding constraint. Decode: the binding constraint is HBM capacity plus weight-read bandwidth, and MoE must keep every expert resident while touching only k. So MoE's efficiency advantage is much larger in training than in single-stream decode.
- Batch statistics change. Prefill (thousands of tokens/step) resembles training; decode (batch_size tokens/step) does not.
- Numerics/kernels differ: training often uses fused grouped-GEMM with a fixed capacity shape; drop-less inference needs variable-length grouped GEMM or padding, which can waste FLOPs or force recompilation on shape changes.

Boundary condition: none of the imbalance story matters if experts are *replicated* rather than sharded — with all experts on every GPU there is no all-to-all, so imbalance costs only idle FLOPs. That layout is feasible only while total expert weights fit in per-GPU HBM alongside the KV cache; once they do not, you are forced into expert parallelism and the straggler effect returns.

Falsifiable hypothesis: for a fixed model, moving from expert-parallel to expert-replicated serving reduces p99 TPOT at batch size 1 but reduces max concurrency (fewer KV-cache slots). Test by measuring both layouts at iso-hardware.
Evidence required: HBM breakdown (weights vs KV vs activations), per-expert token counts, all-to-all time share, TTFT/TPOT percentiles, max concurrent sequences, output-parity check between layouts.
Rollback gate: abandon the expert-parallel layout if it fails the p99 SLO at target concurrency, or if KV-cache capacity forces a preemption rate above the agreed threshold.

Explain how MoE changes between training and inference. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Assumptions: MoE placed in FFN blocks, top-k routing, attention dense. Claims are structural; anything numeric below is an explicitly labeled estimate.

Mechanism (concrete): the load-balancing objective is removed at inference. At serving time the router is frozen and there is no balancing pressure; a decode step routes only batch_size tokens per layer. Under expert parallelism the per-layer all-to-all (dispatch then combine) is a synchronizing collective, so step latency = slowest expert rank. What else genuinely differs:
- Resource bound flips: active-FLOP savings (training's win) vs all-expert HBM residency and weight-read bandwidth (decode's cost).
- Failure mode flips: training absorbs imbalance as dropped tokens (quality); inference absorbs it as tail latency (SLO).
- Phase asymmetry: prefill behaves like training because tokens/step is large; decode does not. This motivates disaggregating prefill and decode onto separate pools with different parallelism, as in Mooncake/Dynamo-style architectures, so the all-to-all runs where it is amortized.

Estimate (not measured): with 64 experts and k=2, you need on the order of hundreds of tokens per step before per-expert counts are statistically stable. Below that, expect high variance; above it, MoE decode approaches its training-time efficiency profile.

- P1: expert-load coefficient of variation scales roughly as 1/sqrt(tokens per step).
- P2: disabling expert parallelism (replicating experts) removes the correlation between load imbalance and step latency.

Give one misleading intuition about MoE and correct it. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Misleading intuition: "A Mixture-of-Experts model with N total parameters but only k active experts costs about the same to serve as a dense model with that active parameter count." People read '8x7B, ~13B active' as '13B to deploy'.

Why it is wrong (concrete mechanism): active parameters determine *FLOPs per token*, not *bytes resident* and not *bytes moved*. Every expert must sit in HBM because the router may select any of them at any token, so memory capacity scales with total parameters, not active ones. Worse, in autoregressive decode the kernel is weight-bandwidth-bound: at small batch you pay to read a fresh set of expert weights per token, and different tokens in the same batch may select different experts, so the batch cannot amortize a single weight read the way a dense FFN can. Add the per-MoE-layer all-to-all (dispatch + combine) under expert parallelism, which is a synchronizing collective whose cost tracks the *most loaded* expert rank, and the deployment cost of the MoE is much closer to its total-parameter footprint than to its active-parameter FLOP count.

Corrected statement: MoE buys you dense-model-quality at reduced *compute* per token; it does not buy you reduced *memory* or reduced *serving complexity*. Budget HBM against total expert weights plus KV cache; budget latency against all-to-all and expert-load imbalance.

Boundary condition (when the naive intuition is nearly right): in large-batch prefill or offline batch scoring, where thousands of tokens per step are routed, per-expert weight reads are amortized across many tokens and the workload becomes compute-bound. There the MoE really does behave close to its active-parameter cost. The intuition fails hardest at batch size 1 decode.

Falsifiable prediction: measure tokens/s/GPU for the MoE and for a dense model with the same active parameter count. Prediction: near parity at large-batch prefill, and a significant MoE deficit at batch-size-1 decode; the MoE will also support fewer concurrent sequences at equal HBM because expert weights crowd out KV cache.
Evidence required: HBM breakdown (weights/KV/activations), tokens-per-step per-expert histograms, all-to-all fraction of step time, TTFT/TPOT percentiles at matched concurrency, max concurrency at fixed SLO.
Rollback gate: if MoE cannot meet the p99 TPOT SLO at the concurrency needed for the cost target, revert to the quality-matched dense baseline.

Give one misleading intuition about MoE and correct it. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Misleading intuition: "MoE routing is basically free — it is just a small linear layer picking top-k experts, so the overhead is negligible."

Why it is wrong (concrete mechanism): the router matmul is indeed tiny, but the router's *output* triggers a data movement pattern, and that is the real cost. After gating you must permute tokens so each expert receives a contiguous block, exchange them across ranks with an all-to-all (dispatch), run grouped GEMMs of ragged sizes, then all-to-all again (combine) and un-permute. Under expert parallelism this is two synchronizing collectives per MoE layer per step. Because it is synchronizing, its cost is set by the most-loaded expert rank, not the average — so a frozen router that happens to favor a few experts on a small decode batch inflates every step. The permute/un-permute and ragged grouped-GEMM also cost real memory traffic and can force padding or shape-driven kernel recompiles.

Corrected statement: routing compute is negligible; routing-induced communication, memory permutation, and load imbalance are not. Model MoE overhead as 2 all-to-alls per MoE layer plus a load-imbalance multiplier, not as one small GEMM.

Boundary condition (when the intuition is approximately true): if experts are replicated on every GPU rather than sharded, there is no all-to-all at all — routing collapses to a local mask and its overhead really is small. This layout is only viable while total expert weights plus KV cache fit in per-GPU HBM. Likewise, in a single-node deployment with high-bandwidth intra-node interconnect and large batches, the all-to-all can be small relative to compute.

Falsifiable prediction: profile the same model with expert parallelism on and off at fixed batch size. Prediction: with EP on, all-to-all plus permute occupies a measurable, non-trivial share of MoE-layer time and that share grows as batch size shrinks and as EP degree grows; with EP off the share is ~0 but HBM headroom and max concurrency drop.
Evidence required: NCCL/comm profile split into dispatch vs combine, kernel-level timeline showing permute/un-permute, per-expert token counts, TPOT percentiles vs EP degree and batch size, HBM breakdown.
Rollback gate: if the measured collective share exceeds the pre-agreed budget of step time at target load, roll back to expert replication or reduce EP degree.

Misleading intuition: "Adding more experts adds capacity for free, because active compute per token stays fixed at top-k." The implied conclusion is that scaling experts is a costless quality lever.

(2) Communication: under expert parallelism, more experts usually means a larger expert-parallel group, and the all-to-all's message-count/latency term grows with group size, while each message shrinks — pushing the collective toward the latency-bound regime where interconnect round-trips, not bandwidth, dominate. Since the all-to-all is synchronizing, tail load sets step latency.

Corrected statement: more experts trades *memory and communication* for *quality at fixed active FLOPs*. It is a real lever but its price is paid in HBM footprint, collective latency, and tail-latency variance — none of which appear in an active-parameter count.

A single request's tokens therefore scatter across many experts at every MoE layer, and the set changes between layers. Misleading intuition: "MoE load balancing is solved — the auxiliary balance loss during training guarantees experts stay evenly used in production."

Why it is wrong (concrete mechanism): the balance loss is a *training-time* gradient signal computed over a large, diverse global batch. It shapes the router weights so that assignments are uniform *in expectation over that distribution*. At serving time the router is frozen, the loss no longer exists, and each decode step routes only batch_size tokens per layer — a tiny sample. Even a perfectly calibrated router yields high relative variance when tokens per step is small compared to num_experts/k. Worse, production traffic is not i.i.d. with the training mixture: a burst of same-language or same-format requests correlates token distributions and reliably creates hot experts. Because the expert-parallel all-to-all is a synchronizing collective, the slowest rank sets the step time, so imbalance shows up as tail latency (p99 TPOT), not as an averaged-away inefficiency.

Corrected statement: training-time balancing makes the *expected* distribution uniform; it does nothing about small-sample variance or distribution shift at serving. Balance must be monitored and mitigated at runtime — via larger effective batches, expert replication for hot experts, capacity-aware scheduling, or dropping expert parallelism entirely.

Boundary condition (when the intuition is nearly right): large-batch prefill or offline batch inference over a diverse corpus, where tokens per step >> num_experts/k and traffic resembles the training mixture. There, measured utilization really can be close to uniform and the residual imbalance is second-order.

Goal: decide, with a falsifiable test, whether an MoE checkpoint beats a quality-matched dense baseline for a specific serving workload. Everything below is a design; no results are claimed.

Null (H0): the MoE meets neither the throughput gain threshold nor the SLO, or its gain vanishes once concurrency is matched.

Controls to hold fixed (state these or the experiment is meaningless): hardware and interconnect topology, dtype/quantization, tokenizer, max context, scheduler and batching policy (continuous batching), KV-cache layout and eviction, sampling parameters, request trace (replayed, identical seed and arrival times), and server version. 1. Quality gate first. Run the held-out eval; if the MoE is not within the agreed quality band of the dense baseline, stop — no throughput number is meaningful.
2. Sweep offered load from 10% to 120% of expected peak on the replayed trace, with two length mixes (e.g. 2k in / 256 out and 8k in / 1k out).

5. Repeat each point at least 3 times; report medians and dispersion. Discard the first run as warm-up (compile/graph capture, cache fill).

If the MoE wins on tokens/s/GPU only at a concurrency it cannot actually sustain within SLO, or only after its HBM footprint has cut max concurrency below the production requirement, the win is not real. Also, results at batch size 1 do not generalize to large-batch prefill and vice versa — report both phases separately.

Decision / rollback gate: adopt the MoE only if (i) quality is within band, (ii) tokens/s/GPU improves by more than the measured run-to-run dispersion at the target SLO, and (iii) max concurrency meets the production requirement. Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating MoE. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

RUNBOOK: MoE serving - uneven decode latency / step-time spikes

Scope: MoE model served with expert parallelism. Symptom: p99 inter-token latency far above p50 while GPU utilization looks "high" but ragged.

Mechanism to keep in mind (concrete): each MoE layer performs dispatch and combine all-to-all collectives. These are synchronizing: every rank waits for the slowest expert rank. At inference the router is frozen and there is no load-balance loss, so a small, correlated decode batch can send a disproportionate share of tokens to a few experts. Result: FLOPs are unchanged but step time tracks the max-loaded expert.

Triage steps:
1. Confirm the symptom is per-step, not per-request: pull the server's ITL/TPOT histogram, not the average. If p50 is fine and p99 is bad, continue; if both are bad, this is a capacity problem, not a routing problem.
2. Dump per-expert token counts for a few hundred decode steps. Compute utilization entropy or Gini. Skew rising with small batches is the signature.
3. Check whether the spike correlates with all-to-all time. Use NCCL timing (NCCL_DEBUG=INFO for topology, a profiler trace for durations). If all-to-all is <10% of step time, routing skew is not your bottleneck - look at KV cache preemption and recompute counters instead.
4. Rule out the boring causes before blaming MoE: thermal/power throttling (nvidia-smi dmon, check clocks and power cap), a straggler GPU or link (per-rank step time spread), ECC/retired pages, and any rank sharing a NUMA node or PCIe root with another job.
5. Check the fabric: for RoCE, confirm PFC/ECN are actually configured and that you are not silently falling back from GPUDirect RDMA to a host-staged path (NCCL_DEBUG=INFO shows the selected transport). A silent fallback looks exactly like "MoE is slow".

Mitigations, in order of reversibility:
- Increase batching window / max-num-seqs so routing averages out. Cheapest, fully reversible.
- Switch to drop-less routing or raise capacity factor if tokens are being dropped or queued.
- Replicate experts instead of sharding them (removes all-to-all entirely) if HBM allows.
- Disaggregate prefill and decode so the all-to-all cost lands where batches are large.

RUNBOOK: MoE training - loss plateau or divergence with suspected router collapse

Scope: multi-GPU MoE pretraining/fine-tuning. Symptom: loss stalls or spikes, and throughput drifts, without an obvious data or LR cause.

Mechanism (concrete): top-k routing is trained jointly with the model. Without a sufficient auxiliary load-balance loss (and often a router z-loss), the router has a positive-feedback failure mode: experts that receive more tokens train faster, become more attractive, and receive still more tokens. Utilization collapses onto a few experts, effective capacity drops toward the dense-with-fewer-params case, and with a finite capacity factor the overflow tokens get dropped, silently removing supervision.

Triage steps:
1. Plot per-expert token counts per step and the utilization entropy over training. A monotone entropy decline is router collapse; a sudden discontinuity is more likely a data-shard or checkpoint-restore bug.
2. Plot the dropped-token fraction. If it is climbing, you are losing gradient signal, and the loss plateau is an artifact of the capacity factor, not of model capacity.
3. Check the router z-loss / logit magnitude. Exploding router logits precede collapse and are the earliest actionable signal.
4. Confirm the balance loss is actually applied and correctly scaled after any gradient-accumulation or parallelism change - this coefficient is a classic casualty of a refactor.
5. Rule out infrastructure causes of "plateau-looking" curves: a rank silently restarting, mismatched data sharding after resume, or an NCCL timeout retry loop. Cross-check step time variance and per-rank loss.

Mitigations:
- Raise the balance-loss coefficient and/or z-loss, restarting from the last healthy checkpoint (not from the collapsed one - a collapsed router rarely recovers in place).
- Raise capacity factor to reduce dropping, accepting the memory and all-to-all cost.
- Add router jitter/noise during training to break the feedback loop.

Boundary condition: an entropy decline is only pathological if it is not what you asked for. Some domain-specialized setups intentionally encourage expert specialization, and moderate imbalance with a stable drop rate and improving held-out loss is healthy. Judge on held-out loss plus drop rate together, never on entropy alone.

Evidence required: per-expert token counts, entropy and drop-rate curves, router logit norms, per-rank loss curves, and the exact balance-loss coefficient in the effective config (dumped from the running job, not from the repo default).

Rollback gate: if held-out loss does not improve within a fixed token budget after the intervention, roll back to the last checkpoint with healthy entropy and drop rate rather than continuing to spend compute.

RUNBOOK: MoE capacity planning - "will this model fit and serve on our GPUs?"

Scope: pre-deployment sizing for an MoE checkpoint on a fixed GPU fleet.

Mechanism (concrete): MoE decouples *active* parameters from *total* parameters. Active params per token = shared trunk + k * expert size, and that drives FLOPs. Total params = shared + E * expert size, and that drives HBM residency, because every expert must be resident even though only k are read per token. Any sizing done on active params alone will underestimate memory by roughly E/k.

Procedure:
1. Compute total weight bytes: total_params * bytes_per_param (2 for bf16/fp16, ~1 for fp8/int8, ~0.5 for 4-bit). Do this from the checkpoint's actual shapes, not from the model card.
2. Subtract weights, activations, and framework overhead from per-GPU HBM to get the KV cache budget. KV bytes per token = 2 * num_layers * num_kv_heads * head_dim * bytes_per_elem; divide the budget by that to get the concurrency ceiling in tokens.
3. Decide the layout: expert parallelism (shards experts, adds two all-to-all per MoE layer per step) versus full replication per instance (no collectives, but every GPU group must hold all experts). Replication is preferred when it fits, because it removes the synchronizing collective from the decode path.
4. If EP crosses hosts, verify the fabric first: NCCL topology (NCCL_DEBUG=INFO), GPUDirect RDMA actually in use rather than a host-staged fallback, and RoCE PFC/ECN configured. Cross-host all-to-all on a misconfigured fabric will dominate every other design choice.
5. Validate with a short load test at the target concurrency before committing; sizing arithmetic gives a bound, not a measurement.

Boundary condition: the arithmetic above assumes weights and KV cache are the only significant consumers and that no preemption/recompute occurs. Once the scheduler starts preempting sequences, effective concurrency falls well below the computed ceiling, and long-context workloads can make KV cache, not experts, the dominant term - in that regime MoE-versus-dense is nearly irrelevant to fit. Quantization changes bytes_per_param but also kernel support and accuracy; do not assume a 4-bit path exists for MoE experts on your stack until you have run it.

Evidence required: checkpoint shape dump, measured HBM high-water mark under load, preemption counters, measured p99 TTFT/ITL at target concurrency, and the NCCL transport actually selected.

Rollback gate: do not promote a config whose measured HBM high-water mark exceeds 90% of per-GPU capacity at target concurrency, or which shows any preemption at steady state; fall back to the replicated or smaller-concurrency configuration.

RUNBOOK: MoE upgrade validation - promoting an MoE model over an incumbent dense model

Scope: change-management checklist for swapping a dense served model for an MoE one. The failure mode this runbook prevents is promoting on offline benchmarks and discovering the regression in production tail latency.

Mechanism (concrete): MoE reduces active FLOPs per token via top-k routing but keeps all E experts resident in HBM and, under expert parallelism, inserts two synchronizing all-to-all collectives per MoE layer per step. So the quality-per-FLOP win and the latency-per-request cost are decided by two different mechanisms, and a benchmark that measures only one of them cannot justify the promotion.

Validation gates, all required:
1. Quality gate: held-out evaluation on your own task distribution, not just public benchmarks, with contamination checks. Report per-slice results; MoE models can shift capability unevenly across domains because of expert specialization.
2. Memory gate: measured HBM high-water mark at target concurrency, with headroom >=10%, and zero preemption/recompute events at steady state.
3. Latency gate: p99 TTFT and p99 ITL under a replayed production trace, compared arm-to-arm on identical hardware, identical server version, and locked clocks. Means are not acceptable evidence here.
4. Fabric gate (only if EP spans hosts): confirm GPUDirect RDMA is actually selected and that RoCE PFC/ECN are configured; record the NCCL transport from NCCL_DEBUG=INFO. A silent host-staged fallback will pass a smoke test and fail production.
5. Failure gate: kill one rank and confirm the serving layer degrades or restarts as designed. EP raises the blast radius of a single GPU failure relative to a replicated dense deployment - that is an availability change, not just a performance change.

Rollout: shadow traffic first, then a canary at low percentage with automatic rollback wired to p99 ITL and error rate, then ramp.

Boundary condition: this checklist assumes the incumbent and candidate are served by the same stack at the same precision. If the MoE arm is also quantized or moved to a different server version, you have confounded the experiment and cannot attribute any delta to MoE; change one variable per promotion.

Evidence required: side-by-side latency histograms, HBM high-water marks, per-slice quality tables with contamination notes, NCCL transport logs, and a recorded rank-failure drill.

Rollback gate: automatic revert to the dense model if canary p99 ITL regresses >10%, error rate rises above baseline, or any preemption is observed; the dense checkpoint stays warm and loadable for the entire canary window.

Define quantization and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Definition: quantization is the replacement of a model's high-precision numeric representation (typically bf16/fp16) with a lower-bit representation (fp8, int8, int4, or block/group-scaled formats), together with the scales and zero-points needed to map back to the original range. It is a representation change, not an approximation of the architecture: the graph is unchanged, only the numeric format and the kernels that consume it.

Why it matters in LLM infrastructure: LLM decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, not FLOP-bound. Each decoded token requires reading essentially the whole weight set from HBM. Halving bytes per parameter roughly halves that traffic, so decode throughput at low batch size tracks the precision reduction almost linearly. Quantization also frees HBM, and the freed memory usually converts into a larger KV cache, which raises the concurrency ceiling - often a bigger operational win than the raw speedup.

Concrete mechanism: weight-only int4 with group-wise scales. Weights are split into groups (e.g. 128 elements) along the input dimension; each group stores a scale (and possibly a zero-point) in fp16. The kernel loads the packed 4-bit weights, dequantizes into registers/shared memory, and does the matmul in fp16/bf16. The win is in bytes moved from HBM; the arithmetic is still done at higher precision. This is why weight-only quantization helps decode a lot and helps compute-bound prefill much less.

Boundary condition: the speedup only materializes if a fused kernel exists for that exact format, shape, and GPU architecture. On an architecture without native fp8 tensor cores, an fp8 path may dequantize and run at fp16 anyway, giving memory savings but no compute gain, and possibly a slowdown from dequantization overhead. Likewise, at large batch prefill the workload becomes compute-bound and weight-only quantization stops helping. Accuracy has its own boundary: activation outliers in specific channels dominate int8 activation quantization error, which is why outlier-aware schemes and per-channel/per-group scaling exist.

Falsifiable hypothesis for any adoption: H1 - int4 weight-only quantization increases decode tokens/s by >=1.6x at batch 1 with held-out task accuracy within 1 point of the bf16 baseline. Falsified by measuring both on the same hardware and stack.

Evidence required: tokens/s and p99 ITL at matched concurrency, HBM high-water mark, per-task accuracy against the bf16 baseline on your own eval set, and confirmation of which kernel was actually selected.

Rollback gate: revert to bf16 if any tracked task regresses beyond the pre-agreed accuracy budget, regardless of the throughput gain.

Define quantization and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Definition: quantization maps model tensors from a high-precision format (bf16/fp16) to a lower-bit one (fp8/int8/int4) plus the scale metadata needed to reconstruct approximate values. Applied to weights, to activations, or to the KV cache - three separate decisions with different cost/benefit profiles.

Why it matters in LLM infrastructure: it is the main lever that converts a memory-bound serving problem into a cheaper one. It reduces HBM residency (fit a larger model, or more KV cache, per GPU), reduces HBM traffic per decoded token (raising decode throughput), and on architectures with native low-precision tensor cores it also raises compute throughput for prefill.

Concrete mechanism: KV cache quantization. The KV cache grows as 2 * num_layers * num_kv_heads * head_dim * bytes_per_elem per token, and at long context it dominates HBM. Storing K and V in fp8 or int8 with per-token or per-head scales halves or quarters that term, which directly raises the number of concurrent sequences the scheduler can admit before it must preempt and recompute. The attention kernel dequantizes on read. Note that K and V are not equally tolerant: K enters the softmax logits, so K quantization error is amplified through the exponential, while V errors average out - quantize V more aggressively than K if you must choose.

Boundary condition: the benefit is real only while KV cache is the binding constraint. In short-context, low-concurrency serving, weights dominate HBM and KV quantization buys almost nothing while still costing accuracy and kernel compatibility. There is also a hard boundary at kernel support: paged-attention kernels must support the chosen KV dtype and block layout, or the server silently falls back to a slower path or refuses the config.

Falsifiable hypothesis: H1 - fp8 KV cache raises the maximum SLO-conformant concurrency by >=1.7x at 32k context with no measurable degradation on long-context retrieval evaluations. Falsified by measuring concurrency-at-SLO and a needle-in-haystack style long-context eval on both arms.

Evidence required: HBM high-water mark versus context length, preemption/recompute counters, concurrency at fixed p99 SLO, and long-context accuracy against the bf16 KV baseline.

Rollback gate: revert to bf16 KV if long-context accuracy drops beyond the agreed budget or if preemption rates do not actually fall; do not accept the change on memory-savings arithmetic alone.

Define quantization and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Definition: quantization is the reduction of numeric precision used to store and/or compute a model's tensors, paired with scaling metadata (per-tensor, per-channel, per-group, or per-block) that defines the mapping back to real values. Formats commonly used in LLM serving include fp8 (E4M3/E5M2), int8, and 4-bit group-scaled weight formats.

Why it matters in LLM infrastructure: it changes the two quantities that actually decide serving cost - bytes resident in HBM and bytes moved per token - without changing the model architecture or the API. In practice it decides whether a given model fits on a given GPU count at all, which is usually a more consequential decision than a percentage of throughput.

Concrete mechanism: calibration for post-training quantization. To pick per-channel or per-group scales you run a few hundred representative samples through the model, record activation ranges, and choose scales that minimize a chosen error (min-max, percentile clipping, or MSE-optimal). The calibration set matters: scales fitted on generic web text can clip activations produced by your production prompt distribution, and the resulting damage shows up as a targeted capability regression rather than as a uniform accuracy drop. This is why "the benchmark score barely moved" is weak evidence for a quantization rollout.

Boundary condition: quantization error is not uniformly distributed across a model. A small number of layers - typically the first and last blocks, and layers with heavy activation outliers - carry disproportionate sensitivity, and quantizing them at the same bit width as the rest is where most accuracy loss originates. Mixed-precision schemes that keep those layers at higher precision exist precisely because the uniform assumption fails. A second boundary: below roughly 4 bits, weight-only quantization typically requires additional machinery (rotations, learned transforms, outlier channels kept in higher precision), and results reported at 2-3 bits generally do not transfer across model families.

Falsifiable hypothesis: H1 - the quantized model matches the bf16 baseline within the agreed accuracy budget on every tracked task slice, not just on the aggregate score. Falsified by per-slice evaluation, which is the test that catches calibration-set mismatch.

Evidence required: per-slice accuracy tables versus bf16, the calibration set composition, the actual selected kernel and format, HBM high-water mark, and p99 latency at matched concurrency.

Rollback gate: revert if any tracked slice regresses beyond budget, or if the calibration set cannot be shown to be representative of production traffic; keep the bf16 checkpoint warm through the canary window.

Definition: quantization maps high-precision tensors (FP16/BF16) to lower-bit representations (INT8, FP8, INT4, NVFP4) plus metadata (scale, optional zero-point), so that value = scale * (q - zero_point). It is a *representation* change, not an algorithmic change to attention or FFN math.

Why it matters in LLM infrastructure: autoregressive decode is memory-bandwidth bound, not FLOP bound. Each decode step must stream all weights (and the KV cache) from HBM once per token. Halving bytes-per-weight roughly halves the mandatory HBM traffic, so decode throughput at low batch size scales close to the byte reduction. That is the dominant reason quantization is deployed, not FLOP savings.

Concrete mechanism: W4A16 group-wise weight-only quantization (e.g. GPTQ/AWQ, group size 128). Weights are stored INT4 with one FP16 scale per 128-element group along the input-channel axis. Prediction: a batch sweep 1,2,4,8,16,32,64 will show W4A16 tokens/s above FP16 at batch 1-8 and crossing below at some batch B*; if no crossover appears, my model of the bottleneck is wrong.
