Contrast quantization with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Naive baseline: keep all weights and activations in BF16/FP16 and run cuBLAS/cutlass GEMMs directly. No scales, no calibration, no custom kernels.

Contrast, per axis:

1. Memory footprint. Naive BF16 for a 9B-parameter model needs ~18 GB of weights, which alone nearly fills a 24 GB A30 and leaves little room for KV cache. W4A16 group-wise quantization stores weights INT4 plus one FP16 scale per 128 elements, giving ~4.5-5 GB, freeing ~13 GB for KV cache and CUDA graphs. The practical consequence is not "faster math" but a much larger admissible concurrent-request count before preemption/recompute kicks in.

2. Bandwidth. Decode streams weights once per step. Naive BF16 must read ~18 GB per step; the quantized path reads ~5 GB. On a device with ~933 GB/s HBM2 (A30), that is the difference between a hard floor of ~19 ms/step and ~5 ms/step for the weight read alone.

3. Cost. Naive BF16 pays dequant-free kernels: no extra ALU ops, no calibration pipeline, no accuracy risk, and full kernel coverage for every op. Quantization pays with calibration data, kernel availability gaps (custom ops, LoRA adapters, MoE routers often fall back to FP16), and an accuracy regression that must be measured, not assumed.

Concrete mechanism that makes the quantized path work at all: per-group scales along the input-channel axis. Weight magnitude varies by orders of magnitude across channels; a single per-tensor scale would push most channels into a couple of quantization levels. Group size 128 bounds the dynamic range each scale must cover, which is why group-wise INT4 is usable while per-tensor INT4 generally is not.

Boundary condition (falsifiable): the quantized path only beats naive BF16 while decode is weight-read bound. In prefill, or in decode at large batch, the GEMM is compute bound and dequantization overhead makes quantized throughput equal or worse. Prediction: measure prefill tokens/s for both; I expect quantized prefill to be within noise of, or slower than, BF16. If quantized prefill is materially faster, my bottleneck model is wrong and the measurement setup should be audited first.

Evidence required: side-by-side tokens/s and TPOT across a batch sweep, achieved HBM read bytes from ncu, peak memory from torch/nvidia-smi, and held-out task accuracy for both. Rollback gate: revert to naive BF16 if accuracy loss exceeds the pre-registered budget or if any production-critical op silently falls back to an unfused FP16 path that erases the latency gain.

Axis 1 - what actually changes. Quantization does not reduce the number of multiply-accumulates. It reduces bytes moved and, on hardware with low-precision tensor cores, the cost per MAC. Naive BF16 KV at long context is often a larger consumer than the weights themselves at high concurrency. FP8 KV cache halves that, roughly doubling the number of concurrent sequences at fixed context length. This is usually the highest-leverage quantization in a serving stack and is independent of weight quantization.

Axis 3 - operational cost. The naive path has one failure mode: OOM. The quantized path adds calibration drift, kernel coverage gaps, and silent accuracy loss that unit tests do not catch.

Naive implementation: everything in BF16, no scales, no calibration. The contrast is clearest if we separate the two things quantization can buy, because the naive path fails differently in each.

Case A - weight-only quantization (W4A16/W8A16). Naive BF16 reads full-precision weights from HBM every decode step. Case B - activation quantization too (W8A8, FP8 e4m3 both sides). Naive BF16 has no dynamic-range problem; W8A8 does. Transformer activations after layernorm contain persistent outlier channels whose magnitude is orders of magnitude above the median. A per-tensor activation scale sized to those outliers crushes the rest of the distribution. This is why naive per-tensor INT8 activation quantization on an unmodified LLM typically produces a visible quality regression, while SmoothQuant-style channel-wise migration of scale from activations into weights, or per-token dynamic scales, recovers most of it.

Concrete mechanism: SmoothQuant. Choose a per-input-channel factor s_j and replace X W with (X / s) (diag(s) W). The activation dynamic range shrinks by s_j and the weight range grows by s_j; s is chosen (typically s_j = max|X_j|^a / max|W_j|^(1-a), a around 0.5) to balance quantization difficulty between the two operands. The transform is mathematically exact in full precision and can be folded into the preceding layernorm, so it costs nothing at runtime.

If outlier positions move per token, a static per-channel s cannot capture them and only per-token dynamic activation scaling helps. Naive implementation: BF16 weights and activations everywhere, stock kernels, no calibration step in the release pipeline. The most important contrast is operational, not numerical.

Numerical contrast, briefly: the naive path has zero representation error and full kernel coverage. The quantized path trades a bounded, measurable representation error for a large reduction in HBM bytes per decode step, which is the binding constraint for autoregressive serving.

Operational contrast, which is where the naive path actually wins:
- Naive BF16 is deterministic across framework versions in a way quantized paths often are not. Quantized checkpoints bind to a specific kernel implementation; upgrading the serving engine can change the dequant path, the group layout, or the fallback rules, and silently change outputs.
- Naive BF16 has one artifact: the checkpoint. A quantized deployment has a checkpoint plus a calibration dataset plus a quantization config, and all three must be versioned or the build is not reproducible.
- Naive BF16 degrades by OOM, which is loud. Quantization degrades by accuracy loss, which is quiet and only shows up in evals you actually run.

The packed bytes are not a portable representation of the quantized tensor; they are a representation of the quantized tensor *for one kernel*. Loading them under a different kernel requires an unpack/repack step that engines sometimes do implicitly.

Prediction: hash the logits of a fixed prompt set under the same quantized checkpoint across two serving-engine minor versions. I expect BF16 to be bitwise-stable or near-stable and the quantized path to diverge more often. Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with quantization. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Two failure modes, each with the mechanism and the boundary where it bites.

Failure mode 1 - outlier-driven accuracy collapse under coarse scaling. Transformer activations, especially after layernorm in mid-to-late layers, contain a small number of channels with magnitudes far above the median. A per-tensor scale must cover the maximum, so the effective resolution for the bulk of the distribution collapses to a handful of levels. Mechanism: with symmetric INT8 and scale = max|x| / 127, a channel whose typical magnitude is max/100 gets about one usable level. The trade-off is that finer granularity (per-channel weights, per-token activations, group size 64/128) fixes this but costs more scale metadata and more complex kernels, and per-token dynamic scaling adds a reduction over the activation before the GEMM. Boundary: this failure is severe for activation quantization and mild for weight-only quantization, because weights are far better behaved than activations. Falsifiable prediction: per-tensor INT8 activations will lose materially more accuracy than per-token INT8 activations on the same model; if they are equal, that model does not have the outlier structure and finer scaling is wasted overhead.

Failure mode 2 - negative speedup from kernel coverage gaps. Quantization only pays off if the fused low-precision kernel actually runs. In practice some ops (MoE routers, LoRA adapters, unusual head dims, small residual GEMMs) fall back to dequantize-then-FP16-GEMM. That path reads the packed weights, materializes FP16, then does the original GEMM, so it moves *more* total bytes than plain BF16 and adds ALU work. Mechanism: an unfused dequant writes the FP16 tensor to HBM and reads it back. Boundary: the failure is invisible in aggregate throughput if only a few layers fall back, and only shows up as a per-kernel anomaly. Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with quantization. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Two failure modes, stated as mechanisms with boundaries.

Failure mode 1 - calibration-set mismatch producing silent domain regression. Post-training quantization derives activation ranges (and, for GPTQ-style methods, the Hessian used to choose weight rounding) from a small calibration corpus, typically a few hundred sequences. Mechanism: GPTQ minimizes layer-wise output error weighted by the empirical input second-moment from the calibration data. If serving traffic is code or a non-English language and calibration was generic English web text, the rounding is optimized for the wrong input distribution and error concentrates exactly on the deployed domain. Trade-off: calibrating on in-domain data fixes this but couples the artifact to a traffic distribution that drifts, so the quantized checkpoint acquires an expiry date and needs re-validation whenever traffic shifts. Boundary/falsifiable prediction: quantize the same model twice, once with generic and once with in-domain calibration, and evaluate on the in-domain held-out set. I predict a measurable gap. If the two are within noise, this model is insensitive to calibration choice and the extra pipeline is unjustified.

Failure mode 2 - throughput regression at high batch because the bottleneck moved. Weight-only quantization helps when weight reads dominate. As batch grows, weight bytes are amortized across more tokens and the GEMM becomes compute bound; dequantization then sits on the critical path as pure added ALU work. Mechanism: arithmetic intensity rises with batch, so the roofline crossing moves from bandwidth-bound to compute-bound. Trade-off: you can pick the precision that wins at your production batch size, but you cannot win at both ends with one artifact unless the engine supports switching. Boundary/falsifiable prediction: sweep batch 1 to 64 and expect a crossover batch B* above which BF16 tokens/s exceeds W4A16. If none exists in range, the kernel is bandwidth bound throughout and the concern does not apply at those sizes.

Evidence required: in-domain and generic held-out accuracy per calibration variant, calibration-set hash recorded with the artifact, batch sweep of tokens/s and p99 TPOT, and ncu counters distinguishing bandwidth- from compute-bound regimes. Rollback gate: revert if in-domain accuracy loss exceeds the pre-registered budget, or if p99 TPOT at the production batch size regresses, even when mean throughput improves.

Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with quantization. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Two failure modes with mechanisms and boundary conditions.

Failure mode 1 - error amplification through long generations. Quantization error per layer is small, but autoregressive decoding feeds outputs back as inputs. Mechanism: a perturbation that flips one low-margin token early in a chain-of-thought or a tool-call argument changes every subsequent conditioning step. The damage is therefore not proportional to per-layer MSE; it is concentrated on tasks with long dependency chains and low-margin decisions, such as multi-step arithmetic, structured JSON emission, and agentic tool calls. Trade-off: perplexity, the cheapest metric, averages over all positions and is dominated by high-margin tokens, so it is close to blind to this failure. Boundary/falsifiable prediction: quantized and BF16 models will show a small perplexity gap but a disproportionately larger gap on exact-match structured-output or multi-step reasoning evals. If the structured-output gap tracks the perplexity gap proportionally, this amplification hypothesis is not supported for that model.

Failure mode 2 - interaction with KV-cache quantization and long context. Weight quantization and KV quantization are usually validated separately and then shipped together. Mechanism: both inject error into the attention path; weight error perturbs the K/V projections, KV quantization then re-quantizes the already-perturbed values, and at long context the softmax aggregates over many more perturbed keys, so small logit errors can change which positions dominate attention. Trade-off: KV quantization is what actually unlocks concurrency at long context, so refusing it costs real capacity. Boundary/falsifiable prediction: run a 2x2 factorial (BF16/W4 weights) x (BF16/FP8 KV) on a long-context retrieval eval. If the combined setting loses more than the sum of the individual losses, the interaction is real and the two must be validated jointly.

Evidence required: exact-match structured-output eval and multi-step reasoning eval alongside perplexity; the 2x2 factorial at the target context length; per-token error statistics if available. Rollback gate: ship BF16 KV, or unquantized weights, if the factorial shows super-additive degradation beyond the pre-registered threshold, regardless of the memory savings.

Scope note: these are claims about numerics and evaluation methodology; they say nothing about any particular deployment's capability.

Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with quantization. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Two failure modes, each with mechanism, trade-off, and a boundary that makes it testable.

Failure mode 1 - hardware/format mismatch producing no speedup at all. Low-precision formats only accelerate math when the tensor cores implement them. FP8 tensor-core math requires Hopper-class or newer; Ampere-class parts (including A30/A100) have INT8 and INT4 tensor-core paths but no native FP8 GEMM. Mechanism: on Ampere, an FP8 checkpoint is typically upconverted to FP16/BF16 before the GEMM, so you keep the smaller HBM footprint but gain nothing on the math and pay conversion ALU cost. Trade-off: the memory saving is still real and may be the whole point (larger KV cache, larger model resident), but framing it as a compute win is wrong. Boundary/falsifiable prediction: on an Ampere-class device, FP8 weights will improve peak-memory and low-batch decode throughput but will not improve prefill FLOP throughput versus BF16. If prefill throughput improves materially, the kernel is doing something other than upconvert-then-GEMM and the assumption should be re-checked.

Failure mode 2 - accuracy cliff at 4 bits without error compensation. Round-to-nearest INT4 without any reconstruction-error minimization degrades sharply compared to INT8, because the number of levels per group drops from 256 to 16 while weight distributions are roughly Gaussian with heavy-ish tails. Mechanism: GPTQ-style methods reduce this by processing columns sequentially and updating the not-yet-quantized weights to compensate the error already committed, using an inverse-Hessian estimate from calibration activations; AWQ instead protects the channels with the largest activation magnitude by rescaling. Trade-off: both require a calibration pass and both bind the artifact to that calibration data. Boundary/falsifiable prediction: RTN-INT4 will lose noticeably more held-out accuracy than GPTQ/AWQ INT4 at the same group size; the gap should shrink as group size shrinks from 128 to 64 to 32. If RTN matches GPTQ at group 128, the model's weights are unusually well conditioned and the extra pipeline is not justified.

Evidence required: device compute-capability and the actual kernel selected (from engine logs or ncu), prefill vs decode throughput separately, and held-out task accuracy across RTN/GPTQ/AWQ at group sizes 128/64/32. Rollback gate: do not ship 4-bit if held-out accuracy loss exceeds the pre-registered budget at every group size tested, or if profiling shows the low-precision kernel is not actually being dispatched.

Scope note: hardware generation is stated only as a constraint on which kernels can run; it is not a claim about model capability.

Explain how quantization interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Quantization interacts with latency, throughput and memory through three separate channels, and conflating them is the usual source of wrong predictions.

Channel 1 - memory capacity. Bits per weight directly set resident weight bytes: a 9B-parameter model is ~18 GB at BF16, ~9 GB at 8-bit, ~5 GB at 4-bit with group-128 FP16 scales (the scales add roughly 0.06 bits-equivalent overhead per weight at group 128, so the packing is close to nominal). On a 24 GB device, the freed capacity converts almost entirely into KV-cache blocks, which is what sets maximum concurrency. Effect: higher achievable throughput via larger running batch, not lower single-stream latency.

Channel 2 - memory bandwidth, which sets decode latency. Time per decode step has a hard floor of (resident weight bytes + KV bytes read) / achieved HBM bandwidth. This is the channel where quantization lowers latency directly, and it dominates at batch 1. Concrete mechanism: W4A16 group-wise quantization with the packed weights dequantized inside the GEMM kernel into registers, so the FP16 weights are never written back to HBM. Only the fused form gives the bandwidth win; an unfused dequantize-to-HBM-then-GEMM path moves more bytes than BF16.

Channel 3 - compute. Only helps if low-precision tensor cores are actually used (INT8/INT4 on Ampere-class, FP8 and below on Hopper-class and newer). W4A16 does not touch this channel at all: accumulation stays FP16, so prefill FLOP throughput is unchanged or slightly worse due to dequant ALU work.

Boundary condition (falsifiable): the latency benefit is confined to the bandwidth-bound regime. As batch grows, weight bytes amortize across more tokens, arithmetic intensity rises, and the kernel crosses to compute bound; past that crossover W4A16 latency is equal to or worse than BF16. Prediction: a batch sweep 1,2,4,8,16,32,64 at fixed input/output length shows W4A16 TPOT below BF16 at low batch and a crossover batch B* where they meet. Additionally, prefill latency should show no improvement. If prefill improves materially, the roofline model above is wrong for this kernel.

Evidence required: p50/p99 TPOT and TTFT separately across the batch sweep; achieved dram__bytes_read from ncu to confirm the byte reduction; peak memory and max concurrent sequences at the target context length; held-out task accuracy on the exact served artifact. Rollback gate: revert to BF16 if p99 TPOT at the production batch size regresses, if the measured DRAM byte reduction is materially below the nominal bit-width ratio (indicating an unfused path), or if accuracy loss exceeds the pre-registered budget.

Explain how quantization interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Mechanism. Autoregressive decode is memory-bandwidth bound: every generated token must re-read all weights from HBM. Time per output token (TPOT) is approximately (weight_bytes + kv_bytes_touched) / effective_HBM_bandwidth, plus kernel launch and communication overhead. Weight-only INT4 (W4A16) on a 9B model drops weight traffic from ~18 GB (BF16) to ~5 GB, so the bandwidth-limited floor of TPOT drops roughly 3-3.5x. On an A30 (933 GB/s HBM2, ~24 GB), the BF16 floor is ~19 ms/token single-stream and the W4A16 floor is ~5-6 ms/token; measured values will be worse because dequantization is done in-kernel and adds ALU work.

Separately, quantization frees capacity: 13 GB of weight savings converts directly into KV-cache blocks, which raises the maximum concurrent sequence count and therefore throughput even if per-token latency were unchanged. FP8 KV cache is a second, independent lever: it halves kv_bytes_touched, which matters at long context where KV traffic exceeds weight traffic.

Boundary condition. The latency win inverts at high arithmetic intensity. In prefill, and in decode at large batch, the GEMM is compute bound, not bandwidth bound; W4A16 then pays dequantization cost on the critical path with no traffic saving to recover it, and can be 10-30% *slower* than a well-tuned BF16 or FP8 tensor-core path. The crossover is where batch * activation_bytes approaches weight_bytes. Concretely: W4A16 is the right choice for low-concurrency, latency-sensitive decode; W8A8/FP8 (which quantizes activations too, so tensor cores run at reduced precision) is the right choice for high-throughput batched serving. On A30 there is no hardware FP8 tensor core (that starts at Hopper/SM90), so FP8 there is emulated or storage-only and the compute-side win does not exist.

Falsifiable claim and gate. Claim: W4A16 reduces p50 TPOT by >=2x at concurrency 1 and by <1.2x at concurrency 64. Gate: reject the quantized build if held-out task accuracy drops more than 1 point absolute, or if p99 TTFT regresses at the target concurrency.

Explain how quantization interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Mechanism (memory side). Quantization changes three distinct budgets and they must not be conflated. (1) Weight residency: BF16 weights are 2 bytes/param, INT4 with group-128 scales is ~0.53 bytes/param including metadata. For a 9B model that is 18 GB -> ~4.8 GB. (2) KV cache: bytes = 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes * seq_len per sequence; FP8 KV halves it, INT4 KV quarters it. (3) Activation/workspace, which quantization usually does not shrink and sometimes grows because dequantized tiles are staged in registers or shared memory.

The throughput consequence is indirect but dominant in practice: freed HBM becomes KV blocks, KV blocks become admitted concurrent sequences, and concurrency is what fills the tensor cores during decode. A vLLM-style scheduler reports this as a higher gpu_cache_usage ceiling and fewer preemptions/recomputations. That path often yields a larger throughput gain than the per-token bandwidth saving does.

Boundary condition. Freed memory only converts to throughput while the workload is memory-limited on KV. Once the batch is large enough that decode becomes compute or scheduler bound, adding KV capacity buys nothing and W4A16 dequant overhead becomes pure loss. A second boundary: group-wise INT4 with very small groups (g=32) improves accuracy but inflates scale metadata and shrinks the memory win, while per-tensor INT8 has the smallest metadata but is the most vulnerable to activation outliers in later layers.

Falsifiable claim and gate. Claim: at fixed 24 GB, W4A16 raises the sustainable concurrent-sequence count at 8k context by >=2x and raises aggregate tokens/s by >=1.5x. Gate: roll back if preemption rate rises, if p99 TTFT exceeds SLO, or if accuracy regression exceeds the agreed threshold on a held-out set.

Explain how quantization interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Mechanism (kernel side). A quantized linear layer is only fast if a fused kernel exists for that exact (weight dtype, activation dtype, group size, layout) tuple. W4A16 kernels such as Marlin/Machete load INT4 tiles, dequantize in registers, and feed BF16 tensor cores; the dequant is hidden behind the memory fetch only while the layer is bandwidth bound. If no fused kernel matches the checkpoint's scheme, the runtime falls back to dequantize-to-BF16-then-GEMM, which materializes the full-precision weight tile in memory and is strictly slower than never quantizing at all. This is the single most common cause of 'we quantized and got no speedup'.

The latency impact is therefore discontinuous, not smooth: it is a function of kernel availability, not of bit width. Checking which kernel was selected (server logs naming the quant backend, or a Nsight kernel trace showing the fused GEMM name) is a prerequisite to any latency claim.

Boundary condition. Kernel coverage is architecture gated. Marlin-class W4A16 kernels require Ampere (SM80) or newer; FP8 tensor cores require Hopper (SM90) or newer; NVFP4 requires Blackwell. On A30 (SM80) INT4/INT8 tensor-core paths exist but FP8 compute does not, so an FP8 checkpoint runs emulated and shows no throughput gain. A second boundary: tensor-parallel sharding must divide cleanly by the quantization group size, or the runtime silently falls back or refuses to load.

Falsifiable claim and gate. Claim: the fused quantized kernel is selected and per-layer GEMM time drops >=2x at concurrency 1. Gate: if the kernel trace shows a separate dequant kernel, treat the quantized build as failed and do not report a latency number for it.

Mechanism (accuracy side, which bounds the latency win you are allowed to keep). Quantization error is dominated by outliers, not by average magnitude. Transformer activations develop a small number of channels with magnitudes 10-100x the rest, concentrated in later layers and in the down-projection input. With per-tensor scaling, one such channel forces a large scale, which collapses the effective resolution of every other channel in that tensor. The standard mitigations are mechanically different: per-channel or group-wise scaling (finer scales, more metadata), SmoothQuant (algebraically migrate activation range into the weights before quantizing both), GPTQ/AWQ (choose weight rounding using calibration-set second-order or salience information rather than nearest-rounding), and keeping a small outlier fraction in FP16.

Calibration is a real dependency: GPTQ/AWQ need a calibration corpus, and if that corpus is off-distribution from production traffic the damage appears specifically on production-like inputs, not on the benchmark.

Boundary condition. Weight-only INT4 is usually safe for accuracy because weight distributions are well behaved; activation quantization (W8A8, FP8 activations) is where outliers bite, and long-context or multilingual traffic degrades first. Perplexity is a poor detector here: a build can lose <0.1 perplexity and still lose several points on structured output, tool-call JSON validity, or long-context retrieval, because those depend on low-probability token discrimination.

Falsifiable claim and gate. Claim: W4A16 with group-128 AWQ loses <=1 point absolute on the held-out task suite while W8A8 per-tensor loses >=2 points on the same suite. Gate: block promotion on any regression in tool-call schema validity or long-context retrieval, regardless of perplexity, and keep the BF16 checkpoint hot for immediate rollback.

Give a measurement plan for validating whether quantization helps a serving workload. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Measurement plan. Step 0, freeze the comparison: identical model revision, identical server version and flags except the quantization scheme, identical max_model_len, identical scheduler settings, pinned clocks (nvidia-smi -lgc) to remove DVFS drift, and a fixed random seed for request generation. Record device compute capability and driver/CUDA versions.

Step 1, define the SLO first, then measure under it. Report p50 and p99 for TTFT and TPOT at fixed input/output token lengths, and report throughput only as goodput: tokens/s among requests that met the SLO. Peak tokens/s without an SLO is not a decision-grade number.

Step 2, sweep concurrency (1, 4, 16, 64, 128) rather than reporting one point, because the quantized and baseline curves cross. Use a load generator with a fixed arrival process; discard the first 60 s as warmup so autotuning and CUDA graph capture do not contaminate results. Run 3 repetitions and report the spread, not a single run.

Step 3, confirm the mechanism, do not infer it. Check the server log for the selected quantization kernel, and take an nsys/ncu sample to confirm dram bytes per decode step actually fell. If traffic did not fall, any observed speedup came from something else and the experiment is invalid.

Step 4, quality gate in the same harness: held-out task accuracy, tool-call schema validity, long-context retrieval.

Mechanism being tested: reduced weight traffic lowers the bandwidth-bound TPOT floor and frees HBM for KV blocks.

Boundary condition. This plan is only valid while the benchmark's input/output length distribution matches production. A benchmark with 128-token outputs is dominated by prefill and will understate a decode-side win; one with 4k-token outputs will overstate it. Bind the length distribution to sampled production traces.

Gate: adopt only if SLO-constrained goodput improves >=20% and no quality metric regresses beyond the agreed threshold; otherwise roll back to the BF16 build.

Measurement plan, memory-capacity framing. The question 'does quantization help' has two separable answers: does it lower per-token latency, and does it raise the concurrency ceiling. This plan isolates the second.

Step 1, measure the static budget: total HBM, weight bytes after quantization (including scale/zero-point metadata, which is not free), CUDA graph and activation workspace, and the residual left for KV. Get this from server startup logs or torch.cuda.memory_allocated at steady state, not from a paper formula.

Step 2, compute and then verify KV bytes per token: 2 * num_layers * num_kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes. Verify by admitting sequences until the scheduler reports the cache full, and compare the observed sequence count against the predicted one. A gap means workspace or fragmentation is larger than assumed.

Step 3, run a capacity sweep at fixed context length (2k, 8k, 32k) and record: max admitted concurrent sequences, preemption/recompute counts, and SLO-constrained goodput. The quantization win shows up as a higher admitted count at equal p99.

Step 4, separate the KV-quantization variable from the weight-quantization variable; changing both at once makes the result uninterpretable.

Mechanism: weight bytes freed convert one-for-one into KV blocks, and KV blocks set the concurrency ceiling under paged attention.

Boundary condition. The conversion stops helping once decode is no longer KV-capacity limited (compute bound at high batch, or bound by CPU-side scheduling and detokenization). At that point extra KV capacity raises queueing latency instead of goodput, and preemption counts stay at zero while p99 still climbs, which is the signature to look for.

Gate: accept only if admitted concurrency rises >=1.5x at 8k context with p99 TTFT inside SLO and zero increase in preemption-driven recomputation; otherwise revert.

Mechanism under test: fewer weight bytes per decode step lowers the bandwidth-bound floor.

What assumptions must be stated before making a performance claim about quantization? Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Assumptions that must be stated before any quantization performance claim. (1) Hardware: exact GPU model, compute capability, HBM capacity and bandwidth, NVLink/PCIe topology, and clock policy (pinned or not). An INT4 or FP8 claim is arch-specific: FP8 tensor cores start at Hopper SM90, so on Ampere A30 an FP8 claim is about storage, not compute. (2) Model identity: parameter count, layer/head/head_dim geometry, GQA kv_heads, and checkpoint hash. (3) Quantization scheme, stated in full: which tensors are quantized (weights only, or weights and activations, or KV too), bit width, granularity (per-tensor / per-channel / group size), and the calibration method and corpus. 'INT4' alone is not a specification. (4) Runtime: server and kernel backend actually selected, tensor-parallel degree, attention backend, chunked prefill on/off, CUDA graph on/off, max_num_seqs and max_model_len. (5) Workload: input and output token length distributions, concurrency, and arrival process. (6) Metric definition: which percentile, TTFT vs TPOT vs end-to-end, and whether throughput is peak or SLO-constrained goodput. (7) Measurement hygiene: warmup discarded, repetition count, variance reported. (8) Which numbers are measured on this system versus estimated from bandwidth arithmetic or quoted from a vendor.

Mechanism, stated so the claim is checkable: the expected win is reduced weight/KV bytes moved per decode step against a fixed HBM bandwidth, plus freed capacity converting into KV blocks and higher admitted concurrency.

Boundary condition. The claim is void outside the measured regime. A speedup measured at concurrency 1 with 512-token outputs does not transfer to concurrency 64 with 128-token outputs, where the workload is compute and prefill dominated and the same build can be slower. State the regime with every number.

Gate: if any of the above is unknown, report the result as provisional and non-transferable rather than as a performance claim, and keep the baseline checkpoint available for rollback.

What assumptions must be stated before making a performance claim about quantization? Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Assumptions that must be stated before any quantization performance claim.

1) Scheme, not just bit width. "INT4" is underspecified. State weight-only vs weight+activation (W4A16 vs W8A8/FP8), group size (per-tensor / per-channel / group-128), symmetric vs asymmetric, and whether the KV cache is quantized independently. W4A16-g128 and W4A16 per-tensor differ by several accuracy points on the same model.
2) Kernel and hardware path. A quantized checkpoint is not a speedup; the speedup lives in the kernel. State the backend (Marlin, Machete, exllama, bitsandbytes, cutlass W8A8) and the SM version. Explain how quantization changes between training and inference. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Quantization means different things in training and inference, and conflating them is a common source of wrong claims.

Training. During training, quantization is almost always about *compute and memory for gradients*, and the constraint is numerical stability of the update. Mixed precision keeps a master copy of weights in FP32 (or BF16 with stochastic rounding), computes matmuls in BF16/FP16, and accumulates in FP32. BF16 is preferred over FP16 because its FP32-matched exponent range removes the need for loss scaling. Optimizer state (Adam m and v) usually stays FP32 or 8-bit, and this state, not the weights, dominates memory: a 9B model needs ~18 GB BF16 weights plus ~72 GB FP32 Adam state plus gradients plus activations. Low-bit quantization of weights during training is possible only through QAT or QLoRA, where a frozen NF4 base is dequantized on the fly and gradients flow into higher-precision adapters; the backward pass never sees a genuinely 4-bit weight.

Inference. At inference there is no backward pass and no optimizer state, so the constraint changes from stability to *memory traffic and accuracy preservation under a fixed forward pass*. Post-training quantization (GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant) is applied once, calibrated on a few hundred samples, and the goal is to minimize output error, not to keep gradients well-conditioned. Weight-only 4-bit is viable here precisely because there is no accumulation of quantization error across thousands of update steps.

Concrete mechanism. The reason 4-bit is safe at inference but not in the training loop: quantization error at inference perturbs a single forward pass and is bounded by the group-wise scale, whereas in training the same error enters every gradient and compounds multiplicatively across steps, and small gradient magnitudes are exactly where a coarse quantization grid has the worst relative error (values below the quantization step round to zero, so the update vanishes).

Boundary condition. QAT breaks the clean split: it simulates inference-time quantization inside the training loop using a straight-through estimator, so the model learns weights robust to the quantization grid. The cost is a full training run, and the STE gradient is biased, so QAT is only worth it when PTQ accuracy loss already exceeds the tolerance budget.

Falsifiable claim and gate. Claim: QLoRA fine-tuning of a 9B on an NF4 base reaches within 1 point of BF16 LoRA on held-out task accuracy, while PTQ-to-INT4 of a BF16-trained model loses <1 point; but naive INT4 weights inside a full-precision training loop diverges or plateaus within 500 steps. Evidence: paired runs with identical data order and seed, logging grad-norm and the fraction of weight updates rounding to zero. Gate: abort the low-bit training run if grad-norm collapses below 10% of the BF16 reference or if >30% of updates quantize to zero; fall back to BF16 mixed precision.

The training-time and inference-time meanings of "quantization" are governed by different constraints.

Training: constrained by gradient numerics. Standard practice is mixed precision, not low-bit quantization. BF16 for matmuls, FP32 accumulation, FP32 (or 8-bit) master weights and optimizer state. BF16's wide exponent range removes FP16's loss-scaling requirement. The dominant memory consumer is optimizer state, not weights, so "quantizing the model" saves far less in training than people expect: for a 9B model, BF16 weights are ~18 GB but FP32 Adam state is ~72 GB. That is why 8-bit optimizers and ZeRO sharding, not weight quantization, are the training-side memory levers. True low-bit training exists only as QAT (fake-quant with straight-through estimator) or QLoRA (frozen NF4 base, higher-precision trainable adapters).

Inference: constrained by memory traffic and single-pass accuracy. No optimizer state, no backward pass, so weights can be pushed to 4 bits with per-group scales. GPTQ/AWQ calibrate on a few hundred sequences and solve for scales that minimize layer output error. KV cache quantization is a separate, inference-only lever with no training analogue.

Concrete mechanism. Decode re-reads all weights per token, so it is HBM-bandwidth bound and low-bit weights translate almost linearly into lower TPOT. Training is dominated by large-batch GEMMs over long sequences, which are compute bound and already saturate tensor cores at BF16; making weights 4-bit does not speed those GEMMs up, because they must be dequantized to a tensor-core-supported dtype before the multiply. This asymmetry (bandwidth-bound decode vs compute-bound training) is the reason the same bit width helps one and not the other.

Boundary condition. The split is not absolute. FP8 training on Hopper/Blackwell does give a real compute-side win because the tensor cores natively execute FP8 with FP32 accumulation and per-tensor scaling; this does not exist on A30/SM80, where FP8 is storage-only at best. Conversely, at very long inference context, KV traffic dominates weight traffic and weight quantization stops paying.

Training and inference quantization differ in objective, in what is quantized, and in what breaks.

What is quantized.
- Training: activations and matmul inputs are cast (BF16/FP16, or FP8 on Hopper+), but a higher-precision master weight and FP32 accumulation are retained. Optimizer state may be 8-bit. Weights themselves are effectively never below 8 bits in a from-scratch loop.
- Inference: weights are the primary target (INT4/INT8), optionally activations (W8A8/FP8), optionally KV cache (FP8/INT8). Nothing needs to be differentiable.

Objective.
- Training minimizes divergence of the optimization trajectory. The failure mode is silent: gradients underflow, updates round to zero, loss plateaus.
- Inference minimizes output error of a fixed function under a memory-traffic budget. The failure mode is measurable immediately on a held-out eval.

Concrete mechanism. Adam's second-moment estimate divides by sqrt(v); when gradient magnitudes fall below the quantization step of a coarse grid they round to zero, the effective update vanishes for those parameters, and the model silently stops learning in exactly the layers with small gradients. Inference has no such accumulation channel: a group-wise scale bounds per-tensor relative error at a single forward pass, and GPTQ/AWQ explicitly solve for scales that minimize that error against calibration activations.

Boundary condition. QLoRA sits between the two regimes and is the practical exception: the base model is stored NF4 (inference-style quantization) and dequantized per-block during the forward and backward pass, while gradients accumulate only into BF16 LoRA adapters. This works because no quantized tensor is ever the target of an update. It buys memory, not speed - the dequantization overhead typically makes QLoRA steps 20-40% slower than BF16 LoRA at the same batch size.

Falsifiable claim and gate. Claim: on 8x A30 24GB, full BF16 fine-tuning of a 9B is infeasible without offload (weights + FP32 Adam + gradients + activations exceed aggregate 192 GB at useful sequence lengths), whereas QLoRA on an NF4 base fits per-GPU with headroom, at a 20-40% step-time penalty. Evidence required: measured peak per-GPU memory from torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated and wall-clock step time for both configurations at identical batch and sequence length. Gate: abort the QLoRA run if eval loss is not within 2% of the BF16 LoRA reference at matched token count; abort a low-bit training experiment if grad-norm collapses or the fraction of zero updates exceeds 30%.

Short answer: in training, quantization is a numerics problem; at inference, it is a memory-bandwidth problem. Different constraints, different valid bit widths.

Inference side. The forward pass is fixed and there is no state to preserve, so post-training quantization can go to 4 bits per weight with group-wise scales. On Hopper/Blackwell, FP8 tensor cores make FP8 a genuine *training* compute win, so the "quantization does not help training speed" statement is false there. Misleading intuition: "4-bit quantization makes the model 4x faster because it is 4x smaller."

Correction. Size and speed are related only through one specific channel - HBM traffic - and only in one specific regime. Compression on disk buys nothing by itself. Three things must all hold before size becomes speed:

1) A fused dequant-GEMM kernel must exist for the target architecture. Without it, the runtime dequantizes to BF16 into a temporary buffer and then runs a normal GEMM, which reads *more* bytes than the BF16 path and is strictly slower.
2) The operator must be memory bound at the actual operating point.
3) The compression ratio must apply to the tensors actually being re-read. Excluded layers (embeddings, lm_head, sometimes first/last block) and the KV cache are usually not 4-bit, so the effective ratio is well below 4x. A "4-bit" 9B model is typically ~5-5.5 GB, not 4.5 GB - about 3.3x, not 4x.

Concrete mechanism. During decode, each generated token requires re-reading the whole weight tensor from HBM, so TPOT_floor ~ (weight_bytes + kv_bytes_touched) / effective_bandwidth. Cutting weight_bytes ~3.3x cuts the floor by at most 3.3x, and only if kv_bytes_touched is negligible. Measured speedup is lower still because dequantization adds ALU work on the critical path and because kernel-launch and sampling overhead form a fixed floor per token that does not shrink at all.

Boundary condition. In prefill and in large-batch decode the GEMM is compute bound; weight traffic is amortized over many tokens, so the quantization "speedup" goes to roughly 1.0x and can invert to 0.7-0.9x because dequantization is pure added work. The crossover is roughly where batch * activation_bytes approaches weight_bytes.

Falsifiable claim and gate. Claim: measured W4A16 speedup over tuned BF16 is <=3.0x at concurrency 1, and <1.2x at concurrency 64, on identical hardware and stack. Evidence required: concurrency sweep reporting p50/p99 TTFT and TPOT, plus held-out task accuracy, plus confirmation of which kernel was selected (log the backend, do not assume it). Gate: reject the quantized build if held-out accuracy drops more than 1.0 absolute point or if p99 TTFT regresses more than 10%; keep the BF16 checkpoint warm for rollback.

Misleading intuition: "quantization degrades all layers a little, so the accuracy loss is uniform and small."

Correction. Quantization error is highly non-uniform and concentrated in a small number of outlier channels. Transformer activations, especially after LayerNorm and in the FFN down-projection input, contain channels with magnitudes 10-100x the median. A per-tensor scale sized to cover those outliers wastes almost the entire quantization grid, so ordinary channels collapse into a handful of levels. The damage is therefore localized and, at INT8 per-tensor, can be catastrophic rather than gentle - which is exactly why the whole family of methods exists: per-channel and group-wise scales bound the error locally, AWQ keeps the salient channels in higher precision or rescales them, SmoothQuant migrates activation outliers into the weight tensor where they are easier to represent, and GPTQ solves a layerwise reconstruction that compensates already-quantized columns.

Concrete mechanism. With symmetric per-tensor INT8, the step size is max|x| / 127. If one channel has magnitude 100 and the rest have magnitude 1, ordinary values map to roughly one of two levels, so the effective precision for most of the tensor is ~1 bit, not 8. Group-wise scaling with group size 128 restores per-group dynamic range and largely eliminates the failure.

Boundary condition. The outlier problem is a property of activations, not weights. Weight distributions are far better behaved, which is why weight-only INT4 with group-128 scales is routinely near-lossless while W8A8 requires SmoothQuant or similar to be safe. So the correction has a limit: for weight-only schemes the "small uniform loss" intuition is closer to true, and the real risk shifts to a small number of sensitive layers rather than a small number of sensitive channels.

Misleading intuition: "quantization frees memory, so I can raise concurrency proportionally."

Correction. Quantization frees *weight* memory. Concurrency is limited by KV cache capacity, which is a different tensor and usually unquantized. The relationship is additive, not proportional, and depends entirely on how much of the GPU was weights to begin with.

Concrete mechanism. On a 24 GB A30, serving a 9B model: BF16 weights ~18 GB, leaving ~4-5 GB for KV after runtime overhead. Quantizing weights to INT4 (~5 GB) leaves ~17-18 GB for KV - roughly a 3.5-4x increase in KV capacity, hence a similar increase in max concurrent sequences. But on an 80 GB H100 serving the same model, weights are 18 of 80 GB; quantizing to 5 GB raises KV from ~58 GB to ~71 GB, only about 1.2x. Same quantization, same model, wildly different concurrency benefit, because the benefit is (total - weight_bytes_new) / (total - weight_bytes_old), not a fixed multiple.

Furthermore, raising concurrency does not raise goodput indefinitely. Beyond the point where decode becomes compute bound, additional sequences increase per-token latency roughly linearly, so tokens/sec/user degrades even as aggregate tokens/sec plateaus. And per-request KV grows linearly with context length, so at long context the concurrency gain evaporates: 2 GB of KV per 32k-token sequence means 17 GB supports only ~8 concurrent sequences regardless of weight precision.

Boundary condition. When KV already dominates the memory budget - long context, large batch, or a small model on a large GPU - weight quantization is close to useless for concurrency, and the correct lever is KV cache quantization (FP8/INT8 KV), paged attention with better block utilization, GQA/MLA-style KV reduction, or offload/disaggregation (e.g. Mooncake-style KV pooling, Dynamo-style prefill/decode disaggregation) so that KV lives outside the decode GPU's HBM.

Controlled experiment: does KV-cache quantization (FP8/INT8) buy usable concurrency without breaking long-context quality?

Hypothesis. On one A30 (24 GB) serving a 9B model in FP16 weights, quantizing the KV cache to 8 bits roughly halves KV bytes and therefore allows ~1.8-2.0x more concurrent 8k-token sequences before preemption, with <= 1 point degradation on a long-context retrieval metric.

Independent variable. kv_cache_dtype in {fp16, int8/fp8}. Weights stay FP16 so the weight term is not a confound.

Mechanism. KV bytes = 2 (K and V) x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x seq_len x bytes_per_elem. With GQA the kv_heads term is already reduced; halving bytes_per_elem halves the remainder, which directly raises the number of blocks the paged allocator can hold, which is what sets max concurrency.

Controls. Identical weights, engine version, block size, scheduler policy, max_model_len, and gpu_memory_utilization. Identical prompt distribution and identical output lengths (force fixed max_tokens) so KV growth is comparable across arms.

Primary metrics. Number of concurrently running sequences before the scheduler starts preempting/swapping; goodput at fixed p95 TTFT SLO; KV blocks allocated (engine metric); long-context accuracy (needle-style retrieval at 8k, plus the standard task suite as a regression guard).

Boundary condition. The benefit is real only when the workload is KV-capacity bound. If the deployment runs short prompts at low concurrency, KV is not the binding constraint and the experiment should show no goodput change - that null result is expected, not a bug.

Known risk. 8-bit KV degrades most visibly on long-range retrieval and on tasks needing exact copying, because attention scores are formed from quantized K. Short-context perplexity can look unchanged while retrieval quality drops, so perplexity alone must not be the acceptance metric.

Rollback gate. Revert if long-context retrieval drops more than the declared budget, or if p99 TTFT regresses due to extra quant/dequant work in the attention kernel. Record which of the two failure modes occurred.

Mechanism. Per-tensor activation scales are set by the max activation. A few channels with 20-100x median magnitude compress the usable range for all other channels in that tensor, so the layers hosting those channels dominate the error.

1. Baseline: FP16 accuracy on the fixed suite, greedy decoding, fixed seed.
2. Full W8A8 per-tensor accuracy, same conditions. Compute the gap.
3. On a held-out calibration set, record per-layer activation max/median ratio; rank layers.
4. Ablation arms: keep top-k layers in FP16 for k in {1, 2, 4, 8, 16}; measure accuracy per arm.
5. Negative control: keep k randomly chosen layers in FP16 for the same k values. If random keep-lists recover as much as ranked keep-lists, the outlier ranking has no explanatory power and the hypothesis is falsified.

Controls. Identical calibration data across arms; identical eval prompts and seeds; the only difference between arms is the keep-list.

Boundary condition. The result is specific to per-tensor scaling. With per-channel or group-wise scales the outlier pressure is already largely absorbed, so the ablation is expected to show a much flatter profile - that is a consistency check, not a contradiction.

Cost note. Each keep-list arm changes kernel dispatch; measure throughput too, because a keep-list that restores accuracy but costs 30% throughput may be worse than simply using W4A16.

Rollback gate. If no keep-list of <= 10% of layers reaches the accuracy budget, abandon W8A8 per-tensor for this model and record the negative result rather than expanding the keep-list until the metric passes.

Controlled experiment: is the observed quantization speedup real, or an artifact of the measurement harness?

Motivation. Most reported quantization speedups are confounded by warmup, clock drift, tokenizer overhead, differing output lengths, and comparing arms at different batch sizes. This experiment is designed to falsify a speedup claim before it is trusted.

Hypothesis to test. The FP16 -> W4A16 speedup measured by the harness is a property of the kernel and memory traffic, not of the harness.

Design (each check can independently kill the claim).
1. Warmup control. Discard the first N=20 iterations; report median of the remaining, plus interquartile range. If the claimed gain disappears after warmup, it was compilation/autotune noise.
2. Clock control. Lock SM and memory clocks (nvidia-smi -lgc / -lmc) and re-measure. If the gain shrinks materially, it was boost/thermal variance. Record GPU temperature and power throughout.
3. Output-length control. Force identical total generated tokens per arm. A quantized model that emits shorter outputs will appear faster in end-to-end wall clock while being no faster per token.
4. Isolation control. Confirm no other process shares the GPU (nvidia-smi pmon); MPS or a co-tenant invalidates the comparison.
5. Mechanism check. Capture dram__bytes.sum and achieved occupancy per decode step with nsight-compute. If bytes moved did not drop roughly in line with the weight compression ratio, the speedup does not have the claimed cause even if the wall clock improved.

Runbook: investigating a suspected quantization accuracy regression in production.

Trigger. Task metric or user-visible quality drops after a quantized build is rolled out, or a canary shows elevated malformed/truncated outputs.

Step 0 - stop the bleeding. If the canary is user-facing, shift traffic back to the FP16 build first, then investigate. Do not debug in the blast radius.

Step 1 - confirm it is the model, not the harness. Pin the weight hash, engine version, sampling params, and prompt template for both builds. A changed chat template or a changed default temperature explains more "quantization regressions" than quantization does. Diff the rendered prompt bytes between builds.

Step 2 - reproduce offline, greedy. Re-run the frozen eval suite with temperature 0 and a fixed seed on both builds on the same GPU. If the gap does not reproduce offline, the problem is in serving config or routing, not in the weights.

Step 3 - localize the scheme. Record scheme details: bit width, weight-only vs weight+activation, group size, symmetric/asymmetric, KV cache dtype, and the kernel backend. Re-test with KV cache forced back to FP16. KV quantization and weight quantization fail differently: KV failures show up on long context and exact-copy tasks, weight failures show up broadly.

Step 4 - localize the layers. On a calibration sample, collect per-layer activation max/median ratios. Run keep-in-FP16 ablations on the top-ranked layers. A small keep-list restoring most of the gap confirms an outlier-driven failure.

Step 5 - check calibration hygiene. Verify calibration data was in-domain and disjoint from the eval set (exact-hash overlap check). Misfit calibration is a common root cause and is cheap to rule out.

Boundary condition. Everything above assumes the quantized checkpoint itself is intact. Verify file hashes first; a truncated or partially-downloaded shard produces symptoms that mimic quantization damage.

Exit criteria. Either (a) a keep-list or scheme change brings accuracy within the declared budget and passes a fresh canary, or (b) the build is reverted to FP16 and the negative result is recorded with the layer attribution data.

Runbook: quantized model will not load, or loads and OOMs.

Trigger. Engine startup fails on a quantized checkpoint, or it loads and then OOMs under load while the FP16 build was stable.

Step 1 - verify the artifact. sha256 every shard against the source manifest. Confirm the config declares the quantization method and that the method matches what the engine was told to use. A checkpoint quantized with one toolchain and loaded with another quantization flag fails in confusing ways.

Step 2 - verify kernel/hardware compatibility. Map the scheme to a kernel and the kernel to the SM version. On A30 (SM80) there is no hardware FP8 tensor-core path; requesting FP8 weights or FP8 KV there either errors or silently falls back to an emulated path that is slower than FP16. Record compute capability from nvidia-smi and the engine's chosen kernel from startup logs, not from assumption.

Step 3 - account for memory honestly. Quantized weights shrink; KV cache, CUDA graphs, activation workspace, and the allocator's reserved pool do not. Engines size the KV pool from a utilization fraction of total memory, so a smaller weight footprint usually causes a LARGER KV pool and therefore more admitted concurrency - which is exactly how a "smaller" model OOMs under load. Reduce gpu_memory_utilization or cap max_num_seqs / max_model_len before blaming the quantization.

Step 4 - separate load-time from run-time OOM. Load-time OOM points at weights plus workspace and dequant buffers. Run-time OOM under concurrency points at KV admission and CUDA-graph capture. Read the traceback location before changing anything.

Step 5 - fall back deliberately. Try, in order: disable CUDA graphs (eager) to remove graph memory, lower gpu_memory_utilization by 0.05 steps, lower max_model_len, then change scheme. Change one variable at a time and record the result of each.

Boundary condition. All of this assumes a single-GPU load. Under tensor parallelism the group size must divide the per-rank shard of the quantized dimension; a group size incompatible with TP degree fails at shard time with a shape error, and the fix is the group size or the TP degree, not the memory settings.

Exit criteria. Engine serves at the target concurrency for a sustained soak with stable memory and no preemption storm; otherwise revert to the FP16 build.

Runbook: deciding whether to adopt quantization at all, and how to review the proposal.

Trigger. Someone proposes quantizing a production model to cut cost or raise throughput.

Step 1 - state the binding constraint first. Quantization only helps if the constraint it relieves is the actual bottleneck. Classify the workload: capacity-bound (model does not fit / KV pool too small), decode-bandwidth-bound (low batch, latency-sensitive), or prefill-compute-bound (long prompts, high batch). Weight-only quantization mainly helps the first two. It does little for prefill-compute-bound traffic, where the GEMMs are already compute-saturated and dequant adds ALU work.

Step 2 - require the scheme to be fully specified. Reject any proposal that says only a bit width. Required: weight-only vs weight+activation, group size, symmetric/asymmetric, KV dtype, kernel backend, and target SM version. Without these, no performance or accuracy claim is checkable.

Step 3 - require a declared accuracy budget before measurement. The budget must be written down first (for example, <= 1.0 absolute point on the frozen task suite, and no regression beyond noise on the safety/refusal set). Budgets chosen after seeing results are not budgets.

Step 4 - require measurement at production operating points. Batch 1 numbers are marketing. Ask for the batch x context grid that matches real traffic, with p50/p95 TTFT and TPOT, plus goodput under the SLO.

Step 5 - require a rollback plan. Both builds resident or quickly loadable, traffic shiftable, a canary with an automatic revert threshold, and the FP16 checkpoint retained for at least one full release cycle.

Boundary condition. If the model is already comfortably resident and the cluster is idle at peak, quantization buys nothing and costs accuracy risk plus a second artifact to maintain. The correct decision is often "no".

Exit criteria. Approve only if the measured gain at the production operating point exceeds the pre-declared threshold and the accuracy budget is met. Otherwise record the negative result and keep FP16.

Runbook entry — investigating a quantization regression on an LLM serving deployment.

Scope: you are asked whether quantization (weight-only INT4/INT8, or W8A8/FP8) is the cause of a latency, throughput, or accuracy anomaly.

Concrete mechanism. Weight-only quantization (e.g. AWQ/GPTQ INT4) does not make the GEMM cheaper in FLOPs; it makes it cheaper in bytes. Decode is memory-bandwidth bound: time per layer is roughly (bytes of weights read) / (achieved HBM bandwidth). Cutting weights from FP16 (2 B/param) to INT4 (~0.5 B/param plus scales/zero-points per group) reduces weight traffic ~3.5-4x, so decode tokens/s can rise nearly proportionally. The dequant-to-FP16 step is fused into the kernel prologue, so the arithmetic is still done in FP16/BF16 tensor cores.

Boundary condition. That speedup only holds while the kernel remains memory bound, i.e. at small effective batch. Once batch x sequence makes the GEMM compute bound (prefill, or decode with large continuous-batching batch size), the INT4 kernel has the same or worse FLOPs than the FP16 path and can be *slower*, because dequantization and group-scale handling add instructions and reduce tensor-core utilization. On A30 (no FP8 tensor cores; INT8 and FP16/BF16 available) there is no hardware FP8 path at all, so an "FP8 quantization" plan must be rejected or emulated, which is not a win.

Falsifiable hypotheses to test, in order:
1. "The regression is bandwidth, not accuracy." Predicts: decode throughput scales with weight bytes; prefill latency roughly unchanged. Test with a fixed-batch decode-only microbenchmark at batch 1, 8, 32 for FP16 vs quantized.
2. "The kernel falls off a supported path." Predicts: a specific (group_size, hidden_dim, batch) shape drops to a slow fallback. Test by sweeping batch and logging kernel names with Nsight Systems / nvprof-style tracing.
3. "The accuracy loss is outlier driven." Predicts: damage concentrates in a few channels of down_proj / o_proj. Test per-layer activation kurtosis and compare a per-channel or SmoothQuant-style variant.

Evidence required before any conclusion: (a) identical tokenizer, sampling params, and seed between arms; (b) throughput measured at matched output length and matched concurrency, not aggregate QPS; (c) accuracy measured on a held-out generative eval, not on perplexity alone, because perplexity can move less than task accuracy; (d) the quantized checkpoint's hash and the quantization config (bits, group size, calibration set) recorded.

Rollback gate: revert to the FP16 checkpoint if held-out task accuracy drops more than the pre-agreed threshold (e.g. > 1 absolute point on the primary eval), or if p99 latency at target concurrency regresses at all, or if any shape falls back to an unfused kernel. Rollback is a weight-path swap plus a serving restart; keep both checkpoints resident so the swap does not require a re-download.

Define NCCL and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library) is the library that implements multi-GPU / multi-node collective operations — all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, broadcast, all-to-all, plus point-to-point send/recv — with topology-aware algorithms and transport selection. Frameworks do not talk to NVLink, PCIe, or the NIC directly; they call NCCL, and NCCL decides how the bytes actually move.

Why it matters in LLM infrastructure: it is the transport under every parallelism strategy. Data parallel / FSDP / ZeRO issue reduce-scatter + all-gather every step; tensor parallelism issues an all-reduce (or reduce-scatter + all-gather) inside every transformer block, twice per layer; expert parallelism issues all-to-all. So NCCL sits on the critical path of both training step time and, for TP-sharded inference, per-token decode latency.

Concrete mechanism. For an all-reduce of N bytes over R ranks, NCCL's ring algorithm moves 2*(R-1)/R * N bytes per rank and takes about 2*(R-1) steps; the tree algorithm reduces the step count to O(log R) at the cost of less bandwidth utilization. NCCL picks between ring, tree, CollNet, and NVLS based on message size, rank count, and the topology it discovers at init, and it exposes that choice via NCCL_ALGO / NCCL_PROTO. It also selects a transport per peer pair: P2P over NVLink or PCIe when the peers are on the same node and access is permitted, otherwise SHM, otherwise the network path (IB verbs / RoCE, with GPUDirect RDMA if the NIC and GPU sit under a compatible PCIe topology and nvidia-peermem or the DMA-BUF path is present).

Boundary condition. The bandwidth advantage is real only above the algorithm's latency floor. For small messages — which is exactly the regime of TP all-reduce during single-token decode, often tens to a few hundred KB — the collective is latency bound, and per-call overhead (kernel launch, ring traversal, protocol handshakes) dominates; adding GPUs then makes decode *slower* per token even though aggregate FLOPs went up. The crossover is hardware specific: on NVLink-connected GPUs it sits far lower than on a PCIe-only box such as an 8xA30 node, where inter-GPU traffic crosses PCIe switches and possibly the host root complex.

Falsifiable claim and evidence: "TP=4 improves decode latency on this node" predicts a monotone latency drop from TP=1 to TP=4 at batch 1. Verify with nccl-tests all_reduce_perf at the actual message sizes, plus an end-to-end decode benchmark; record NCCL_DEBUG=INFO output showing the selected algorithm, protocol, and whether GPUDirect RDMA / P2P was enabled. Rollback gate: if measured p50 decode latency at TP=4 is not better than TP=2 by a pre-agreed margin, revert to the lower TP degree and take the memory cost elsewhere (quantization or KV-cache paging).

Define NCCL and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

NCCL is NVIDIA's collective communication library: it provides all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, broadcast, all-to-all and send/recv for GPUs, choosing both the algorithm and the physical transport automatically from the topology it discovers when a communicator is created.

Why it matters: in LLM infrastructure, NCCL is the thing that turns a pile of GPUs into one logical accelerator. Every gradient synchronization in DDP/FSDP, every tensor-parallel activation reduction inside an attention or MLP block, and every expert dispatch in an MoE layer is an NCCL call. Its cost is therefore not overhead you can amortize away — it recurs per layer, per step, and for TP inference, per generated token.

Concrete mechanism — transport selection. At init NCCL walks the PCIe/NVLink topology and builds per-peer transports in a strict preference order: NVLink/P2P, then PCIe P2P, then shared memory, then the network plugin. On the network path it will use GPUDirect RDMA (the NIC DMAs straight to/from GPU HBM, skipping a bounce buffer in host memory) only if the GPU and NIC are close enough in the PCIe hierarchy and the peer-memory support (nvidia-peermem or DMA-BUF) is loaded. Otherwise it silently falls back to staging through host memory, which roughly doubles PCIe traffic and adds copy latency. The fallback is silent — this is the single most common cause of "our fabric is 400G but the all-reduce is slow".

Boundary condition. GPUDirect RDMA helps only when the GPU-NIC pair is under the same PCIe switch (or otherwise has a short path). If the traffic must cross the CPU root complex or a socket-to-socket link, GDR can be *slower* than the staged path, and NCCL's own heuristics (NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL) will disable it. So "enable GDR everywhere" is not a valid tuning rule; it is a topology-dependent decision.

Evidence required: NCCL_DEBUG=INFO logs showing the chosen transport per peer ("via NET/IB/0/GDRDMA" vs a non-GDR line), nvidia-smi topo -m for the GPU/NIC affinity matrix, ibstatus or ethtool counters for the fabric, and nccl-tests bus bandwidth at the message sizes your job actually issues.

Rollback gate: any tuning change (NCCL_ALGO, NCCL_PROTO, NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL, NCCL_IB_HCA pinning) must be reverted unless it improves measured end-to-end step time or decode latency by more than run-to-run variance across at least three runs. Improving a microbenchmark alone is not sufficient evidence.

NCCL is the GPU collective communication library — all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, broadcast, all-to-all, and point-to-point — used by PyTorch distributed, DeepSpeed, Megatron, vLLM and essentially every other LLM stack as the process-group backend on NVIDIA hardware.

Why it matters: it determines the scaling efficiency of both training and sharded inference. A training step is compute time plus exposed communication time; NCCL both performs the communication and, through stream/overlap semantics, determines how much of it can be hidden behind compute.

Concrete mechanism — overlap. NCCL collectives run on their own CUDA stream(s). FSDP and ZeRO exploit this by prefetching the next layer's all-gather while the current layer's matmuls execute, so the exposed cost is max(compute, comm) per layer rather than compute + comm. This works because the collective is asynchronous with respect to the compute stream and is only joined by an event wait at the point the tensor is consumed.

Boundary condition. Overlap only hides communication while compute per layer is longer than communication per layer. That ratio degrades as you scale out (compute per rank shrinks with more data-parallel ranks at fixed global batch, while all-reduce volume per rank stays near 2N) and as you shrink micro-batch size for memory reasons. Past the crossover, the step becomes communication bound and adding GPUs buys almost nothing. A second boundary: NCCL kernels occupy SMs, so heavy overlap can measurably slow the compute kernels it is supposedly hidden behind — the two are not free of each other.

NCCL is NVIDIA's collective communications library. It implements the collective and point-to-point primitives that multi-GPU and multi-node LLM workloads depend on, and it is the default backend of torch.distributed on NVIDIA GPUs.

Why it matters in LLM infrastructure: correctness and liveness, not just speed. NCCL collectives are strictly collective — every rank in a communicator must issue matching operations in the same order with matching sizes and datatypes. This makes NCCL the place where distributed bugs surface, usually as a hang or a watchdog timeout rather than an exception.

Concrete mechanism. NCCL collectives are implemented as CUDA kernels that spin waiting for their peers' data. If one rank fails to enqueue the matching collective — because it took a different branch (e.g. a rank-dependent `if` around a logging all-reduce), because its dataloader stalled, or because it crashed — the remaining ranks' kernels spin until the PyTorch watchdog fires (default around 10 minutes, TORCH_NCCL_BLOCKING_WAIT / NCCL timeout) and abort the whole job. The GPU appears at 100% utilization the entire time, because a spinning collective kernel is indistinguishable from useful work at the utilization-counter level.

Boundary condition. Raising the timeout is only correct when the cause is genuine straggling (slow checkpoint write, uneven data shard, a slow node), never when the cause is a mismatched collective schedule. A mismatch is not slow — it will never complete — so a longer timeout only lengthens the outage and burns GPU hours.

Distinguishing evidence, in order: (a) NCCL_DEBUG=INFO plus the watchdog message names the collective and the ranks that did not arrive; (b) py-spy dump or a stack dump on each rank shows whether the missing rank is inside NCCL, inside the dataloader, or dead; (c) per-rank step-time histograms distinguish a persistent straggler node from a schedule mismatch; (d) checking whether the collective count per rank diverges before the hang.

Rollback gate: if the diagnosis is a schedule mismatch, roll back the code change that introduced rank-conditional collectives — do not tune timeouts. If the diagnosis is a straggler node, drain that node and re-run; only accept a timeout increase when the straggler is a known bounded event (e.g. periodic checkpoint) and the increase is smaller than the job's failure-detection budget. Never raise the timeout to a value that exceeds your willingness to leave a dead job holding the cluster.

Contrast NCCL with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.

Contrast: NCCL versus a naive hand-rolled multi-GPU synchronization.

Naive implementation. The obvious way to synchronize gradients across R GPUs is: every rank copies its gradient buffer to host memory, an MPI or socket layer gathers all R buffers on rank 0, rank 0 sums them on CPU, then broadcasts the result back. Cost per step: 2 * N bytes over PCIe per rank in each direction, N*R bytes into one node's host memory, a CPU-side reduction, and a serialized broadcast. The link into rank 0 becomes a hard bottleneck that scales as O(R), so step time grows linearly with GPU count — the opposite of what you bought the GPUs for.

What NCCL does instead. Ring all-reduce splits the buffer into R chunks and runs reduce-scatter then all-gather around the ring. Each rank sends and receives exactly 2*(R-1)/R * N bytes — under 2N, and independent of R in the limit — and all links are used simultaneously rather than funneling into one rank. The reduction arithmetic happens in a CUDA kernel on the GPUs, not on the CPU. Data moves peer-to-peer over NVLink or PCIe, or NIC-to-GPU via GPUDirect RDMA on the network path, so it never touches host memory when the topology allows it. For large rank counts NCCL can switch to tree or NVLS algorithms that trade bandwidth optimality for O(log R) latency.

Concrete mechanism worth internalizing: the win is that ring all-reduce is bandwidth-optimal (2N per rank is the information-theoretic floor for all-reduce) and congestion-free, whereas the naive gather-on-rank-0 is O(R*N) on one link.

Boundary condition. Ring's advantage is asymptotic in message size. Its latency term is proportional to 2*(R-1) hops, so for small buffers — many small gradient tensors, or TP all-reduces during single-token decode — ring can be worse than a tree or even than a naive approach with fewer hops. This is exactly why NCCL buckets gradients (DDP's bucket_cap_mb) before reducing them, and why tuning bucket size matters: too small and you pay the latency floor repeatedly, too large and you lose compute/communication overlap.

Contrast: NCCL versus not using it.

Without NCCL you are choosing one of two naive paths, and both are worse for a specific, mechanical reason.

Path 1 — CPU-mediated collectives (Gloo, MPI over host memory, or hand-written sockets). Every gradient or activation tensor must be device-to-host copied, reduced or forwarded by the CPU, then host-to-device copied back. The PCIe round trip alone is a fixed tax proportional to tensor bytes, the CPU reduction is orders of magnitude slower than a GPU reduction kernel, and the copies serialize against your compute stream unless you hand-manage pinned buffers and streams. For an FSDP or tensor-parallel workload that communicates several times per layer, this dominates step time completely.

Path 2 — parameter server / gather-on-one-rank. All R ranks send N bytes to a coordinator, which reduces and broadcasts. The coordinator's link carries O(R*N) bytes, so scaling efficiency falls off roughly as 1/R. Ring all-reduce, by contrast, moves 2*(R-1)/R * N bytes per rank with every link busy at once, which is the bandwidth-optimal bound.

Concrete mechanism NCCL provides that you would otherwise have to build: topology discovery and transport selection. NCCL inspects NVLink/NVSwitch, PCIe switch hierarchy, and NIC affinity at communicator-init time, then picks per-peer transports (NVLink P2P > PCIe P2P > SHM > net) and per-call algorithms (ring/tree/CollNet/NVLS) and protocols (LL, LL128, Simple) based on message size. Reproducing even a fraction of that correctly — including GPUDirect RDMA so the NIC DMAs into HBM without a host bounce — is a multi-year effort.

Boundary condition. NCCL is not universally the right answer. It requires NVIDIA GPUs and a homogeneous communicator; it does not handle CPU-only tensors (Gloo does, which is why many stacks keep a Gloo group for small control-plane collectives and metadata broadcast); it has no built-in fault tolerance — a single failed rank aborts the communicator, so elastic training needs an external layer. And at very small message sizes with few ranks, the fixed launch and handshake cost can exceed a trivial cudaMemcpyPeer.

Evidence required: side-by-side nccl-tests vs the alternative backend at your real message sizes, plus end-to-end tokens/s at matched global batch. Rollback gate: if switching a control-plane collective to NCCL does not improve end-to-end step time beyond run variance, keep it on Gloo, since NCCL's abort-on-failure semantics make it the riskier choice for non-critical paths.

Contrast: NCCL versus a naive non-NCCL implementation, from the operational-risk angle rather than only the performance angle.

Performance side. Naive gather-to-one-rank all-reduce moves O(R*N) bytes across a single rank's links; NCCL's ring moves 2*(R-1)/R * N bytes per rank with all links active, which is bandwidth optimal for all-reduce. Naive host-staged reduction pays two PCIe crossings plus a CPU-side sum; NCCL reduces on the GPU and, where the PCIe/NIC topology allows, uses P2P over NVLink or GPUDirect RDMA so the bytes never enter host memory.

Concrete mechanism you would have to reimplement: chunked pipelining. NCCL splits a buffer into many chunks and pipelines them around the ring, so a rank is sending chunk k while receiving chunk k-1 and reducing chunk k-2. That is what keeps every link saturated; a naive blocking send/recv per whole tensor leaves most links idle most of the time and turns a bandwidth-bound problem into a latency-bound one.

Boundary condition and the honest trade-off. NCCL buys performance at the cost of failure semantics. A NCCL communicator has no partial-failure mode: if one rank dies or diverges from the collective schedule, the surviving ranks spin inside a kernel until a watchdog aborts the job, and GPU utilization reads 100% the whole time. A naive socket-based implementation, however slow, can time out per peer and degrade gracefully. So for control-plane operations (rendezvous, metadata exchange, health checks) a slower, individually-timeoutable backend such as Gloo is often the safer choice, and most production stacks keep both process groups.

Falsifiable hypothesis: "our collective path is the bottleneck." Prediction: exposed NCCL kernel time on an Nsight timeline should be a large fraction of step time, and step time should improve materially when message sizes are bucketed differently. Test both before changing topology.
