H0: at the 70/30 short/long mix, disaggregating prefill and decode onto separate
replica pools does NOT improve goodput by more than 10 percent versus a single
co-located continuous-batching pool at equal total GPU count.
H1: it does, because decode-phase TPOT is currently degraded by long prefill chunks
sharing the same scheduler step.
Discriminating measurement: per-step timeline of prefill tokens vs decode tokens,
and TPOT conditioned on 'a long prefill was co-scheduled in the same step'. If TPOT
inflation under co-scheduling is < 5 percent, H1 is refuted and disaggregation
(which adds KV transfer cost over the interconnect) is not justified. Cross-node KV
transfer for a disaggregated design must itself be budgeted: measure the KV bytes
per request and the achieved RDMA bandwidth, and confirm transfer time < the TTFT
budget you are trying to protect.

8. Reporting artifact
One table per arm: config hash, mix, arrival rate, req count, warmup
excluded, TTFT p50/p95/p99, TPOT p50/p95/p99, output tok/s, goodput,
queue-wait p99, preempt count, peak KV utilization, clock/throttle log.
Raw per-request records are archived alongside; any claim not derivable
from those records is withdrawn.

0. Non-claims
This is a serving-system measurement protocol only. It is not evidence about model
quality, and no number here transfers across engine commit, weight hash, quantization,
sequence-length regime, tenancy, or GPU SKU without a full re-run.

1. Fixed setup (record it or the run is void)
- Engine commit + launch flags, weights hash, quantization scheme, tokenizer version,
  driver/CUDA version, container image digest.
- Persistence mode on, clocks pinned (nvidia-smi -pm 1, -lgc), MIG topology declared.
  Unpinned DVFS makes thermal drift readable as a treatment effect; that is the single
  most common way these studies lie.
- Open-loop Poisson arrivals from an off-host generator; generator CPU < 60% at peak
  and RTT recorded. Closed-loop harnesses self-throttle under overload and delete
  exactly the tail samples the P99 claim depends on.
- Seeded length mixture over four strata S/M/L/XL, byte-identical across arms.
- ignore_eos with fixed max_tokens per stratum, otherwise output length is an
  uncontrolled random variable and TPOT is uninterpretable.

2. Metric definitions frozen before the first run
- TTFT = server ingress -> first output token flushed to the socket. Also record
  client-side TTFT; the delta is the queue + network component.
- TPOT = (E2E - TTFT) / (out_tokens - 1), per request; undefined and excluded when
  out_tokens < 2. Never a global mean over pooled requests.
- Queueing delay = ingress -> prefill admission, reported as its own distribution.
- Throughput split into req/s, prefill tok/s, decode tok/s. Prefill is compute-bound,
  decode is memory-bandwidth-bound at small batch; one aggregate tok/s number hides
  the trade and is not falsifiable.
- Goodput = req/s meeting a pre-declared per-stratum SLO, not raw completions.
- P99 computed per stratum from raw per-request records, never pooled across strata
  or across repeats.

3. Procedure
Warmup discarded (first 2 min or 500 requests, whichever is larger); >= 5 fresh-process
repeats per arm; randomized arm order to break drift-vs-treatment aliasing; load ladder
of >= 6 points up to 130% of measured saturation so the knee and the post-knee behavior
are both visible.

4. Falsifiable hypothesis (H1: prefill/decode disaggregation improves TTFT tail without
paying an unacceptable KV-transfer cost at this cluster's interconnect)
H1: splitting prefill and decode onto separate GPU pools, with KV handed over via
RDMA, improves S-stratum P99 TTFT >= 30% at 90% saturation while total cluster
output tok/s degrades <= 8%.
Null: TTFT gain inside the noise band, or throughput loss > 8%.
Mechanism and the boundary that decides it: handover cost is KV bytes per request
divided by achieved (not line-rate) fabric bandwidth. Compute this number first. If
per-request KV is on the order of hundreds of MB and the fabric delivers only a few
tens of GB/s achieved, transfer time lands in the same order as the prefill it was
meant to offload and H1 cannot hold; the experiment then becomes a falsification of
the design, which is a valid and cheap outcome.
5. Controlled experiment
Arms: colocated (control) vs disaggregated at matched total GPU count. Instrument the
handover path separately: transfer bytes, achieved bandwidth, completion latency, and
whether transfer overlaps decode of other sequences. Report interconnect type
explicitly (RoCEv2 vs InfiniBand vs PCIe/host-staged) because the conclusion is not
portable across them; a host-staged copy through system memory is a different
experiment with a different ceiling.

Confounders instrumented on every run
- Prefix/KV cache hit rate. A divergence > 2 percentage points between arms voids the
  comparison outright; it is not a covariate to adjust away.
- Continuous-batching batch-size distribution over time, not just its mean.
- Preemption / recompute / swap counts, KV block utilization, allocator OOM retries.
- Sampling parameters and EOS behavior (output length is itself a treatment).
- NUMA/CPU-affinity placement, CPU governor, tokenizer-thread saturation, generator RTT.
- Co-tenant activity on the same host and any NIC/PCIe contention.

Stop / rollback gates (pre-committed, before seeing data)
- Any throttle reason reported by nvidia-smi (thermal, power, reliability) => the sample
  is invalid, not noisy; abort and rerun the arm.
- Error rate > 0.5% at a load point => abort that load point, record it as saturation.
- Promote only if the pre-registered primary metric beats a noise band of 2x the control
  arm's across-repeat spread AND no stratum regresses > 5% on P99 end-to-end latency.
- Roll back within one deploy cycle on > 10% P99 E2E regression, observed starvation of
  any stratum, or an increase in preemption/OOM counters.

Honest limit: a P99 estimated from a few thousand requests carries a wide interval.
Quote a bootstrap or binomial CI next to it; an effect smaller than that interval is
not a result, and reporting it as one is the failure mode this plan exists to prevent.

  enable/tune swapping, raise gpu_memory_utilization only after OOM headroom

  interval histogram shows spikes aligned with prefill admissions. Fix: enable

  from the config and validate against observed KV block consumption. A > 10%
  mismatch means the engine is doing something you have not modelled.

confounder is active; investigate before reporting any speedup.

Analysis framing (Performance Analysis variant 1195)
Build a roofline-style capacity model before tuning, then falsify it.
- Prefill is compute-bound: expected time ~ (2 * P_active * in_tokens) / achieved
  FLOP/s. Measure achieved FLOP/s at a fixed prompt length; do not assume peak.
- Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound: expected per-step time ~ (bytes of weights +
  KV read) / achieved HBM BW. TPOT should be near-flat in batch size until the
  batch is large enough to become compute-bound - the batch size at which TPOT
  starts rising is the measured crossover point.

  from the config and validate against observed KV block consumption. A > 10%
  mismatch means the engine is doing something you have not modelled.
Predicted vs measured gap > 20% on either phase means the model is wrong or a
confounder is active; investigate before reporting any speedup.

Diagnostic framing (Troubleshooting variant 1200)
Symptom triage first: P99 latency regressions in mixed traffic almost always
resolve to one of four mechanisms. Test them in this order, cheapest first.
H-T1 Queueing-bound: queue_wait/TTFT > 0.5 at target load. Evidence: scheduler
  queue depth > 0 persistently while SM util < 70%. Fix: admission control,
  more replicas, lower max_num_seqs to shorten head-of-line blocking.
H-T2 KV-exhaustion / preemption: nonzero preemption counters, bimodal TPOT,
  KV utilization pinned near 100%. Fix: cap max_num_seqs, reduce max context,
  enable/tune swapping, raise gpu_memory_utilization only after OOM headroom
  is measured.
H-T3 Prefill/decode interference: long prompts stall decode steps; decode-step
  interval histogram shows spikes aligned with prefill admissions. Fix: enable
  chunked prefill and tune chunk size; or split prefill/decode across replicas
  (disaggregated serving) and re-measure the KV transfer cost explicitly.
H-T4 Hardware/collective: throttle reasons nonzero, or NCCL allreduce time
  variance high on TP>1. Fix: check `nvidia-smi topo -m`, power caps, and NIC
  path before touching engine flags.
Each hypothesis is falsified by a single-variable experiment against the frozen
baseline trace; if the predicted counter does not move, discard and move on.

Performance-analysis framing.
Primary falsifiable hypothesis H-P: enabling chunked prefill (chunk = 512 tokens)
on the production mix reduces short-prompt TTFT P99 by >=25% at fixed QPS while
degrading output-token throughput by <=5%. Null H0: no change in TTFT P99 beyond
trial noise (overlapping bootstrap CIs).
Controlled experiment: single-variable A/B on the same node, same weights hash,
same seeded workload trace replayed identically to both arms, randomized arm
order across >=5 trial pairs. Mechanism being tested: chunking bounds the length
of any single prefill occupancy of the scheduler step, so decode steps interleave
and head-of-line blocking of short prompts shrinks; the cost is more scheduler
iterations and reduced prefill arithmetic intensity.
Boundary conditions: the effect should be near zero when prompts are uniformly
short (no long prefill to chunk) and should grow with the long-prompt tail. If
TTFT improves in the short-prompt-only cell too, the mechanism claim is wrong and
something else changed - discard the hypothesis.

0. Scope and non-claims
This is a serving-system measurement protocol only. It characterizes the
deployment (engine build, weights hash, quantization, scheduler policy, GPU SKU,
tenancy, workload mix), not model domain capability. No number here transfers
across any of those axes; changing one invalidates the baseline and requires a
re-run. Results are provisional until the falsification experiment below is
executed on real hardware.

1. Assumptions to record before any run (a run without these is unreportable)
- Engine + commit SHA (e.g. vLLM / SGLang / TensorRT-LLM), CUDA + NCCL version,
  driver version.
- Weights: repo + revision hash, dtype, quantization (fp16 / fp8 / awq / gptq),
  KV-cache dtype.
- Parallelism: TP / PP / DP degrees, `nvidia-smi topo -m` output, NVLink vs PCIe,
  NIC model and whether GDR is active (`ibv_devinfo`, NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL).
- Scheduler knobs: max_num_seqs, max_num_batched_tokens, chunked-prefill on/off
  and chunk size, preemption/swap policy, gpu_memory_utilization.
- Workload: prompt-length and output-length distributions (report percentiles,
  not means), arrival process (fixed QPS Poisson vs closed-loop), mix ratio of
  short-prompt vs long-generation requests, and the RNG seed used to draw it.
- Client: request timeout, streaming on/off, concurrency cap, clock source.

2. Metric definitions (ambiguity here is the most common source of bogus deltas)
- TTFT = t(first token received by client) - t(request submitted by client).
  Includes queue wait. Also record queue_wait separately from server traces so
  TTFT can be decomposed into queue_wait + prefill_compute + network.
- TPOT = (t(last token) - t(first token)) / (output_tokens - 1). Report the
  per-request distribution, never a global mean; a global mean silently reweights
  toward long generations.
- Throughput: report output tokens/s AND total (prefill+decode) tokens/s AND
  requests/s. Output-token throughput alone hides prefill cost; total-token
  throughput alone hides decode stalls.
- Queueing: scheduler queue depth sampled at >=10 Hz, plus per-request
  queue_wait, plus preemption/recompute counters.
- P99 latency: end-to-end per request, reported with a bootstrap CI. P99 from
  fewer than ~3000 completed requests per cell is not interpretable; state n.

3. Why prefill and decode must be separated
Prefill is compute-bound and scales ~O(prompt_tokens) (attention adds an
O(L^2) term at long context); decode is memory-bandwidth- and KV-capacity-bound
and scales ~O(batch x model bytes) per step. Mixed traffic therefore has two
different bottlenecks that move in opposite directions under batching: raising
batch size improves decode bandwidth utilization but lengthens prefill-induced
head-of-line blocking, inflating TTFT of short prompts. Any single aggregate
number over the mix is unattributable. Run at minimum three cells:
  A short-prompt-only, B long-generation-only, C the production mix.
A and B calibrate the two regimes; C exposes the interference term. The
interference term is the quantity of interest: I = P99(C) - max(P99(A),P99(B))
at matched load.

4. Experimental protocol
- Warmup: discard the first 60 s or 300 requests, whichever is larger; report
  the discard rule. Warmup covers CUDA graph capture, autotuner, allocator
  steady state, and cache warmup.
- Load: closed-loop concurrency sweep AND open-loop Poisson QPS sweep. Only the
  open-loop sweep produces a meaningful latency-vs-load curve; closed-loop
  self-throttles and will hide queue collapse.
- Repeats: >=5 independent trials per cell, fresh server process per trial,
  randomized cell order to defeat thermal and cache drift. Report median of
  per-trial P99 plus interquartile range, not a pooled P99.
- Duration: each trial long enough that the steady-state window (post-warmup)
  contains >=3000 completions.
- Capture per trial: request-level traces (arrival, schedule, first token, last
  token, output length), scheduler queue depth timeseries, KV-cache utilization,
  preemption count, GPU memory (allocated + reserved + free), SM/DRAM utilization,
  power and clock throttle reasons (`nvidia-smi --query-gpu=clocks_throttle_reasons.active`),
  and for TP>1 the NCCL collective time distribution.

5. Confounders that must be controlled or measured

0. Framing
Design framing: the plan must fix the workload generator and the SLO contract before comparing any two configurations.
The source text is a grading rubric ("Answer should state ..."), not an answer, so it is rewritten into an executable plan.

1. Stated assumptions (must be recorded, not guessed)
- Single model replica per measurement cell; engine (vLLM/SGLang/TensorRT-LLM) and commit SHA pinned.
- Continuous batching with a fixed scheduler policy; KV cache dtype and quantization pinned.
- Workload is open-loop: arrivals are Poisson at target QPS and do NOT slow down when the server slows down.
  A closed-loop client silently caps queueing and will make P99 look healthy; this is the single most common
  measurement error in this scenario.
- Prompt and output length distributions are sampled from a seeded trace, not from a fixed constant.

2. Falsifiable hypothesis
H-D217: separating prefill and decode onto distinct replicas (disaggregated serving) improves short-prompt TTFT p99 by >=25% at equal total GPU count, at a cost of <=10% output-token throughput. Falsified if either bound is missed.
The hypothesis names one variable, one direction, one threshold, and its own falsification condition.

3. Metric definitions (operational, so runs are comparable)
- TTFT = wall clock from client send to first streamed token, including admission and queue wait.
- Queue wait = admission timestamp to first prefill step; reported separately so TTFT can be decomposed.
- TPOT = (end_to_end - TTFT) / (output_tokens - 1), computed per request, then aggregated; never a global average.
- Throughput reported as two numbers: output tokens/s and completed requests/s. Reporting only one hides the
  short-prompt vs long-generation tradeoff, which is exactly the tension in this workload.
- P99 computed per request over post-warmup completions only, with a bootstrap 95% CI.

4. Controlled experiment protocol
- Change exactly one variable per cell (e.g. chunked-prefill on/off, or max_num_seqs, or TP degree).
- Warmup: discard the first 90s and the first 200 completions; record the warmup boundary explicitly.
- >=5 independent trials per cell, >=3000 post-warmup completions per trial, fresh process per trial.
- Sweep QPS upward until output-token throughput stops increasing; report the full latency-throughput curve,
  not one operating point, because a single-QPS comparison cannot distinguish a better config from a lightly loaded one.
- Randomize cell execution order to defuse thermal drift and neighbor noise.

5. Expected confounders and their controls
- Prefill/decode interference: long prefills stall decode of in-flight long generations, inflating TPOT p99.
  Control by logging per-step prefill token count and correlating with per-token decode latency.
- KV cache pressure and preemption: when KV is exhausted the scheduler preempts/recomputes, producing bimodal TPOT.
  Control by logging preemption counters and KV utilization; a bimodal histogram invalidates a single P99 number.
- Thermal/power capping: on a power-capped node clocks drop mid-run. Control by logging clocks and throttle reasons.
- Tokenizer differences between client-side length accounting and server-side counts.
- Multi-GPU cases: NCCL collectives on the tensor-parallel path add per-step latency; verify NVLink vs PCIe topology
  with nvidia-smi topo -m before attributing a regression to the scheduler.

6. Evidence to capture per trial
Engine + driver + CUDA/NCCL versions, weights revision hash, parallelism degrees, scheduler config, request-level
trace (arrival, admission, first token, all inter-token gaps, completion), GPU memory / SM / clock timeseries,
and the raw per-request records so percentiles can be recomputed independently.

7. Decision and rollback gates
- Promote only if the primary metric improves beyond its 95% CI, no secondary SLO regresses more than 5%,
  and the result replicates on a second identical node.
- Canary at <=5% traffic for >=60 minutes; auto-rollback on TTFT p99 breach, error-rate rise, or any preemption
  counter increase versus baseline.
- Keep the previous config and its exact artifact hashes hot for immediate revert; rollback must not require a rebuild.

Boundary conditions: this plan is valid for a single-model, single-cluster endpoint. It does not cover
multi-tenant fairness, cross-region routing, or prefix-cache-hit-dominated traffic, each of which would require
separate hit-rate stratification before percentiles are meaningful.

A service receives a mix of short prompts and long generations. Design an evaluation plan that reports TTFT, TPOT, throughput, queueing, and P99 latency. Scenario variant 224: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.

Scope and assumptions (variant 224, framing: Troubleshooting). Assume a single vLLM/TensorRT-LLM-class decoder-only serving tier on homogeneous GPUs, continuous batching enabled, paged KV cache, one model replica per GPU group with tensor parallel degree TP fixed for the whole study. Traffic is bimodal: short prompts (about 128-512 input tokens) with long generations (about 512-2048 output tokens) mixed with short-in/short-out requests. If any of these are false the plan must be re-derived, because prefill/decode ratios drive every metric below.

Mechanism. TTFT is dominated by queueing delay plus prefill compute, which is compute-bound and scales roughly linearly with total prefilled tokens in the batch. TPOT is dominated by the decode step, which is memory-bandwidth-bound: each step reads the full weight set plus the KV cache of every active sequence, so TPOT degrades as concurrent sequence count and context length grow. Throughput (output tokens/s) rises with batch size until either KV-cache blocks are exhausted (admission control starts queueing, TTFT spikes) or HBM bandwidth saturates (TPOT rises proportionally). P99 latency is therefore not a single phenomenon: P99 TTFT is a queueing/admission artifact, P99 end-to-end is dominated by long generations and by prefill requests preempting decode.

Falsifiable hypothesis. H1: with chunked prefill enabled and a prefill token budget of B tokens per step, P99 TTFT at a fixed offered load will drop by at least 30 percent relative to the non-chunked baseline, while mean TPOT increases by no more than 10 percent and total output throughput changes by less than 5 percent. H1 is falsified if P99 TTFT improves by less than 15 percent, or if TPOT regresses by more than 10 percent, or if throughput drops more than 5 percent. A useful null H0 is that queueing, not prefill interference, is the sole driver, in which case chunking changes nothing until offered load is reduced.

Controlled experiment. Fix model, weights, quantization, TP degree, GPU clocks (lock SM and memory clocks, disable auto boost), driver, kernel, and server version. A service receives a mix of short prompts and long generations. Design an evaluation plan that reports TTFT, TPOT, throughput, queueing, and P99 latency. Scenario variant 232: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.

Scope and assumptions (variant 232, framing: System Design). Assume a single vLLM/TensorRT-LLM-class decoder-only serving tier on homogeneous GPUs, continuous batching enabled, paged KV cache, one model replica per GPU group with tensor parallel degree TP fixed for the whole study. Traffic is bimodal: short prompts (about 128-512 input tokens) with long generations (about 512-2048 output tokens) mixed with short-in/short-out requests. If any of these are false the plan must be re-derived, because prefill/decode ratios drive every metric below.

Mechanism. TTFT is dominated by queueing delay plus prefill compute, which is compute-bound and scales roughly linearly with total prefilled tokens in the batch. TPOT is dominated by the decode step, which is memory-bandwidth-bound: each step reads the full weight set plus the KV cache of every active sequence, so TPOT degrades as concurrent sequence count and context length grow. Throughput (output tokens/s) rises with batch size until either KV-cache blocks are exhausted (admission control starts queueing, TTFT spikes) or HBM bandwidth saturates (TPOT rises proportionally). P99 latency is therefore not a single phenomenon: P99 TTFT is a queueing/admission artifact, P99 end-to-end is dominated by long generations and by prefill requests preempting decode.

Falsifiable hypothesis. H1: with chunked prefill enabled and a prefill token budget of B tokens per step, P99 TTFT at a fixed offered load will drop by at least 30 percent relative to the non-chunked baseline, while mean TPOT increases by no more than 10 percent and total output throughput changes by less than 5 percent. H1 is falsified if P99 TTFT improves by less than 15 percent, or if TPOT regresses by more than 10 percent, or if throughput drops more than 5 percent. A useful null H0 is that queueing, not prefill interference, is the sole driver, in which case chunking changes nothing until offered load is reduced.

Controlled experiment. Fix model, weights, quantization, TP degree, GPU clocks (lock SM and memory clocks, disable auto boost), driver, kernel, and server version. The only manipulated variable is the prefill scheduling policy (chunked on/off, and B in a small sweep). Use a closed-loop-free open-loop load generator that issues requests from a fixed, seeded trace so both arms replay byte-identical prompts and identical requested max_new_tokens; do not let sampling change generation lengths between arms (use greedy or a fixed seed and ignore-eos with fixed output length for the primary arm, and a separate realistic-length arm as a secondary). Sweep offered QPS in a staircase (for example 25, 50, 75, 90, 100, 110 percent of the measured saturation point) and hold each step for at least 5 minutes after a discarded warmup of at least 2 minutes or 500 requests, whichever is longer. Run at least 5 independent repetitions per cell, randomizing arm order, and report medians of per-run percentiles with bootstrap confidence intervals rather than pooling all requests.

Measurements. Per request: arrival timestamp, admission timestamp, first-token timestamp, per-token timestamps (or at minimum last-token timestamp plus token count), input and output token counts, and the scheduler state (running/waiting queue depth) at admission. Derive TTFT = first_token - arrival (report the queueing component admission - arrival separately from prefill first_token - admission, otherwise the result is uninterpretable). Derive TPOT = (last_token - first_token)/(output_tokens - 1). Report throughput as both output tokens/s and requests/s, and report goodput under an explicit SLO. Server-side: KV cache utilization and preemption/recompute counts, batch size distribution, prefill vs decode step counts and time. Hardware: sample nvidia-smi or DCGM for SM occupancy, HBM bandwidth utilization, memory used, power and clock throttle reasons at 1 Hz; NCCL/comm time if TP > 1. Always report the input/output length distribution alongside every latency number.

Expected confounders. Client-side bottlenecks and tokenizer overhead in the load generator; open vs closed loop (a closed-loop client hides queueing and makes P99 look artificially good); coordinated omission if the client waits before issuing the next request; thermal/power throttling on long runs; page cache and CUDA graph capture warmup; different realized output lengths between arms making TPOT and throughput incomparable; other tenants on the same host or NIC; prefix caching silently making the second arm faster because it replays the same prompts. Mitigate the last one by clearing or explicitly configuring prefix cache identically in both arms and reporting cache hit rate.

Evidence that would settle it. Paired per-cell distributions of TTFT split into queue and prefill components, TPOT vs concurrent-sequence count, throughput vs offered load curves with the saturation knee identified, KV preemption counts, and a bandwidth-utilization trace showing whether decode is at the memory roofline. If TPOT is flat while HBM bandwidth is below roughly 70 percent, the bottleneck is not decode bandwidth and the hypothesis about batch-size scaling is wrong.

Rollback criteria. Promote the new scheduling policy only if, on the canary at production traffic mix, P99 TTFT improves and P99 end-to-end does not regress, TPOT regression stays under 10 percent, error rate and timeout rate are unchanged, and no increase in KV preemptions is observed over a 24-hour soak. Roll back immediately if P99 end-to-end regresses more than 10 percent, if timeout/5xx rate increases at all, or if OOM or preemption-driven recompute appears. Keep the previous config one flag-flip away and canary at 5 percent for at least one full traffic cycle before wider rollout.

Scope and assumptions (variant 1235, framing: System Design). Traffic is bimodal: short prompts (~128-512 input tokens) paired with long generations (~512-2048 output tokens), interleaved with short-in/short-out requests. Every number below is an estimate to be measured, not a platform fact; if the assumptions break, the plan must be re-derived because prefill/decode ratio drives all five metrics.

Mechanism. TTFT = queue wait + scheduling delay + prefill compute. Prefill is compute-bound and grows roughly with total prefilled tokens (attention adds a superlinear term at long context). TPOT is the steady-state decode step time, dominated by HBM bandwidth for weight and KV reads, so it grows with concurrent batch size and with accumulated KV length. Throughput (output tok/s) rises with batch size until either KV-cache blocks or memory bandwidth saturate; past that knee, added load converts directly into queueing and P99 blowup. These are separate regimes and must never be summarized by a single average latency.

Falsifiable hypothesis (the controlled experiment centers on chunked prefill vs default scheduler). H1: enabling chunked prefill with a token budget of ~2048 tokens per scheduler step reduces decode-phase TPOT p99 by >=20% at 80% of saturation load, while increasing mean TTFT by <=15%. Null: the effect size is within the noise band, defined as the 95% CI half-width of the baseline arm.

Experiment design. Two arms, baseline vs treatment, identical hardware, identical model weights and engine build, only chunked prefill vs default scheduler changed. Use a pre-recorded request trace with fixed seeds and fixed input/output token lengths so realized work is identical across arms; enforce output length with min/max new tokens so the treatment cannot win by generating less. Drive load open-loop with a Poisson arrival process at a staircase of offered rates (e.g. 25/50/75/90/100/110% of the baseline saturation rate) to locate the knee and avoid coordinated omission. Discard a warmup window and demonstrate stationarity before counting samples. Repeat each cell at least 5 times in randomized, interleaved order; report medians with bootstrap CIs, never a single run. Lock GPU clocks or record them, and record power and throttle reasons.

Measurements. Per-request trace with arrival, admission, first-token and last-token timestamps plus input/output token counts, so TTFT can be decomposed into queue wait vs prefill compute, and TPOT computed over the decode phase only. Server-side scheduler counters: batch size distribution, KV block utilization, preemption/recompute counts, prefix cache hit rate. Device telemetry at 1 Hz via DCGM: HBM bandwidth, SM occupancy, power, throttle reasons, memory footprint. For multi-GPU arms also collect NCCL collective time share and topology (nvidia-smi topo -m). Report P50/P90/P99 with sample counts; a P99 from fewer than ~1000 samples per cell is not trustworthy.

Evidence required before believing the result: prefill chunking token budget, plus the per-request trace, the staircase throughput curve with the identified knee, and reproduction on a second independent day.

Rollback criteria and safety. Stage the change in shadow or on a small canary slice first. Roll back immediately if: TPOT p99 regression >25% or TTFT mean regression >15% for two consecutive 10-minute windows; or if error rate, timeout rate, or preemption-induced recompute rises above baseline; or if any correctness check on generated output regresses. Keep the previous engine config and model version hot so rollback is a routing flip, not a redeploy. Do not promote a config whose gain is not reproduced across two independent measurement days.

Experiment design. Arms: BF16 baseline vs FP8. Quality is a gate, not a secondary metric: performance results from a quantized arm are void unless the paired accuracy check runs on the same build. Everything else is held fixed: model weights, engine build, GPU SKU and count, driver/NCCL versions, sampling parameters, and the replayed request trace including arrival timestamps. Randomize arm order across trials to absorb drift in the shared environment.

Measurement protocol. Open-loop load generator with Poisson arrivals; per-request trace records arrival, admission, first token, per-token timestamps, input/output token counts, and workload class. Discard a warmup window (first 3 minutes or until the running throughput mean is stable within 2% over 60s, whichever is later), then hold a 15-minute measurement window. Five independent trials per arm with engine restart between trials to avoid carry-over of cache state; report median with the 5th/95th trial spread, and bootstrap 95% CIs for p99. Sample GPU memory, SM utilization, achieved HBM bandwidth, KV-block occupancy, preemption count, and NCCL/NIC counters at 1s resolution alongside the request trace.

Confounders to control explicitly: warmup and JIT/graph-capture effects; prompt-mix drift between arms (freeze a replayed trace, do not resample); tokenizer differences inflating token counts; client-side bottlenecks (verify the generator can exceed the target rate against a null endpoint); GPU clock throttling (log nvidia-smi clocks and temperature, drop trials with thermal or power capping); other tenants on the node or fabric; and autoscaling or router changes mid-run.

Rollback criteria and gates. Promote the treatment only if the pre-registered effect size holds with a 95% CI excluding the null, error rate stays <=0.1%, no OOM or engine restart occurs across all trials, and quality on the held-out eval is unchanged within tolerance. Roll back immediately if P99 end-to-end for any workload class regresses >10%, preemption/recompute exceeds 1% of requests, or the error rate exceeds 0.5% during a canary at 10% traffic. Canary for at least one full diurnal cycle before fleet-wide rollout; keep the previous engine build resident so rollback is a router flip, not a redeploy.

A service receives a mix of short prompts and long generations. Design an evaluation plan that reports TTFT, TPOT, throughput, queueing, and P99 latency. Scenario variant 259: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.

Assumptions (state explicitly, do not assume vendor-specific behavior): single model replica on a known GPU type and count; continuous batching serving engine (e.g. vLLM-class) with paged KV cache; client and server clock-synced; network RTT measured separately and subtracted from TTFT if the goal is server-side latency. Scenario variant corpus-01259.

Definitions used, with units:
- TTFT (ms) = first output token timestamp minus request-arrival timestamp at the server. It contains queue-wait + prefill compute.
- TPOT (ms/token) = (end-to-end latency - TTFT) / (output_tokens - 1). Decode-side only.
- Throughput = output tokens/s aggregated, and separately requests/s completed; report both, they diverge under a long-generation mix.
- Queueing (ms) = time between admission-eligible and scheduler dispatch; must be instrumented in the engine, not inferred.
- P99 latency (ms) computed over a fixed, pre-registered request population, not over whatever completed in the window (completion bias truncates long generations).

Falsifiable hypothesis (pre-register before running): H1 = "At fixed arrival rate lambda, increasing max batch size from B0 to 2*B0 increases output-token throughput by >=15% while degrading TTFT p99 by <=20%." Null: throughput gain <15% or TTFT p99 degradation >20%. This is falsifiable because both quantities are directly measured with a fixed workload trace and fixed decoding params.

Controlled experiment:
1. Freeze the workload: replay a recorded trace with fixed prompt-length and output-length distributions (log them: e.g. prompt p50/p95, output p50/p95) and a fixed arrival process (Poisson at lambda, or closed-loop with fixed concurrency - say which, they are not interchangeable).
2. Fix decoding: temperature, max_tokens, ignore_eos on/off. ignore_eos=true makes output length deterministic and is the cleaner throughput measurement; ignore_eos=false is the realistic latency measurement. Run both, do not mix.
3. Warmup: discard the first N requests (or first 60 s) until TTFT p50 is stationary; report the discarded count and the stationarity check.
4. Repeat: >=3 independent trials per configuration, randomized order, report mean and CI or min/median/max. A single run cannot distinguish a 10% effect from run-to-run noise.
5. Sweep lambda upward until the system is saturated (queue-wait grows without bound); report the knee, not just one operating point.

Instrumentation to capture per request: arrival, admission, first-token, last-token timestamps; prompt and output token counts; batch size and number of running sequences at admission; KV-cache utilization; preemption/recompute events. Plus GPU-level: memory used vs reserved, SM/tensor-core utilization, power and clocks (thermal or power capping silently changes TPOT).

Design emphasis: the harness must be able to change one factor at a time (batch policy, max_num_seqs, chunked-prefill on/off) without changing the workload trace.

Expected confounders: (a) prefill/decode interference - a large prefill inflates TPOT of unrelated in-flight sequences unless chunked prefill bounds it; (b) KV-cache pressure causing preemption/recompute, which shows as bimodal TTFT; (c) client-side bottleneck (single-threaded client, TLS, tokenizer on the hot path) masquerading as server latency - validate by running the client on a second host; (d) power/thermal drift over long runs; (e) other tenants on the same node or NIC; (f) completion bias in the percentile window.

Rollback / stop criteria (pre-agreed, not negotiated after the fact): revert the configuration if TTFT p99 regresses >20% versus baseline, or if preemption rate >1% of requests, or if any request errors/timeouts appear above the baseline rate, or if the throughput gain is inside the trial-to-trial CI. Roll back by config flag only - keep the previous engine build deployed so rollback is a restart, not a rebuild.

Evidence needed before claiming a win: the raw per-request trace files, the config diff, the GPU counters for the same window, and the >=3-trial variance. Absent those, any single-number improvement is an estimate, not a measured fact.

A service receives a mix of short prompts and long generations. Design an evaluation plan that reports TTFT, TPOT, throughput, queueing, and P99 latency. Scenario variant 273: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.

Scenario variant 273 — evaluation plan for a mixed short-prompt / long-generation LLM serving endpoint.

Analysis lens: treat the mixed short-prompt/long-generation workload as two coupled queues (prefill-bound and decode-bound) sharing one KV-cache budget; the metric of record is where the P99 tail is manufactured, not the mean.

1. Assumptions (state them, they bound every number below)
- Single model replica class, continuous batching (vLLM-style) with paged KV cache; no speculative decoding unless declared as a separate arm.
- Closed-loop clients with a fixed concurrency ladder, not open-loop Poisson, unless the production traffic is genuinely open — the two produce different queueing tails and are not comparable.
- Tokenizer is fixed; all token counts are measured with the serving tokenizer, never estimated from characters.
- Hardware, driver, CUDA, and serving-engine versions are pinned and recorded per run; a version delta invalidates cross-run comparison.

2. Metric definitions (ambiguity here is the most common source of bogus results)
- TTFT = wall clock from request admission at the HTTP/gRPC boundary to first streamed token. Record client-side and server-side separately; the gap is queueing + network.
- TPOT = (end-to-end latency - TTFT) / (generated_tokens - 1), per request, then aggregated. Never derive it from a global token/s counter.
- Throughput reported as three separate numbers: prefill tokens/s, decode tokens/s, and completed requests/s. A single "tokens/s" figure hides the prefill-decode tradeoff.
- Queueing delay = time in scheduler waiting queue before first forward pass, exported by the engine, not inferred.
- P99 latency reported per workload class (short-prompt-short-gen, short-prompt-long-gen, long-prompt-long-gen) — pooled P99 across classes is meaningless because the mixture ratio dominates it.

3. Falsifiable hypothesis
H1: "Under the production mixture, P99 TTFT degradation above 60% concurrency is caused by prefill chunking limits (long generations holding KV blocks and shrinking the admissible prefill batch), not by raw GPU compute saturation."
Prediction if H1 is true: increasing max_num_batched_tokens (chunked prefill budget) at constant KV-cache size moves P99 TTFT down by a measurable margin while decode TPOT rises, and GPU SM occupancy during the TTFT spike is below saturation.
Prediction if H1 is false: P99 TTFT is flat under that change and SM occupancy is pegged near saturation during spikes — the bottleneck is compute, and the fix is replica scaling or quantization, not scheduler tuning.
H1 is refuted by either the flat-TTFT observation or the saturated-occupancy observation; both are recorded automatically.

4. Controlled experiment
- Factor A: chunked-prefill token budget (3 levels). Factor B: max concurrent sequences / KV-cache utilization cap (3 levels). Factor C: mixture ratio of long generations (2 levels: production ratio, and 2x long-generation share as a stress arm).
- Full factorial where affordable, otherwise a screening design with the production point replicated; randomize run order to de-confound thermal drift.
- 5 minutes warmup discarded, then >=3 independent repeats per cell on separate process starts. Report median and the spread across repeats; a cell whose repeat spread exceeds the effect size is reported as inconclusive, not as a result.
- Fixed request corpus with a frozen seed so prompt lengths and generation lengths are identical across arms; max_tokens forced rather than left to EOS, otherwise the arms differ in work, not in scheduling.

5. Confounders to control explicitly
- Prefix caching / KV reuse silently reducing prefill work on repeated corpora — either disable it or report cache hit rate per arm.
- Client-side bottlenecks (single-threaded tokenizer, HTTP connection limits) masquerading as server latency; validate with a no-op echo endpoint at the same concurrency.
- GPU clock throttling and ECC/thermal drift over long sweeps; log clocks and temperature per run.
- Cross-tenant interference if the GPU is shared (MPS/MIG or other processes); require exclusive placement for the record runs.
- Autoscaler or load-balancer behavior changing replica count mid-run.

6. Instrumentation and evidence to collect
- Per-request trace: arrival, admission, first token, completion, prompt_tokens, generated_tokens, scheduler queue depth at admission.
- Engine counters: running/waiting sequence counts, KV-cache utilization, preemption/recompute events, chunked-prefill batch composition.
- GPU: memory in use vs reserved, SM occupancy/achieved FLOPs sample, NVLink/PCIe traffic if tensor-parallel.
- Nsight Systems or engine-native profile on one representative cell only — profiling perturbs timing and must not be part of the record runs.

7. Rollback / decision gates
- Ship a scheduler change only if P99 TTFT improves by more than the measured repeat-to-repeat spread AND P99 end-to-end latency for the long-generation class does not regress beyond the SLO budget.
- Canary at <=5% of traffic for at least one full diurnal cycle; automatic rollback on P99 TTFT above the pre-change baseline, on any preemption-rate increase, or on OOM/KV-eviction events appearing where the baseline had none.
- Keep the previous engine configuration as a single-flag revert; no partial migrations.

8. Reporting
Publish the workload manifest, engine version, config matrix, raw per-request traces, and the aggregation script. A result without the raw traces is not reproducible and should be treated as provisional.

2. Metric definitions (ambiguity here is the most common source of bogus results)
- TTFT = wall clock from request admission at the HTTP/gRPC boundary to first streamed token. Record client-side and server-side separately; the gap is queueing + network.

H2 (secondary): "Enabling chunked prefill reduces P99 TTFT under mixed load by >=20% at equal throughput, at the cost of <=10% TPOT regression." Falsified if TPOT regresses more than 10% or TTFT gain is within trial noise.

- TTFT = arrival timestamp at the front door (not engine admission) to first streamed token. Measuring from engine admission hides queueing and is the single most common benchmarking error.

- Fix the workload distribution: a frozen request trace (seeded input/output length pairs sampled from the production distribution) replayed identically across arms. Do not let the client sample fresh lengths per arm - that confounds arm with workload.
- Open-loop Poisson arrivals at fixed request rates, sweeping rate, not a closed-loop fixed-concurrency client. Closed-loop clients self-throttle and structurally hide queueing, which is exactly the variable under test.
- Warmup: discard the first 60-120s (CUDA graph capture, torch.compile, KV allocator steady state, autotuner) and confirm steady state by a flat rolling-median TTFT before counting.
- >=3 repeated trials per cell, arms interleaved (A,B,A,B) rather than blocked, to absorb thermal and clock drift.
- One variable per arm; changing batch policy and tensor-parallel degree together makes the result uninterpretable.

- Engine scheduler counters: running/waiting/swapped queue depths, preemption count, cache hit rate for prefix caching.
- If multi-GPU/multi-node: NCCL collective time (NCCL_DEBUG=INFO once, then off), interconnect counters - NVLink/PCIe for intra-node, RoCE/IB port counters for inter-node, plus PFC pause and ECN-marked packet counts. - Tokenizer differences making token counts non-comparable across arms.
- Noisy neighbours, MIG/MPS partitioning, and power/thermal capping.
- Coordinated omission from closed-loop load generators.

- Ship only if: P99 TTFT and P99 E2E improve or hold within the pre-registered non-inferiority margin (e.g. <=5%) at the target rate, with non-overlapping bootstrap CIs across >=3 trials, and no increase in preemption or error rate.
- Roll back immediately if: error/timeout rate rises above baseline+0.1pp, OOM or preemption events appear, P99 TTFT regresses >10%, or goodput drops >5%.
- Canary at <=5% traffic for >=1 hour covering a peak window before full rollout; keep the previous engine config loadable so rollback is a config flip, not a rebuild.

Report per-arm tables of TTFT/TPOT/E2E at P50/P90/P99 plus goodput, each with CI and trial count, alongside the frozen trace hash, engine version, and full config diff. Any number without workload trace + version + trial count attached is not reproducible and should not be used for a capacity decision.

- Open-loop, Poisson arrivals at a fixed target rate lambda. A closed-loop client with fixed concurrency suffers coordinated omission: when the server slows, the client stops offering load and P99 is structurally understated.

A long-context workload intermittently hits OOM after several concurrent requests. Give a prioritized diagnosis and mitigations. Scenario variant 1: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.

Scope: intermittent OOM on a long-context workload appearing only after several concurrent requests. Scenario variant 1. Emphasis: the durable fix is admission control and an explicit memory budget, not one-off flag tuning.

0) Assumptions
- Single-node or TP-sharded deployment on a paged-attention engine (vLLM/SGLang class). Model dtype, TP degree, max_model_len, max_num_seqs and gpu_memory_utilization are known and recorded.
- "Intermittent, after several concurrent requests" is the key signal: it points at a demand-side term that scales with concurrency x sequence length (KV cache and activation peaks), not at a fixed weight-loading error. A deterministic OOM at startup would be a different failure class.

1) Mechanism: where the memory goes
Total = weights + KV cache pool + activation/workspace peak + fragmentation + non-torch allocations (NCCL buffers, CUDA graphs, cuBLAS workspace, comm buffers).
Per-token KV bytes = 2 (K and V) x num_layers x num_kv_heads x head_dim x bytes_per_element.
Per-request KV = per-token bytes x (prompt_len + generated_len). Under TP, KV heads are sharded, so per-GPU KV is divided by TP degree only when num_kv_heads is divisible by TP; GQA with few KV heads often replicates instead, which silently doubles or quadruples the expected per-GPU footprint. Compute this number explicitly for the deployed config — a large fraction of "mysterious" long-context OOM is arithmetic that was never done.
Note the concurrency coupling: the pool is sized once at startup, so OOM appearing only under concurrency usually means either (a) the paged pool is exhausted and the engine should preempt but a non-paged allocation is racing it, or (b) the true OOM is in the activation/workspace peak during a large prefill batch, not in the KV pool at all.

H1 (alternative): the OOM is KV-pool exhaustion or fragmentation. Prediction: capping prefill tokens does NOT help, while lowering max_num_seqs or raising the pool does.
These make opposite predictions under the same intervention, so one experiment discriminates them.

- Replay a fixed trace that reproduces the OOM within a bounded time (record trace hash and reproduction rate over >= 5 runs; if reproduction is < 100%, all conclusions need the same repetition count).
- Arm A: baseline. Arm B: max_num_batched_tokens = 4096, everything else identical. Arm C: max_num_seqs halved, everything else identical.
- One factor per arm; >= 5 replays per arm; report OOM occurrence rate with a binomial CI, not a single pass/fail.
- Instrument torch.cuda.memory_stats() (allocated, reserved, active, inactive_split) and dump a memory snapshot at the failing step.

1. Compute the KV budget arithmetically and compare with the pool actually allocated. Fix a wrong max_model_len or a GQA/TP sharding assumption. Zero risk, config-only.

5. Verify prefix/paged cache is actually on and that block size and eviction are sane; a disabled paged cache reintroduces contiguous per-request allocation.
6. Lower max_model_len or max_num_seqs to a value the budget arithmetic supports. This is a capability reduction and needs product sign-off.

- Other processes on the same GPU (MPS, monitoring, a stale worker) consuming memory -> check nvidia-smi per-process usage.
- CUDA graph capture reserving memory after warmup, so the first OOM appears minutes in.
- NCCL/comm buffers growing with TP degree and message size (multi-node).
- Memory growth from a leak in the request path, distinguishable because it rises monotonically across runs rather than tracking concurrency.
- Preemption/recompute masking the problem as a latency spike in some runs and an OOM in others.

6) Evidence required
Per-request prompt/generation lengths at failure, KV blocks free/used over time, torch memory snapshot at the failing step, engine preemption counters, nvidia-smi per-process memory, engine config dump, and the reproduction rate over >= 5 replays.

7) Rollback criteria
Any mitigation ships behind a canary at <= 5% traffic. Auto-rollback if OOM recurs at all, if P99 TTFT worsens > 15%, or if rejection rate exceeds 0.5%. Steps 6 and 7 additionally require an accuracy/functional gate because they change model behaviour, not just resource limits.

Scope: intermittent OOM on a long-context LLM serving deployment that only manifests after several concurrent requests. Intermittency is the key signal: a deterministic allocation bug would fail on the first request, so the failure is a function of aggregate concurrent state (KV-cache working set, activation peaks of the largest scheduled batch, and allocator fragmentation), not of any single request. Assumptions stated up front: single-node inference engine with paged KV cache, static weights, CUDA caching allocator, no other tenants on the GPUs; if any of these is false the ranking below changes and must be re-derived.

Mechanism. GPU memory at steady state = weights + optimizer-free runtime buffers + CUDA/NCCL context and communication buffers + activation peak of the currently scheduled batch + KV cache pool. Only the last two scale with concurrency. KV bytes = 2 (K and V) * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes * total_tokens; with GQA the kv_heads term is much smaller than attention heads, so long context, not head count, dominates. Because the engine preallocates a KV pool, true KV exhaustion should present as preemption/queueing, not OOM. An actual OOM therefore points to memory outside the pool: transient activation peaks (prefill of a long prompt, chunked-prefill boundary, logits tensor of vocab*batch), fragmentation of the non-pool arena, or a pool sized from an optimistic profiling run.

Primary falsifiable hypothesis (H1): the OOM is caused by the transient activation peak of concurrent long prefills, not by KV-cache exhaustion; if true, memory_reserved spikes at prefill boundaries while KV blocks in use stays below the pool ceiling.

Controlled experiment. Freeze one replayable trace captured at failure time (request arrival timestamps, input_len, output_len) and hash it; replay it against a dedicated replica with identical weights, engine version and driver. Run A = current config. Run B = single variable changed: enable chunked prefill with a fixed chunk size so no single scheduler step prefills more than a bounded token count. Hold everything else fixed, run each arm three times in alternating order to absorb thermal and page-cache drift. H1 is refuted if run B shows the same OOM at the same trace offset within run-to-run variance; it is supported only if B survives the full trace AND the instrumented metric moves in the predicted direction. A latency-only improvement is not evidence.

Prioritized mitigations, cheapest and most reversible first.
1. Admission control: cap max_num_seqs and max_num_batched_tokens so the worst-case scheduled batch is bounded rather than emergent. This trades throughput for a hard memory ceiling and is instantly revertible.

3. Lower the KV pool utilization fraction (e.g. 0.90 -> 0.85) to leave explicit headroom for activation peaks. Costs concurrency linearly in the freed fraction.
4. Enable chunked prefill so a long prompt is processed in bounded token chunks, capping the activation peak independent of prompt length.
5. Enable prefix/prompt caching only if the trace shows real shared prefixes; otherwise it adds memory without reducing peak.
6. Set an expandable-segments allocator policy to let the arena grow/shrink instead of fragmenting.
7. KV quantization (fp8) or a smaller-KV model variant. This is last because it changes numerics and requires a quality re-evaluation, not just a latency check.

Expected confounders: autoscaling or replica restarts mid-experiment change the traffic each replica sees; NVML reports process-level memory that includes the caching allocator's unreturned blocks, so nvidia-smi will look flat even while the arena fragments; and a warm page cache makes the first replay artificially faster.

Roll back immediately on any OOM, on >10 percent p99 regression, or on preemption rate exceeding 2 percent of requests. Keep the previous config in the deployment manifest so rollback is a single revert, not a rebuild.

Explicitly out of scope: this is a memory-headroom and admission-control problem. Adding GPUs or replicas raises aggregate capacity but does not bound the per-replica peak, so it can mask the defect while leaving the tail failure mode intact.

4. 1. With tensor parallelism the KV cache is sharded across ranks, but the NCCL communicator, its buffers, and CUDA graphs are per-rank overhead that does not shrink. On 24GB cards this overhead is a material fraction and is commonly left out of capacity math.

3. Check that the OOM is not a secondary symptom of a hang: a stuck collective can keep memory pinned while new requests continue to be admitted. Correlate with NCCL timeout logs before concluding it is capacity.

H1: memory is imbalanced across ranks by >15%, and rank-0 is the consistent OOM victim.

Controlled experiment

Expected confounders
TP changes compute efficiency and communication volume simultaneously, so latency comparisons across TP degrees are not clean; restrict the claim to memory. NVLink vs PCIe topology changes collective cost substantially and must be recorded (topology matrix) alongside results.

Choose TP so that kv_heads is divisible by the degree; move sampling buffers off the critical rank; pin NCCL buffer sizes explicitly; reduce concurrency to the per-rank budget.

Multi-GPU angle: with tensor parallelism the OOM is per-rank, and per-rank asymmetry is a common and often missed cause.

Prioritized diagnosis
1. Aggregate KV demand exceeds per-rank pool. KV is sharded across TP ranks by kv_heads, so per-rank kv_bytes_per_token = total / tp_degree only if kv_heads is divisible by tp_degree. With grouped-query attention and a kv_heads count that does not divide evenly, some ranks carry more heads and OOM first. This produces exactly the intermittent, one-rank-crashes-the-server symptom.
2. Rank 0 asymmetry: sampling, logits, and often the tokenizer/scheduler state live on or near rank 0, giving it a larger non-KV footprint.
3. NCCL communication buffers: each rank holds registered buffers whose size depends on the collective sizes and on NCCL_BUFFSIZE; these are outside the framework allocator and reduce the pool invisibly.
4. General capacity and fragmentation as in the single-GPU case.

Falsifiable hypothesis
H6: OOM is rank-asymmetric. Prediction: across 10 induced failures, more than 80% originate on the same rank, and that rank shows persistently higher reserved memory (>5% gap) at identical load.
Refutation: uniformly distributed failure ranks and a per-rank reserved-memory spread under 2% kill H6; the cause is then symmetric capacity.

Controlled experiment
Instrument per-rank reserved/allocated memory at 1 Hz. Ramp concurrency to failure 10 times, cold restart between runs, record the failing rank each time. Independently compute kv_heads mod tp_degree and NCCL buffer footprint from the config. One variable at a time: repeat with tp_degree changed to a divisor of kv_heads if the modulus is non-zero.

Expected confounders
The rank that reports the error is not always the rank that ran out (a collective can surface the failure elsewhere) — trust the per-rank memory trace, not the traceback location. NUMA/PCIe topology affecting which rank also hosts other work. Persistent NCCL buffers allocated lazily on the first collective, so early samples understate the footprint.

1. Choose tp_degree that divides kv_heads.
2. Size the KV pool from the worst-case rank, not the average.
3. Bound NCCL buffer memory explicitly and account for it in the capacity model.
4. Admission control on projected tokens, as always.

Rollback criteria
Changing tp_degree changes throughput and latency materially, so it goes through a canary with a pre-registered p99 and tokens/sec envelope; revert if either regresses beyond 15%. Any NCCL tuning that increases collective latency beyond the measured baseline is reverted.

Evidence required
Per-rank memory traces at matched load, the failing-rank histogram over 10 induced failures, the kv_heads/tp_degree arithmetic, and before/after throughput at fixed p99.

1. In an aggregated engine, long prefill and steady decode share one memory pool, so a burst of long prompts starves decode and OOMs. This is the default hypothesis.
2. In a disaggregated deployment, the failure moves: prefill workers OOM on activation peaks, decode workers OOM on KV accumulation, and the KV transfer path itself (RDMA-registered staging buffers) holds pinned memory that is not visible to the framework allocator.
3. KV-cache offload tiers (host DRAM, NVMe via GDS) reduce device pressure but add pinned-host-memory and bandwidth constraints; an offload path that cannot keep up silently backs up into device memory.

H7: prefill/decode interference is the mechanism. Prediction: running the same total load with prefill and decode separated (either disaggregated workers, or chunked prefill in one engine) eliminates OOM at loads that previously failed, at equal or better p99 TTFT.

Three arms, same model/dtype/version: (A) baseline aggregated, (B) aggregated with chunked prefill, (C) disaggregated prefill/decode if available. 2. Admission control on projected tokens.

Disaggregation reverts if p99 TTFT regresses >20%, if KV transfer becomes the bottleneck (transfer time > 30% of TTFT), or if any new failure mode (transfer timeout, worker desync) appears in canary. Cause to measurement map
Aggregate KV capacity -> engine-reported KV blocks used vs total at the moment of failure.
Prefill activation spike -> peak reserved memory during a single long-prompt request at batch 1.
Fragmentation -> failing allocation size in the OOM traceback versus reserved memory.
Leak -> reserved memory slope at constant load over 2 hours.
Co-tenancy -> process list on the device.
Per-rank asymmetry -> per-rank reserved memory spread at identical load.

5. Co-tenancy. Discriminating evidence: another process on the device.

H10: exactly one of the five causes accounts for >80% of observed OOMs. Prediction: classifying 20 captured OOM events by the discriminating evidence above puts more than 16 into a single bucket.

Do not experiment yet. Scenario variant 73.

Assumptions (state before acting): single-node LLM serving (vLLM/TGI-class engine) with paged KV cache; homogeneous GPUs; OOM is CUDA out-of-memory on the device, not host RAM; the workload is long-context (prompt >= 8k tokens) and failures appear only after several concurrent requests, i.e. the failure is load-dependent, not single-request-dependent. If any assumption is false (e.g. host OOM, MIG partitioning, multi-tenant GPU sharing), stop and re-scope.

Mechanism. Steady-state GPU memory = weights + activation/workspace peak + KV cache + allocator fragmentation + CUDA/NCCL context. Weights are constant; KV cache scales as 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes * sum(seq_len over active sequences). With paged KV, growth is in block granularity, so admitted concurrency times average context length is the dominant term. Intermittency is the signature: the scheduler admits a batch whose projected KV plus transient prefill activation exceeds free memory only for certain arrival patterns. Prefill of a long prompt also allocates a large transient attention/logits workspace that is not accounted for in the KV budget, so an OOM often lands at admission of the Nth long request, not at decode.

Falsifiable hypothesis H1: OOM is caused by KV-cache admission overcommit — i.e. peak resident KV blocks plus prefill workspace exceed the free pool — and NOT by allocator fragmentation. Prediction: if H1 holds, capping max concurrent sequences (or max_num_batched_tokens) so that worst-case KV blocks <= 85% of the KV pool eliminates OOM with zero change in fragmentation metrics; and reserved-minus-allocated bytes at the crash point stays below ~10% of reserved.
Competing hypothesis H2 (fragmentation): reserved memory stays high while allocated drops, and OOM occurs with large free-but-unusable reserved bytes (>20% of reserved). H2 predicts that setting PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True materially raises the failure threshold while concurrency caps do not.
H1 and H2 make opposite predictions on the reserved-vs-allocated gap, so one experiment discriminates them.

Controlled experiment. Fix model, dtype, GPU count, and engine version. Replay a captured trace at fixed input-length distribution; sweep concurrency 1,2,4,8,16 with 3 repeats each, randomized order. At each step record: torch.cuda.memory_allocated / memory_reserved / max_memory_reserved, engine KV-cache utilization (gpu_cache_usage_perc), num_running/num_waiting sequences, preemption/recompute counts, and nvidia-smi used MiB. Identify the concurrency at which OOM first appears (C*). Then run two arms against C*: (A) concurrency cap at 0.7*C*, (B) expandable_segments allocator at original concurrency. Arm A fixing it and arm B not => H1. Arm B fixing it and arm A not => H2. Both failing => a third cause (see confounders).

Prioritized diagnosis, cheapest and most reversible first:
1. Read engine config actually in effect: max_model_len, max_num_seqs, max_num_batched_tokens, gpu_memory_utilization, enable_prefix_caching, chunked prefill on/off. Misconfiguration is the most common root cause and costs nothing to check.
2. Inspect live active sequences and their lengths at crash time; confirm the long tail of context length rather than a mean shift.
3. Measure per-request KV growth empirically (KV bytes per 1k tokens) and compute worst-case = max_num_seqs * max_model_len; compare to the KV pool size.
4. Check the reserved-minus-allocated gap for fragmentation (distinguishes H1 from H2).
5. Rule out non-KV consumers: another process on the same device, CUDA graph capture memory, LoRA adapters, or logits buffers scaling with vocab * batch.

Mitigations, ordered by risk. (a) Admission control: lower max_num_seqs and max_num_batched_tokens, and enforce a request-level max context; fully reversible, costs throughput. (b) Enable chunked prefill so long prompts do not create a single large transient workspace; moderate risk, changes latency profile. (c) Enable prefix caching if prompts share long system prefixes; reduces KV pressure but only if the sharing hypothesis is measured, not assumed. (d) Set expandable_segments:True if the fragmentation gap is real. (e) Lower gpu_memory_utilization slightly to enlarge headroom — this is a symptom-level buffer, not a fix. (f) KV quantization (fp8) or a smaller max_model_len — real capacity gain but changes output quality, so it needs a quality gate. (g) Tensor parallelism or a larger GPU — capital change, last resort.

Confounders to control: engine version differences in the memory profiler; background processes on the same device; prefix-cache hit rate drifting between arms; nondeterministic arrival timing; thermal/clock variation affecting timing but not memory; CUDA graph capture inflating baseline once at warmup.

Evidence required before declaring root cause: crash-time allocator snapshot, KV utilization time series, concurrency-vs-OOM curve with repeats, and the A/B arm result. A single reproduction is not sufficient because the failure is intermittent.

Rollback gate: apply one change at a time behind a config flag. Promote only if, over a 30-minute replay at production concurrency, OOM count is 0 and p95 latency regression is under 10% and throughput regression is under 15%. Roll back immediately if OOM recurs, if p95 exceeds the SLO, or if preemption/recompute counts rise more than 2x versus baseline. Keep the previous config pinned and revertible in one step.

Operational safety: do not raise gpu_memory_utilization toward 1.0 to 'buy room' — it removes the margin that absorbs transient prefill spikes and converts intermittent OOM into hard crashes. Do not change several knobs at once; you lose attribution. Do not restart the server to clear symptoms before capturing the allocator snapshot.

Uncertainty: without the actual engine, model dimensions, and trace, the numeric thresholds above are estimates, not measured facts.

Design emphasis: make capacity explicit in the architecture — budget KV pool size from an SLO-derived worst case (max_concurrency * max_context), enforce context limits at the gateway, and separate long-context traffic into its own pool or replica class so a long-context tail cannot evict short-request capacity. Prefill/decode disaggregation is worth evaluating only after the single-pool budget is proven insufficient.

Scenario variant 75.

Assumptions (state before acting): single-node LLM serving (vLLM/TGI-class engine) with paged KV cache; homogeneous GPUs; OOM is CUDA out-of-memory on the device, not host RAM; the workload is long-context (prompt >= 8k tokens) and failures appear only after several concurrent requests, i.e. the failure is load-dependent, not single-request-dependent. If any assumption is false (e.g. host OOM, MIG partitioning, multi-tenant GPU sharing), stop and re-scope.

Mechanism. Steady-state GPU memory = weights + activation/workspace peak + KV cache + allocator fragmentation + CUDA/NCCL context. Weights are constant; KV cache scales as 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes * sum(seq_len over active sequences). With paged KV, growth is in block granularity, so admitted concurrency times average context length is the dominant term. Intermittency is the signature: the scheduler admits a batch whose projected KV plus transient prefill activation exceeds free memory only for certain arrival patterns. Prefill of a long prompt also allocates a large transient attention/logits workspace that is not accounted for in the KV budget, so an OOM often lands at admission of the Nth long request, not at decode.

Falsifiable hypothesis H1: OOM is caused by KV-cache admission overcommit — i.e. peak resident KV blocks plus prefill workspace exceed the free pool — and NOT by allocator fragmentation. Prediction: if H1 holds, capping max concurrent sequences (or max_num_batched_tokens) so that worst-case KV blocks <= 85% of the KV pool eliminates OOM with zero change in fragmentation metrics; and reserved-minus-allocated bytes at the crash point stays below ~10% of reserved.
Competing hypothesis H2 (fragmentation): reserved memory stays high while allocated drops, and OOM occurs with large free-but-unusable reserved bytes (>20% of reserved). H2 predicts that setting PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True materially raises the failure threshold while concurrency caps do not.
H1 and H2 make opposite predictions on the reserved-vs-allocated gap, so one experiment discriminates them.

Controlled experiment. Fix model, dtype, GPU count, and engine version. Replay a captured trace at fixed input-length distribution; sweep concurrency 1,2,4,8,16 with 3 repeats each, randomized order. At each step record: torch.cuda.memory_allocated / memory_reserved / max_memory_reserved, engine KV-cache utilization (gpu_cache_usage_perc), num_running/num_waiting sequences, preemption/recompute counts, and nvidia-smi used MiB. Identify the concurrency at which OOM first appears (C*). Then run two arms against C*: (A) concurrency cap at 0.7*C*, (B) expandable_segments allocator at original concurrency. Arm A fixing it and arm B not => H1. Arm B fixing it and arm A not => H2. Both failing => a third cause (see confounders).

Prioritized diagnosis, cheapest and most reversible first:
1. Read engine config actually in effect: max_model_len, max_num_seqs, max_num_batched_tokens, gpu_memory_utilization, enable_prefix_caching, chunked prefill on/off. Misconfiguration is the most common root cause and costs nothing to check.
2. Inspect live active sequences and their lengths at crash time; confirm the long tail of context length rather than a mean shift.
3. Measure per-request KV growth empirically (KV bytes per 1k tokens) and compute worst-case = max_num_seqs * max_model_len; compare to the KV pool size.
4. Check the reserved-minus-allocated gap for fragmentation (distinguishes H1 from H2).
5. Rule out non-KV consumers: another process on the same device, CUDA graph capture memory, LoRA adapters, or logits buffers scaling with vocab * batch.

Mitigations, ordered by risk. (a) Admission control: lower max_num_seqs and max_num_batched_tokens, and enforce a request-level max context; fully reversible, costs throughput. (b) Enable chunked prefill so long prompts do not create a single large transient workspace; moderate risk, changes latency profile. (c) Enable prefix caching if prompts share long system prefixes; reduces KV pressure but only if the sharing hypothesis is measured, not assumed. (d) Set expandable_segments:True if the fragmentation gap is real. (e) Lower gpu_memory_utilization slightly to enlarge headroom — this is a symptom-level buffer, not a fix. (f) KV quantization (fp8) or a smaller max_model_len — real capacity gain but changes output quality, so it needs a quality gate. (g) Tensor parallelism or a larger GPU — capital change, last resort.

Confounders to control: engine version differences in the memory profiler; background processes on the same device; prefix-cache hit rate drifting between arms; nondeterministic arrival timing; thermal/clock variation affecting timing but not memory; CUDA graph capture inflating baseline once at warmup.

Evidence required before declaring root cause: crash-time allocator snapshot, KV utilization time series, concurrency-vs-OOM curve with repeats, and the A/B arm result. A single reproduction is not sufficient because the failure is intermittent.

Rollback gate: apply one change at a time behind a config flag. Promote only if, over a 30-minute replay at production concurrency, OOM count is 0 and p95 latency regression is under 10% and throughput regression is under 15%. Roll back immediately if OOM recurs, if p95 exceeds the SLO, or if preemption/recompute counts rise more than 2x versus baseline. Keep the previous config pinned and revertible in one step.

Operational safety: do not raise gpu_memory_utilization toward 1.0 to 'buy room' — it removes the margin that absorbs transient prefill spikes and converts intermittent OOM into hard crashes. Do not change several knobs at once; you lose attribution. Do not restart the server to clear symptoms before capturing the allocator snapshot.

Uncertainty: without the actual engine, model dimensions, and trace, the numeric thresholds above are estimates, not measured facts.

Performance-analysis emphasis: express the result as a capacity curve — admitted concurrency vs KV bytes and vs p95 TTFT/TPOT — and identify the knee. Report goodput (requests meeting SLO), not raw throughput, because admission control trades throughput for stability. Attribute time between prefill and decode before optimizing either.
