Mechanism. Weight-only quantization (WOQ) reduces the BYTES OF WEIGHTS READ PER FORWARD PASS. It therefore helps only where the kernel is memory-bandwidth bound, which in LLM serving means small-batch autoregressive decode. Prefill is compute bound; dequantization adds arithmetic there, so TTFT is flat or slightly worse. As batch size rises, decode GEMMs become compute bound too and the advantage decays monotonically toward 1.0x. Any claim of a uniform speedup across the concurrency range is mechanically wrong and should be treated as an instrumentation bug until explained.

Byte-count ceiling (ESTIMATE, derivation inline, not a throughput result). A 9B-parameter model in BF16 is 9e9 x 2 B = 18 GB of weights. INT4 with group-128 FP16 scale and zero point costs about 0.5 + ~0.06 B/param, i.e. ~5.0-5.3 GB. Ratio ~3.2-3.6x. This is pure byte counting with no kernel-efficiency model and no attention or KV traffic included; it is an upper bound on batch-1 decode speedup ONLY. Applying Amdahl with a decode-weight-read fraction f: f=0.4 bounds end-to-end gain near 1.33x, f=0.8 near 2.1x (ESTIMATE).

Mandatory two-arm-plus-one design. Run the quantized configuration TWICE: (a) with KV cache block count clamped to the BF16 baseline's block count, which isolates the kernel/bandwidth effect; (b) at native capacity, which shows the deployable benefit. Freed HBM becomes additional KV blocks and raises throughput by batching alone. If the clamped arm is flat, the honest conclusion is "we bought KV headroom", and tuning KV settings on the BF16 arm must be priced as the cheaper alternative before shipping a second numeric path.

Arm identity is frozen and hashed. Checkpoint hash, bit width, group size, symmetric/asymmetric, outlier or mixed-precision policy, calibration dataset hash, library and engine build, TP/PP layout, activation precision, KV precision, block size, max_num_seqs, max_model_len, chunked-prefill state, speculative-decoding state. The configuration symmetric difference between arms must be exactly the bit-width fields; anything else invalidates the comparison. Weight-only means weight-only: "INT4 plus FP8 KV" is two experiments, and the KV change usually explains most of the throughput delta while none of the quality delta gets attributed correctly.

Comparison point. Compare arms at the intersection of each arm's own latency-throughput frontier with the p95 SLO, never at a fixed batch size; the two arms have different optimal batch sizes, and fixed-batch comparison is the single most common way these studies mislead. Cost unit is GPU-seconds per 1,000 output tokens at that fixed p95 SLO, converted to currency last.

Measurement protocol. At least five concurrency points, at least three repeats per point, steady state with a fixed warmup-exclusion rule, greedy decoding and fixed seed for quality, bootstrap 95% CIs on ABSOLUTE quality deltas. Quality is sliced: long context, structured/JSON output, code, math, safety and refusal behaviour; aggregate scores can stay flat while repetition or truncation degrades, so sampled side-by-side output diffs are part of the evidence, not a nicety. A BF16-vs-BF16 A/A control across seeds and physical GPUs establishes the noise floor that any claimed delta must clear.

Confounders to control and report. Autotune cache warmth; clock and thermal drift over long runs; asymmetric telemetry overhead; prefill/decode mix drift between arms; silent kernel fallback to a dequantize-then-GEMM path (dump per-layer kernel names and timings and diff the arms - a null result with a fallback in the logs is a tooling defect, not a verdict on the method); calibration-set leakage into the eval set, disproved by hash comparison; library defaults silently changing group size across versions.

Evidence required before any decision. Per-request raw records (arrival, TTFT, per-token timestamps, output length, status); per-layer kernel name and achieved-bandwidth traces for both arms; the arm configuration manifest with hashes; per-slice quality scores with CIs plus raw generations; the HBM ledger with KV blocks as the residual and a measured high-water mark; the A/A noise-floor numbers; and matched-window fleet GPU-hour and token accounting, because benchmarks propose and production billing disposes.

Rollback gates, pre-committed. Revert if p95 TTFT or TPOT exceeds SLO at target concurrency; if any eval slice falls more than 1.0 point absolute with a 95% CI excluding zero; if structured-output compliance falls more than 2 points; if measured cost improvement is under 25%; if preemption or recompute rates rise without explanation; or if kernel-fallback evidence appears, in which case fix the tooling and re-run rather than concluding anything. Keep the BF16 arm warm and routable throughout so rollback is a routing flip rather than a redeploy, and rehearse the revert once before the canary.

Mechanism. Weight-only quantization (WOQ) reduces the BYTES OF WEIGHTS READ PER FORWARD PASS. It therefore helps only where the kernel is memory-bandwidth bound, which in LLM serving means small-batch autoregressive decode. Prefill is compute bound; dequantization adds arithmetic there, so TTFT is flat or slightly worse. As batch size rises, decode GEMMs become compute bound too and the advantage decays monotonically toward 1.0x. Any claim of a uniform speedup across the concurrency range is mechanically wrong and should be treated as an instrumentation bug until explained.

Byte-count ceiling (ESTIMATE, derivation inline, not a throughput result). A 9B-parameter model in BF16 is 9e9 x 2 B = 18 GB of weights. INT4 with group-128 FP16 scale and zero point costs about 0.5 + ~0.06 B/param, i.e. ~5.0-5.3 GB. Ratio ~3.2-3.6x. This is pure byte counting with no kernel-efficiency model and no attention or KV traffic included; it is an upper bound on batch-1 decode speedup ONLY. Applying Amdahl with a decode-weight-read fraction f: f=0.4 bounds end-to-end gain near 1.33x, f=0.8 near 2.1x (ESTIMATE).

Mandatory two-arm-plus-one design. Run the quantized configuration TWICE: (a) with KV cache block count clamped to the BF16 baseline's block count, which isolates the kernel/bandwidth effect; (b) at native capacity, which shows the deployable benefit. Freed HBM becomes additional KV blocks and raises throughput by batching alone. If the clamped arm is flat, the honest conclusion is "we bought KV headroom", and tuning KV settings on the BF16 arm must be priced as the cheaper alternative before shipping a second numeric path.

Arm identity is frozen and hashed. Checkpoint hash, bit width, group size, symmetric/asymmetric, outlier or mixed-precision policy, calibration dataset hash, library and engine build, TP/PP layout, activation precision, KV precision, block size, max_num_seqs, max_model_len, chunked-prefill state, speculative-decoding state. The configuration symmetric difference between arms must be exactly the bit-width fields; anything else invalidates the comparison. Weight-only means weight-only: "INT4 plus FP8 KV" is two experiments, and the KV change usually explains most of the throughput delta while none of the quality delta gets attributed correctly.

Comparison point. Compare arms at the intersection of each arm's own latency-throughput frontier with the p95 SLO, never at a fixed batch size; the two arms have different optimal batch sizes, and fixed-batch comparison is the single most common way these studies mislead. Cost unit is GPU-seconds per 1,000 output tokens at that fixed p95 SLO, converted to currency last.

Measurement protocol. At least five concurrency points, at least three repeats per point, steady state with a fixed warmup-exclusion rule, greedy decoding and fixed seed for quality, bootstrap 95% CIs on ABSOLUTE quality deltas. Quality is sliced: long context, structured/JSON output, code, math, safety and refusal behaviour; aggregate scores can stay flat while repetition or truncation degrades, so sampled side-by-side output diffs are part of the evidence, not a nicety. A BF16-vs-BF16 A/A control across seeds and physical GPUs establishes the noise floor that any claimed delta must clear.

Confounders to control and report. Autotune cache warmth; clock and thermal drift over long runs; asymmetric telemetry overhead; prefill/decode mix drift between arms; silent kernel fallback to a dequantize-then-GEMM path (dump per-layer kernel names and timings and diff the arms - a null result with a fallback in the logs is a tooling defect, not a verdict on the method); calibration-set leakage into the eval set, disproved by hash comparison; library defaults silently changing group size across versions.

Evidence required before any decision. Per-request raw records (arrival, TTFT, per-token timestamps, output length, status); per-layer kernel name and achieved-bandwidth traces for both arms; the arm configuration manifest with hashes; per-slice quality scores with CIs plus raw generations; the HBM ledger with KV blocks as the residual and a measured high-water mark; the A/A noise-floor numbers; and matched-window fleet GPU-hour and token accounting, because benchmarks propose and production billing disposes.

Rollback gates, pre-committed. Revert if p95 TTFT or TPOT exceeds SLO at target concurrency; if any eval slice falls more than 1.0 point absolute with a 95% CI excluding zero; if structured-output compliance falls more than 2 points; if measured cost improvement is under 25%; if preemption or recompute rates rise without explanation; or if kernel-fallback evidence appears, in which case fix the tooling and re-run rather than concluding anything. Keep the BF16 arm warm and routable throughout so rollback is a routing flip rather than a redeploy, and rehearse the revert once before the canary.

The recipe and the executed code path are different objects, and conflating them is the most common way a quantization study overstates its gain. A quantized checkpoint loads successfully whether or not an optimised kernel exists for its shapes; when one does not, the runtime typically dequantizes to BF16 and runs the ordinary GEMM, which preserves correctness, preserves the memory saving on resident weights, and delivers no compute benefit while adding dequantization overhead. Prefill is compute bound; dequantization adds arithmetic there, so TTFT is flat or slightly worse. As batch size rises, decode GEMMs become compute bound too and the advantage decays monotonically toward 1.0x. Any claim of a uniform speedup across the concurrency range is mechanically wrong and should be treated as an instrumentation bug until explained.

Byte-count ceiling (ESTIMATE, derivation inline, not a throughput result). A 9B-parameter model in BF16 is 9e9 x 2 B = 18 GB of weights. INT4 with group-128 FP16 scale and zero point costs about 0.5 + ~0.06 B/param, i.e. ~5.0-5.3 GB. Ratio ~3.2-3.6x. This is pure byte counting with no kernel-efficiency model and no attention or KV traffic included; it is an upper bound on batch-1 decode speedup ONLY. Applying Amdahl with a decode-weight-read fraction f: f=0.4 bounds end-to-end gain near 1.33x, f=0.8 near 2.1x (ESTIMATE).

Mandatory two-arm-plus-one design. Run the quantized configuration TWICE: (a) with KV cache block count clamped to the BF16 baseline's block count, which isolates the kernel/bandwidth effect; (b) at native capacity, which shows the deployable benefit. Freed HBM becomes additional KV blocks and raises throughput by batching alone. If the clamped arm is flat, the honest conclusion is "we bought KV headroom", and tuning KV settings on the BF16 arm must be priced as the cheaper alternative before shipping a second numeric path.

Arm identity is frozen and hashed. Checkpoint hash, bit width, group size, symmetric/asymmetric, outlier or mixed-precision policy, calibration dataset hash, library and engine build, TP/PP layout, activation precision, KV precision, block size, max_num_seqs, max_model_len, chunked-prefill state, speculative-decoding state. The configuration symmetric difference between arms must be exactly the bit-width fields; anything else invalidates the comparison. Weight-only means weight-only: "INT4 plus FP8 KV" is two experiments, and the KV change usually explains most of the throughput delta while none of the quality delta gets attributed correctly.

Comparison point. Compare arms at the intersection of each arm's own latency-throughput frontier with the p95 SLO, never at a fixed batch size; the two arms have different optimal batch sizes, and fixed-batch comparison is the single most common way these studies mislead. At least five concurrency points, at least three repeats per point, steady state with a fixed warmup-exclusion rule, greedy decoding and fixed seed for quality, bootstrap 95% CIs on ABSOLUTE quality deltas. Quality is sliced: long context, structured/JSON output, code, math, safety and refusal behaviour; aggregate scores can stay flat while repetition or truncation degrades, so sampled side-by-side output diffs are part of the evidence, not a nicety. Falsifiable hypothesis H92: the quantized arm's throughput advantage shrinks monotonically as batch size rises and approaches zero or turns negative in the compute-bound regime, testable by sweeping concurrency across the full operating range on both arms and plotting the delta against batch size. A single-concurrency benchmark answers a question about one point on a curve and is routinely generalised to the whole curve, which is where quantization comparisons most often mislead. The mechanism is explicit: at small batch the decode step reads the full weight set per token and is bandwidth bound, so fewer weight bytes translates directly into a shorter step, while at large batch the same weight read is amortised across many sequences and the step becomes compute bound, at which point a low-precision kernel whose arithmetic still runs at BF16 rates offers no advantage and may lose to a better-tuned baseline kernel. Note the second-order coupling: freed memory raises the admissible batch size, which pushes the arm toward the regime where its advantage is smallest, so capacity and latency benefits partially cancel and must be reported jointly rather than separately. Mechanism. Weight-only quantization (WOQ) reduces the BYTES OF WEIGHTS READ PER FORWARD PASS. It therefore helps only where the kernel is memory-bandwidth bound, which in LLM serving means small-batch autoregressive decode. Prefill is compute bound; dequantization adds arithmetic there, so TTFT is flat or slightly worse. As batch size rises, decode GEMMs become compute bound too and the advantage decays monotonically toward 1.0x. Any claim of a uniform speedup across the concurrency range is mechanically wrong and should be treated as an instrumentation bug until explained.

Byte-count ceiling (ESTIMATE, derivation inline, not a throughput result). A 9B-parameter model in BF16 is 9e9 x 2 B = 18 GB of weights. INT4 with group-128 FP16 scale and zero point costs about 0.5 + ~0.06 B/param, i.e. ~5.0-5.3 GB. Ratio ~3.2-3.6x. This is pure byte counting with no kernel-efficiency model and no attention or KV traffic included; it is an upper bound on batch-1 decode speedup ONLY. Applying Amdahl with a decode-weight-read fraction f: f=0.4 bounds end-to-end gain near 1.33x, f=0.8 near 2.1x (ESTIMATE).

Mandatory two-arm-plus-one design. Run the quantized configuration TWICE: (a) with KV cache block count clamped to the BF16 baseline's block count, which isolates the kernel/bandwidth effect; (b) at native capacity, which shows the deployable benefit. Freed HBM becomes additional KV blocks and raises throughput by batching alone. If the clamped arm is flat, the honest conclusion is "we bought KV headroom", and tuning KV settings on the BF16 arm must be priced as the cheaper alternative before shipping a second numeric path.

Arm identity is frozen and hashed. Checkpoint hash, bit width, group size, symmetric/asymmetric, outlier or mixed-precision policy, calibration dataset hash, library and engine build, TP/PP layout, activation precision, KV precision, block size, max_num_seqs, max_model_len, chunked-prefill state, speculative-decoding state. The configuration symmetric difference between arms must be exactly the bit-width fields; anything else invalidates the comparison. Weight-only means weight-only: "INT4 plus FP8 KV" is two experiments, and the KV change usually explains most of the throughput delta while none of the quality delta gets attributed correctly.

Comparison point. Compare arms at the intersection of each arm's own latency-throughput frontier with the p95 SLO, never at a fixed batch size; the two arms have different optimal batch sizes, and fixed-batch comparison is the single most common way these studies mislead. Cost unit is GPU-seconds per 1,000 output tokens at that fixed p95 SLO, converted to currency last.

At least five concurrency points, at least three repeats per point, steady state with a fixed warmup-exclusion rule, greedy decoding and fixed seed for quality, bootstrap 95% CIs on ABSOLUTE quality deltas. Quality is sliced: long context, structured/JSON output, code, math, safety and refusal behaviour; aggregate scores can stay flat while repetition or truncation degrades, so sampled side-by-side output diffs are part of the evidence, not a nicety. Mechanism. Weight-only quantization (WOQ) reduces the BYTES OF WEIGHTS READ PER FORWARD PASS. It therefore helps only where the kernel is memory-bandwidth bound, which in LLM serving means small-batch autoregressive decode. Prefill is compute bound; dequantization adds arithmetic there, so TTFT is flat or slightly worse. As batch size rises, decode GEMMs become compute bound too and the advantage decays monotonically toward 1.0x. Any claim of a uniform speedup across the concurrency range is mechanically wrong and should be treated as an instrumentation bug until explained.

Byte-count ceiling (ESTIMATE, derivation inline, not a throughput result). A 9B-parameter model in BF16 is 9e9 x 2 B = 18 GB of weights. INT4 with group-128 FP16 scale and zero point costs about 0.5 + ~0.06 B/param, i.e. ~5.0-5.3 GB. Ratio ~3.2-3.6x. This is pure byte counting with no kernel-efficiency model and no attention or KV traffic included; it is an upper bound on batch-1 decode speedup ONLY. Applying Amdahl with a decode-weight-read fraction f: f=0.4 bounds end-to-end gain near 1.33x, f=0.8 near 2.1x (ESTIMATE).

Mandatory two-arm-plus-one design. Run the quantized configuration TWICE: (a) with KV cache block count clamped to the BF16 baseline's block count, which isolates the kernel/bandwidth effect; (b) at native capacity, which shows the deployable benefit. Freed HBM becomes additional KV blocks and raises throughput by batching alone. If the clamped arm is flat, the honest conclusion is "we bought KV headroom", and tuning KV settings on the BF16 arm must be priced as the cheaper alternative before shipping a second numeric path.

Arm identity is frozen and hashed. Checkpoint hash, bit width, group size, symmetric/asymmetric, outlier or mixed-precision policy, calibration dataset hash, library and engine build, TP/PP layout, activation precision, KV precision, block size, max_num_seqs, max_model_len, chunked-prefill state, speculative-decoding state. The configuration symmetric difference between arms must be exactly the bit-width fields; anything else invalidates the comparison. Weight-only means weight-only: "INT4 plus FP8 KV" is two experiments, and the KV change usually explains most of the throughput delta while none of the quality delta gets attributed correctly.

Comparison point. Compare arms at the intersection of each arm's own latency-throughput frontier with the p95 SLO, never at a fixed batch size; the two arms have different optimal batch sizes, and fixed-batch comparison is the single most common way these studies mislead. Analytical stance under test: memory-accounting-and-fragmentation-first - freed weight bytes do not become usable capacity automatically.

The weight-byte saving is easy to compute from the artefact and is routinely presented as capacity, but the path from freed bytes to admitted requests passes through an allocator, an activation working set, a fragmentation pattern and a safety reserve, each of which can absorb part of it. Mechanism. Weight-only quantization (WOQ) reduces the BYTES OF WEIGHTS READ PER FORWARD PASS. It therefore helps only where the kernel is memory-bandwidth bound, which in LLM serving means small-batch autoregressive decode. Prefill is compute bound; dequantization adds arithmetic there, so TTFT is flat or slightly worse. As batch size rises, decode GEMMs become compute bound too and the advantage decays monotonically toward 1.0x. Any claim of a uniform speedup across the concurrency range is mechanically wrong and should be treated as an instrumentation bug until explained.

Byte-count ceiling (ESTIMATE, derivation inline, not a throughput result). A 9B-parameter model in BF16 is 9e9 x 2 B = 18 GB of weights. This is pure byte counting with no kernel-efficiency model and no attention or KV traffic included; it is an upper bound on batch-1 decode speedup ONLY. Applying Amdahl with a decode-weight-read fraction f: f=0.4 bounds end-to-end gain near 1.33x, f=0.8 near 2.1x (ESTIMATE).

Analytical stance under test: instruction-following-and-format-adherence-first - aggregate accuracy is the wrong instrument; the first thing WOQ breaks is compliance with the prompt contract.

Falsifiable hypothesis H201: under greedy decoding on a fixed instruction-heavy prompt set, the
INT4 arm's format-adherence rate (exact schema match, required-section presence, length-bound
compliance, refusal-when-asked) stays within 0.5 absolute points of BF16. If adherence drops by
more than that while aggregate task scores are flat, the claim "quality preserved" is falsified and
must be restated as "preserved on scored tasks, degraded on instruction compliance".

Mechanism and why this is separable from accuracy. Instruction following is carried by
low-margin logit decisions at a small number of control tokens: the opening brace of a JSON object,
a stop token, a section header, a refusal prefix. Rounding error from group-wise weight
quantization perturbs logits by a bounded but non-uniform amount; where the BF16 margin between the
top two candidates is already small, a small perturbation flips the argmax. Scored benchmarks
average over many tokens and hide this, because a single flipped control token can void an entire
structured response while costing almost nothing in token-level accuracy.

Boundary condition that decides the experiment: the effect scales with how many control-token
decisions a response contains, not with response length in general. A 20-field JSON emission has
roughly 20 independent opportunities to break; free-form prose has almost none. So the comparison
must be run on the production prompt mix weighted by structured-output share, not on a benchmark
suite chosen for score comparability.

Instrumentation. Log, per arm and per prompt: schema-validation pass/fail with the raw failing
output retained, top-1 token agreement against BF16 under identical greedy decoding, and the
per-position logit margin distribution at control-token positions. Agreement is the sensitive
early-warning statistic; validity is the operational one.

Numbers, ESTIMATE with derivation. If per-call schema validity drops from 99.4% to 98.4%, a
10-step agent loop's end-to-end success falls from 0.994^10 = 94.2% to 0.984^10 = 85.1%
(ESTIMATE, derived by independence across steps, which is itself an assumption to be checked since
errors correlate within a session). A one-point per-call regression is therefore a nine-point
product regression, which is why aggregate parity cannot be the release gate.

compresses the stored weight tensors and dequantizes them inside the GEMM epilogue. It reduces BYTES
OF WEIGHTS READ PER DECODE STEP and nothing else: it does not shrink the KV cache, does not reduce
attention FLOPs, and adds dequantization work on the compute path. The structural boundary follows

traffic. Prefill is compute bound, so TTFT is flat or mildly worse, and as batch size grows decode
GEMMs cross into the compute-bound regime and the speedup decays monotonically toward 1.0x.

format varies. Arms are interleaved in time (A/B/A/B) so thermal drift, background tenants and
driver state cannot be aliased into the treatment effect.

threshold, or (d) any arm shows kernel fallback, numerical instability or NaN in a 24-hour soak.

Analytical stance under test: speculative-decoding-interaction-first - WOQ and speculative decoding both target decode; measuring them apart predicts a benefit neither delivers together.

Falsifiable hypothesis H203: the GPU-seconds saving from INT4 measured with speculative decoding
DISABLED overstates the saving measured with the production speculative configuration ENABLED by
more than 30% relative. If the two savings are statistically indistinguishable, the interaction is
negligible and the simpler single-factor study is adequate; if they differ, any decision taken on
the spec-off number is invalid for a fleet that runs spec-on.

Mechanism of the interaction. Speculative decoding verifies K draft tokens in a single target
forward pass, so weights are read once per K accepted tokens instead of once per token. That
directly raises arithmetic intensity of the target step and shrinks the weight-bandwidth fraction f
that WOQ acts on. The two techniques are therefore substitutes for the same bottleneck, not
complements. A team that measures WOQ on a spec-off baseline and then deploys onto a spec-on fleet
will find most of the projected saving absent.

Second-order effects that must be controlled. Quantizing the target model changes its logit
distribution, which changes draft acceptance rate; a lower acceptance rate reduces speculative
efficiency and can make the quantized arm worse end to end even where its per-step cost is lower.
Acceptance rate must therefore be measured per arm, not assumed constant. If the draft model is
also quantized, that is a second variable and needs its own arm.

Experimental design. Four arms at minimum: BF16 spec-off, INT4 spec-off, BF16 spec-on, INT4 spec-on,
all at the same SLO-feasible concurrency. Report acceptance rate and mean accepted length per
spec arm alongside the cost denominator.

fraction available to WOQ is roughly 1/2.5 of the spec-off case (ESTIMATE, derived from weight

mean accepted length from 2.5 to 2.2 costs about 12% of decode throughput (ESTIMATE, derived from
the ratio 2.2/2.5), which can exceed the WOQ gain remaining at that operating point.

Falsifiable hypothesis H204: within the same nominal bit width, the spread in eval-suite score
across scheme variants (group size 32 vs 128 vs per-channel; symmetric vs asymmetric; act-order on
vs off; outlier channels retained in higher precision vs not) exceeds the BF16-to-INT4 gap of the
default variant. If it does, then reporting a single "INT4" result is not a measurement of
quantization at all, and the scheme parameters must be treated as first-class independent variables.

Mechanism. Group-wise quantization fits one scale (and optionally one zero point) per group of
weights along the reduction dimension. Smaller groups track local dynamic range better and cost more
metadata; asymmetric schemes handle skewed distributions but need a zero point; activation-order
permutations change which weights share a group, which matters exactly when outlier channels exist.
Each knob trades accuracy against memory and against kernel availability, and the kernels available
differ per variant, so accuracy and speed are not independently choosable.

Boundary conditions that must be checked, not assumed. Group size must divide the per-shard input
dimension; a tensor-parallel degree change can therefore invalidate a scheme. Some variants have no
fused kernel on some architectures and silently fall back. Metadata overhead grows as group size
shrinks and eats the memory saving that motivated the project.

Design. A scheme sweep run before the headline comparison, reporting for each variant: eval score,
weight bytes including metadata, dispatched kernel names, and decode throughput at the target
concurrency. The headline arm is then the Pareto-selected variant, named explicitly in the report.

metadata per weight is (16+4)/group_size bits. At group 128 that is 0.156 bits/weight, giving 4.16

memory saving claimed from "4-bit" is materially wrong at small group sizes and must be recomputed
per variant from measured artefact size.

Analytical stance under test: engine-version-and-dependency-drift-first - the comparison has a shelf life; an engine bump can invert the result without any model change.

Falsifiable hypothesis H205: re-running both arms unchanged after the next scheduled engine,
kernel-library or driver upgrade reproduces the original GPU-seconds delta within the pre-declared
run-to-run band. If the delta moves outside that band on a pure dependency bump, the result is a
property of one software stack and must be re-certified per upgrade rather than treated as a
standing conclusion.

Mechanism. The WOQ benefit is delivered by kernels, and kernel selection is a runtime decision made
by heuristics that change between releases. A patch-level upgrade can add a faster BF16 path (which
shrinks the quantized arm's relative win), add or remove a fused low-precision kernel for a
particular shape, change autotuning defaults, or change scheduler behaviour that shifts the
prefill/decode mix. None of these are announced as performance changes to your specific shapes.

Operational consequence that the design must absorb. If quantization is adopted, the fleet now runs
two numeric paths, and every dependency upgrade must be validated on both. That is a recurring
engineering cost and a recurring risk of asymmetric regression, where the upgrade is safe on the
baseline and harmful on the quantized arm.

Control procedure. Pin the entire stack by digest for the study, record engine commit, kernel

Analytical stance under test: energy-and-power-envelope-first - if the claim is cost, measure joules per token, because power capping and clocks silently set the answer.

Falsifiable hypothesis H206: the INT4 arm reduces energy per 1,000 output tokens at the fixed

Mechanism. Bandwidth-bound decode leaves compute units idle and draws less power than a
compute-bound phase. WOQ shifts the step toward compute (dequantization plus GEMM at higher

scale even though it was real on an unconstrained single node.

Confound to control explicitly. Clock policy must be identical and preferably locked across arms.
With auto-boost, a short benchmark can run at a boost clock that a sustained production load cannot
hold, so the quantized arm's advantage measured in a two-minute run may not survive a one-hour soak.
Measurement therefore requires a soak long enough to reach thermal steady state, with the warmup
window discarded and the steady-state window verified flat.

Analytical stance under test: multi-tenant-interference-and-isolation-first - a fair comparison on an isolated node can be an unfair prediction for a shared cluster.

Falsifiable hypothesis H207: the INT4 arm's advantage measured on a dedicated node persists,
within the pre-declared band, when both arms are re-measured under the production co-tenancy pattern
(neighbouring jobs on the same host, shared PCIe/NVLink paths, shared storage and network). If the
advantage shrinks materially under co-tenancy, the isolated-node result is not a valid basis for a
fleet decision.

Mechanism. WOQ's benefit is a reduction in memory-bandwidth demand. In a shared environment, the
resources that contend are exactly the ones the benefit is denominated in: HBM bandwidth is private
per GPU, but host memory bandwidth, PCIe, NVLink and network are shared, and a noisy neighbour that
saturates them changes the phase mix. Weight loading, KV offload paths, and any host-side
detokenization or logging contend for host resources whose availability differs between an isolated
benchmark and a packed host.

that reproduces production host packing. Randomize arm order and interleave, because interference is
time-varying and back-to-back runs alias it into the treatment effect. Report per-arm variance under
co-tenancy separately from the mean, since interference typically widens the tail more than it moves
the median, and the SLO is defined on the tail.

number of co-located containers, and whether MIG or time-slicing is in use. MPS or time-slicing in

Falsifiable hypothesis H208: the quantized artefact, loaded by the production serving path,
reproduces the quantization tool's own reported per-layer reconstruction error within tolerance, and
its layer inventory matches the base model exactly in shape, count and naming. If any layer is
missing, mis-shaped, silently left in high precision, or loaded with a different config than the one
recorded, the artefact is not the thing that was validated and every downstream number is void.

Mechanism of the failure. Quantization is a conversion pipeline: load, calibrate, pack, serialize,
then reload under a different runtime. Each stage can drop or alter state. Common concrete failures
are layers skipped because a shape did not match the group size, a config field the serving engine
ignores so it loads with different defaults than the packer wrote, and a partially-written artefact
that loads without error because the format tolerates missing optional tensors. None of these raise
an exception; they produce a model that runs and is quietly wrong or quietly unquantized.

packing match the intended scheme; list deliberately excluded layers explicitly. Compare

the packer's reported reconstruction error. Confirm the loaded quantization config as reported by
the running server, not as written in the file.

Analytical stance under test: admission-control-and-queueing-first - the SLO is set by the queue, not the kernel; compare arms at their admission limits or not at all.

Falsifiable hypothesis H209: at the concurrency where each arm just satisfies the p95 SLO, the
INT4 arm admits at least 20% more requests per second than BF16. If instead the gain appears only at
concurrencies where p95 is already out of contract, the throughput win is unclaimable and the correct
conclusion is that the arm improves saturated throughput but not SLO-bounded capacity.

Mechanism. End-to-end latency is queueing delay plus service time. WOQ reduces per-step service time
in the bandwidth-bound regime, but as offered load rises the system approaches its stability
boundary and queueing delay dominates; near saturation latency is governed by utilisation, not by
per-step cost. So a modest service-time improvement can produce a large capacity gain (by moving the
stability boundary) or almost none (if the admission controller, KV block limit, or max-num-seqs cap
binds first). Which of these holds is a property of the scheduler configuration, not of the kernel.

Design. For each arm, sweep offered load with an open-loop generator using a production-derived
arrival process, find the highest sustainable rate meeting the p95 SLO, and read GPU-seconds per
1,000 output tokens at that point. Closed-loop generators are also run, but only same-generator
comparisons are reported, because closed loop suppresses queueing by construction and systematically
flatters the slower arm.

Binding-constraint identification, which is the actual deliverable. Record, per arm at the SLO
point, which limit is active: KV blocks exhausted, max-num-seqs reached, scheduler preemption rate
nonzero, or pure compute saturation. If the KV block limit binds, the gain is a capacity effect from
freed memory and must be reported as such; if preemption is occurring, the comparison is measuring
scheduler policy rather than precision.

heavy-tailed output lengths will fall short of this, so the analytic figure is an upper bound to be
falsified by measurement, not a prediction.

Analytical stance under test: regression-triage-and-attribution-first - design the study so that a failure is diagnosable, not just detectable.

Falsifiable hypothesis H210: given only the artefacts the study is designed to produce, an
engineer who did not run it can attribute any observed quality or latency regression to one of a
pre-enumerated set of causes (kernel fallback, calibration mismatch, tokenizer or config drift,
scheduler or capacity difference, workload shift, or genuine precision loss) without re-running the
experiment. If attribution requires a re-run, the study's instrumentation is inadequate and should be
fixed before the comparison is trusted, regardless of what the headline numbers say.

Why this is a design constraint and not a postscript. Quantization studies fail in ways that all
present as "the quantized arm is worse", and the remedies are mutually exclusive: a fallback needs a
kernel fix, a calibration mismatch needs more or different data, a config drift needs a packaging
fix, and genuine precision loss needs abandoning the bit width. Without discriminating evidence
collected during the run, the team iterates by guessing, which is expensive and tends to terminate
on whichever hypothesis was checked first rather than the true one.

Discriminating instrumentation, collected on every run. Kernel-name histogram with time attribution
(separates fallback). Per-slice paired quality deltas with calibration-represented and
calibration-absent slices labelled (separates calibration mismatch). Config and tokenizer hashes
plus loaded-config readback (separates drift). KV block occupancy, preemption counts and admitted
concurrency (separates capacity and scheduler effects). Request-mix statistics per measurement window
(separates workload shift). Per-layer output error against the BF16 reference (isolates genuine
numeric loss to specific layers).

Deviation and exclusion log. Every retune, restart or discarded run is recorded with a reason.
Silent exclusion of "bad runs" is the most common route by which a false positive survives review,
and it also destroys the evidence needed for triage.

Numbers, ESTIMATE with derivation. Adding the above instrumentation costs on the order of a few
percent of run wall time (profiler traces are sampled on short windows, not run continuously) and a
few gigabytes of trace storage for a multi-week trial at roughly 200 bytes per request record
(ESTIMATE, derived from request volume times record size). That is negligible against the cost of a
single misattributed iteration cycle.

Analytical stance under test: calibration-set-representativeness-first - the single largest hidden variable in a weight-only quantization (WOQ) comparison is the calibration set, not the bit width. GPTQ/AWQ-style methods solve a per-layer reconstruction objective against activations sampled from a calibration corpus; if that corpus is generic web text while production traffic is code or tool-call JSON, the per-channel scales are fitted to the wrong activation distribution and quality regresses on exactly the traffic you care about.

Falsifiable hypothesis (H0): H0: with calibration drawn from a held-out sample of production traffic, INT4 WOQ accuracy delta versus BF16 on the production task suite is <=1 absolute point, and this delta is strictly smaller than the delta obtained with a generic-web calibration set.

Controlled experiment: Freeze model weights, tokenizer, prompt set, sampling params (greedy, temperature 0, fixed seed), engine version and GPU type. Vary exactly one factor: calibration corpus (generic vs production-sampled), holding sample count and sequence length fixed. Quantize twice, evaluate both on the same held-out production eval set that shares no prompts with calibration.

Confounders to hold fixed or measure: Calibration sample count and max sequence length silently change group-wise scale statistics; sampling nondeterminism; eval set leakage into calibration; different quantization group sizes (g128 vs g64) being changed at the same time as the corpus.

A team wants lower serving cost through weight-only quantization. Define a fair comparison. Scenario variant 267: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.

Analytical stance under test: sampler-and-logits-postprocessing-cost-first - the part of the step that quantization cannot touch sets the floor.

Falsifiable hypothesis H197b: the fraction of decode step time spent outside the quantized linear layers, in attention, normalization, sampling, logit processing and Python or scheduler overhead, is large enough that the end-to-end gain is bounded well below the weight-byte bound, testable by per-kernel and host-side profiling of one representative decode step per arm. If that fraction is small, the weight-byte bound is approximately reachable and the stance's caution is falsified.

The weight-byte reduction bounds only the part of a decode step that reads weights, and a serving engine spends a non-trivial share of each step elsewhere: attention over the KV cache, which weight-only quantization does not shrink; normalization and residual work; the LM-head projection, whose cost scales with vocabulary size and which may or may not be quantized in the arm under test; logit post-processing including repetition, presence and frequency penalties, logit bias and top-k or top-p filtering; the sampling kernel itself; detokenization; and host-side scheduler work between steps. Profile the step and attribute time to these buckets on both arms before interpreting any aggregate. The consequence is an Amdahl bound: if the quantized linear layers account for a fraction of step time, the end-to-end step-time improvement is capped by that fraction regardless of how good the kernel is, and a study that reports only the aggregate cannot distinguish a weak kernel from a small addressable fraction. Two boundary conditions sharpen this. A large vocabulary makes the LM head a significant term, so whether it is quantized changes the addressable fraction materially and must be recorded as an arm property rather than left implicit. Heavy logit post-processing, common in structured-output and tool-calling deployments, adds a fixed per-step cost that dilutes the gain further and does so more at small batch, exactly where the weight-byte argument is strongest. State which buckets the arm addresses and which it cannot. ESTIMATE: with a fraction f of step time in quantized linear layers and a per-layer speedup s, the step-time ratio is one over the quantity one minus f plus f over s, so the ceiling falls steeply as f drops below about one half; derivation is Amdahl's law applied to the profiled buckets, and it is an ESTIMATE, not MEASURED.

Mechanism. Weight-only quantization (WOQ) reduces the BYTES OF WEIGHTS READ PER FORWARD PASS. It therefore helps only where the kernel is memory-bandwidth bound, which in LLM serving means small-batch autoregressive decode. Prefill is compute bound; dequantization adds arithmetic there, so TTFT is flat or slightly worse. As batch size rises, decode GEMMs become compute bound too and the advantage decays monotonically toward 1.0x. Any claim of a uniform speedup across the concurrency range is mechanically wrong and should be treated as an instrumentation bug until explained.

Byte-count ceiling (ESTIMATE, derivation inline, not a throughput result). A 9B-parameter model in BF16 is 9e9 x 2 B = 18 GB of weights. INT4 with group-128 FP16 scale and zero point costs about 0.5 + ~0.06 B/param, i.e. ~5.0-5.3 GB. Ratio ~3.2-3.6x. This is pure byte counting with no kernel-efficiency model and no attention or KV traffic included; it is an upper bound on batch-1 decode speedup ONLY. Applying Amdahl with a decode-weight-read fraction f: f=0.4 bounds end-to-end gain near 1.33x, f=0.8 near 2.1x (ESTIMATE).

Mandatory two-arm-plus-one design. Run the quantized configuration TWICE: (a) with KV cache block count clamped to the BF16 baseline's block count, which isolates the kernel/bandwidth effect; (b) at native capacity, which shows the deployable benefit. Freed HBM becomes additional KV blocks and raises throughput by batching alone. If the clamped arm is flat, the honest conclusion is "we bought KV headroom", and tuning KV settings on the BF16 arm must be priced as the cheaper alternative before shipping a second numeric path.

Arm identity is frozen and hashed. Checkpoint hash, bit width, group size, symmetric/asymmetric, outlier or mixed-precision policy, calibration dataset hash, library and engine build, TP/PP layout, activation precision, KV precision, block size, max_num_seqs, max_model_len, chunked-prefill state, speculative-decoding state. The configuration symmetric difference between arms must be exactly the bit-width fields; anything else invalidates the comparison. Weight-only means weight-only: "INT4 plus FP8 KV" is two experiments, and the KV change usually explains most of the throughput delta while none of the quality delta gets attributed correctly.

Comparison point. Compare arms at the intersection of each arm's own latency-throughput frontier with the p95 SLO, never at a fixed batch size; the two arms have different optimal batch sizes, and fixed-batch comparison is the single most common way these studies mislead. Cost unit is GPU-seconds per 1,000 output tokens at that fixed p95 SLO, converted to currency last.

Measurement protocol. At least five concurrency points, at least three repeats per point, steady state with a fixed warmup-exclusion rule, greedy decoding and fixed seed for quality, bootstrap 95% CIs on ABSOLUTE quality deltas. Quality is sliced: long context, structured/JSON output, code, math, safety and refusal behaviour; aggregate scores can stay flat while repetition or truncation degrades, so sampled side-by-side output diffs are part of the evidence, not a nicety. A BF16-vs-BF16 A/A control across seeds and physical GPUs establishes the noise floor that any claimed delta must clear.

Confounders to control and report. Autotune cache warmth; clock and thermal drift over long runs; asymmetric telemetry overhead; prefill/decode mix drift between arms; silent kernel fallback to a dequantize-then-GEMM path (dump per-layer kernel names and timings and diff the arms - a null result with a fallback in the logs is a tooling defect, not a verdict on the method); calibration-set leakage into the eval set, disproved by hash comparison; library defaults silently changing group size across versions.

Evidence required before any decision. Per-request raw records (arrival, TTFT, per-token timestamps, output length, status); per-layer kernel name and achieved-bandwidth traces for both arms; the arm configuration manifest with hashes; per-slice quality scores with CIs plus raw generations; the HBM ledger with KV blocks as the residual and a measured high-water mark; the A/A noise-floor numbers; and matched-window fleet GPU-hour and token accounting, because benchmarks propose and production billing disposes.

Rollback gates, pre-committed. Revert if p95 TTFT or TPOT exceeds SLO at target concurrency; if any eval slice falls more than 1.0 point absolute with a 95% CI excluding zero; if structured-output compliance falls more than 2 points; if measured cost improvement is under 25%; if preemption or recompute rates rise without explanation; or if kernel-fallback evidence appears, in which case fix the tooling and re-run rather than concluding anything. Keep the BF16 arm warm and routable throughout so rollback is a routing flip rather than a redeploy, and rehearse the revert once before the canary.

Declared unknowns. Kernel efficiency on the specific shapes and TP degree in use, per-layer sensitivity of the specific checkpoint, and the production decode-token fraction are all MEASURED quantities in this design; none of them are asserted here. Every number above is labelled ESTIMATE and carries its derivation.

A team wants lower serving cost through weight-only quantization. Define a fair comparison. Scenario variant 268: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.

Analytical stance under test: continuous-batching-preemption-and-recompute-accounting-first - a capacity gain shows up as fewer evictions, not as a faster kernel.

Falsifiable hypothesis H197c: the quantized arm's throughput advantage under production-shaped load is driven primarily by a reduction in preemption and KV recompute events rather than by per-step kernel speed, testable by recording preemption count, swapped or recomputed token count and the resulting wasted GPU time on both arms under the same replayed trace. If preemption counts are already near zero on the baseline, this channel contributes nothing and any gain must come from the kernel path.

In a continuous-batching engine with paged KV, memory pressure does not surface as an out-of-memory error but as preemption: running sequences are evicted, their KV is dropped or swapped, and the tokens are recomputed when the sequence is rescheduled. That recomputation is pure waste and it is charged to throughput without appearing in any per-step kernel timing, which is why a quantization study that measures only kernel time can miss the dominant effect entirely, in either direction. Instrument the eviction path explicitly: preemption events per minute, tokens recomputed, tokens swapped out and in, queue wait time separated from execution time, and the distribution of sequence lifetimes. Then compare arms under an identical replayed trace with identical arrival timing, because preemption is a function of offered load and memory headroom together and disappears entirely under gentle synthetic load. Two mechanisms must be separated and are routinely conflated. If the baseline arm was preemption-heavy, the quantized arm's extra KV blocks reduce evictions and the gain is a capacity effect that a memory upgrade, a shorter maximum sequence length or a lower concurrency cap would also deliver, at no accuracy risk. If the baseline arm never preempted, the freed memory buys nothing on this channel and the gain must be kernel-side. Distinguish them by running a clamped arm whose KV block count is pinned to the baseline value; the difference between clamped and unclamped is the capacity channel, and the difference between clamped and baseline is the kernel channel. Boundary condition: preemption is bursty and tail-dominated, so its effect appears in p99 latency long before it appears in mean throughput. ESTIMATE: wasted GPU time from recompute is approximately the recomputed token count times the per-token prefill cost, so a preemption rate that looks small in events per minute can consume a large share of capacity when evicted sequences are long; derivation is multiplying event counts by per-token prefill cost, and it is an ESTIMATE, not MEASURED.

Analytical stance under test: quantized-artefact-load-path-and-startup-integrity-first - the artefact must be proven to be what the report says it is, at load time, on the serving host.

Falsifiable hypothesis H197d: the process serving traffic loaded exactly the artefact whose hash appears in the report, with the quantization scheme parameters the report claims, verified by a load-time hash check and a runtime dump of the model's per-layer weight dtypes and quantization configuration from the live process. If the runtime dump disagrees with the report, every number attributed to that arm is void regardless of how carefully it was measured.

A quantization comparison is a claim about an artefact, and the weakest link in most such claims is that nobody verified which artefact the serving process actually loaded. Close that gap mechanically rather than by convention. Hash the artefact files at build time and record the hashes in the run manifest; verify the same hashes on the serving host at load time and fail closed on mismatch rather than logging a warning; and after the server is up, dump from the live process the per-layer weight dtype, the quantization method name, the group size, the symmetric or asymmetric flag, and whether the LM head and any excluded modules were quantized. Diff that runtime dump against the intended arm definition and against the other arm; the symmetric difference must consist only of the quantization axis. This catches several failure modes that silently corrupt results. A stale artefact in a mounted cache or an image layer serves the previous build while the manifest names the new one. A loader that silently falls back to dequantizing weights into the baseline precision at load time produces an arm that is nominally quantized and mechanically identical to the baseline except slower, yielding a null that is a tooling defect rather than a verdict. A partially quantized model, where some modules were excluded by a default configuration nobody read, changes both the memory ledger and the addressable fraction. Also record artefact provenance: base checkpoint identity and licence, the conversion tool and version, the calibration data identity and its retention rights, and the publication path with its access controls, since a quantized checkpoint is a derived artefact that inherits obligations from its inputs. ESTIMATE: the on-disk artefact size implied by the claimed scheme is the parameter count times bytes per weight plus the scale and zero-point overhead implied by the group size, so a size that disagrees with that arithmetic is a cheap early signal of a mismatched artefact; derivation is byte counting against the declared scheme, and it is an ESTIMATE, not MEASURED. Rollback gate: any load-time hash or runtime-dump mismatch voids the arm and stops the study.

Falsifiable hypothesis H197f: the achieved HBM read volume per decode step on the baseline arm is close to the model's weight byte count, verified by hardware memory-traffic counters or profiler-reported achieved bandwidth over a fixed number of steps. If measured read volume is substantially below the weight byte count, some weight traffic is being served from cache or is fused away, and the byte-ratio bound overstates the achievable gain.

The weight-byte argument assumes each decode step reads every weight from HBM exactly once, and that assumption is an approximation that the hardware can violate in both directions. Verify it with counters rather than accepting it as mechanism. Measure achieved HBM read bytes over a fixed number of decode steps at fixed batch size on the baseline arm and compare against the model's weight byte count times the step count; the ratio is the correction factor that the byte-ratio bound needs and it is rarely exactly one. Below one indicates that some weight traffic is absorbed by on-chip cache, which occurs more readily for small tensors and for models whose per-layer working set fits available cache, and it means the quantized arm has less traffic to remove than the naive ratio suggests. Above one indicates extra traffic the argument ignored: activation and KV traffic, which weight-only quantization does not reduce and which grows with batch size and context length, plus any dequantization path that reads the packed weights and writes an expanded intermediate to memory rather than dequantizing in registers or shared memory. That last case is the important asymmetry: a dequantize-to-memory kernel can move more total bytes than the baseline while nominally storing fewer weight bytes, producing a slowdown that the byte argument predicts as a speedup. Inspect the dispatched kernel and its memory behaviour rather than inferring it. Boundary condition: as batch size and context length grow, the KV and activation share of traffic grows and the weight share falls, so the correction factor is regime dependent and must be measured at the concurrency actually served. Falsifiable hypothesis H197g: interleaving the arms in time in a randomised A-B-B-A order yields the same delta as running them back to back, testable by executing both schedules and comparing the deltas against the A/A noise floor. If the two schedules disagree beyond that floor, a time-varying factor such as neighbour load, thermal state, driver state or cache warmth is contributing to the reported result.

Benchmark arms are usually run sequentially, which silently assigns every time-varying factor to the arm that happened to run later. On shared or cloud infrastructure those factors are substantial: co-tenant load on shared host resources, ambient and device temperature affecting sustained clocks, storage and network contention during weight loading and telemetry, page-cache and allocator warmth, and any background maintenance activity on the host. The countermeasure is experimental design rather than more careful measurement. Interleave the arms in short randomised blocks so each arm samples the same distribution of environmental conditions, run at least an A-B-B-A pattern to cancel monotone drift to first order, and repeat across physically distinct devices and hosts so device-to-device variation is inside the error bar rather than confounded with the arm. Record per-run environmental covariates alongside the metrics: device clocks, temperature, power draw, any clock-throttle reason flags, host load, and the exact wall-clock window. Then check whether the delta is stable across blocks; a delta that is large in some blocks and absent in others is a signal that an uncontrolled factor is driving it. Establish the A/A noise floor under the same interleaved schedule, not under ideal quiet conditions, because the floor measured on a quiet machine understates the variance the real comparison faces. Boundary condition: on a dedicated, thermally stable, single-tenant machine the interleaving requirement is weaker, but that condition must be demonstrated with the covariate log rather than asserted, and the resulting number then carries a narrower scope: it describes that machine, not the fleet. Falsifiable hypothesis H197h: the freed weight memory changes the fleet's packing outcome, meaning either more model replicas per device or a shift to a smaller device class while holding the SLO, testable by solving the packing problem with measured per-replica memory and throughput on both arms. If the packing outcome is identical, the memory saving produces no cost change and the study's economic claim fails even if its latency claim holds.

For fleets that serve several models or several replicas per device, the operationally meaningful consequence of weight-only quantization is often not step latency but packing: how many serving instances fit on a device while each holds its SLO. Frame the comparison as a packing problem with measured inputs. For each arm, measure per-replica steady-state memory high-water mark including weights, KV pool, activation peak and allocator headroom, and measure sustainable request rate at the target p95 SLO. Then compute, for the actual fleet mix and its peak-to-mean ratio, the number of devices required under each arm, and price the difference in device-hours rather than in percentages. This framing exposes discontinuities that a latency-percentage framing hides. Memory savings pay off in steps, not continuously: a saving that does not cross the threshold for one more replica per device buys nothing, and a saving that crosses it buys a large discrete gain. Conversely, colocated replicas contend for memory bandwidth and streaming multiprocessors, so two replicas on one device do not each achieve the isolated single-replica rate, and the packing calculation must use the measured colocated rate rather than the isolated one. Interference also raises tail latency for every colocated tenant, so an SLO that was met in isolation can be missed after packing, which converts an apparent saving into an SLO incident. Boundary condition: where the fleet runs one model per device at low utilisation, the binding constraint is request rate rather than memory, and weight memory savings are economically irrelevant no matter how large; state which regime the fleet is in before running the study. Mechanism. Weight-only quantization (WOQ) reduces the BYTES OF WEIGHTS READ PER FORWARD PASS. It therefore helps only where the kernel is memory-bandwidth bound, which in LLM serving means small-batch autoregressive decode. Prefill is compute bound; dequantization adds arithmetic there, so TTFT is flat or slightly worse. As batch size rises, decode GEMMs become compute bound too and the advantage decays monotonically toward 1.0x. Any claim of a uniform speedup across the concurrency range is mechanically wrong and should be treated as an instrumentation bug until explained.

Byte-count ceiling (ESTIMATE, derivation inline, not a throughput result). A 9B-parameter model in BF16 is 9e9 x 2 B = 18 GB of weights. INT4 with group-128 FP16 scale and zero point costs about 0.5 + ~0.06 B/param, i.e. ~5.0-5.3 GB. Ratio ~3.2-3.6x. Applying Amdahl with a decode-weight-read fraction f: f=0.4 bounds end-to-end gain near 1.33x, f=0.8 near 2.1x (ESTIMATE).

Mandatory two-arm-plus-one design. Run the quantized configuration TWICE: (a) with KV cache block count clamped to the BF16 baseline's block count, which isolates the kernel/bandwidth effect; (b) at native capacity, which shows the deployable benefit. Analytical stance under test: dataset-and-slice-freshness-first - a quality verdict expires as the traffic distribution moves.

Falsifiable hypothesis H197j: the evaluation slices used to certify quality still match the current production request distribution, testable by comparing slice proportions and prompt characteristics in the evaluation set against a recent sample of production telemetry. A quantization adoption decision is certified against a fixed evaluation set, and that certification silently decays because production traffic moves while the evaluation set does not. Treat the verdict as having an expiry and a monitoring contract rather than as a permanent property of the artefact. Establish the slice proportions of the evaluation set and compare them against a recent production sample along the dimensions that interact with quantization damage: context length distribution including its tail, structured-output and tool-calling share, language and domain mix, and the share of requests from each SLO class. Where a slice has grown materially in production but is thin or absent in the evaluation set, the certification does not cover it and the correct action is to extend the set and re-run rather than to extrapolate. New product features introduce request shapes that never existed when the study ran, and those shapes are exactly the ones most likely to fall outside the calibration set the quantized artefact was fitted on, which is where weight-only damage concentrates. Model refreshes invalidate the artefact entirely, since a quantized checkpoint is derived from a specific base checkpoint and its calibration must be redone on every refresh; that recurring cost belongs in the economic comparison and is frequently omitted. Analytical stance under test: kv-cache-dtype-and-quantization-interaction-first - the KV cache is a separate precision axis that must be held fixed.

Falsifiable hypothesis H198a: the KV cache dtype and any KV quantization setting are byte-for-byte identical across arms, verified by dumping the engine's effective KV dtype, per-block byte size and any KV quantization scale configuration from each live serving process. If they differ, the comparison confounds weight precision with KV precision and neither the memory ledger nor the quality delta can be attributed to weight-only quantization.

Weight-only quantization is defined by leaving activations and the KV cache alone, yet many quantization toolchains and serving presets change the KV dtype at the same time, either because a preset bundles them or because a lower KV precision is enabled to exploit the freed memory. That single coupling invalidates the entire study, because KV precision moves both the memory ledger and the quality result through a completely different mechanism than weight precision. Separate the axes explicitly. Dump from each live process the effective KV dtype, the per-block KV byte size, whether KV quantization is enabled and with which scale granularity, and assert equality across arms; then, if KV quantization is genuinely of interest, run it as a third arm rather than folding it into the quantized arm. The mechanisms differ in ways that matter operationally. Weight error is fixed at build time and identical for every request, so its damage is stationary and can be certified once per artefact. KV error accumulates along the sequence and interacts with attention softmax sharpness, so its damage grows with context length and is largest exactly in the long-context regime that memory savings are usually sought to serve. A study that conflates them will observe a quality delta that looks context-dependent and will misattribute it to weights. Boundary condition: where the deployment serves short contexts almost exclusively, KV precision contributes little to either memory or quality and the confound is small, but that must be shown from the served context-length distribution rather than assumed. ESTIMATE: KV pool bytes scale as two times layer count times KV head count times head dimension times total cached tokens times bytes per element, so halving KV element bytes changes the memory ledger by roughly the same order as the weight saving at long context; derivation is byte counting over the KV layout, and it is an ESTIMATE, not MEASURED. Rollback gate: if the runtime dumps disagree on any KV precision property, the run is void and must be re-executed with the axes separated.

Falsifiable hypothesis H198b: no item, near-duplicate or source document from the quantization calibration set appears in the evaluation sets used to certify quality, testable by exact-hash and near-duplicate matching between the calibration corpus and every evaluation slice. If overlap exists, the measured quality parity is inflated by fitting rather than earned, and the certification must be re-run on a disjoint set.

Post-training weight-only quantization methods that use calibration data fit scales, group statistics or error-compensation terms to a sample of text, which makes the quantized artefact a data-dependent object even though no gradient update occurred. That creates a contamination channel most quantization studies never check: if the calibration sample overlaps the evaluation set, the artefact has been tuned toward the exact items used to certify it, and the observed parity partly measures fitting rather than robustness. Audit the boundary mechanically. Record the calibration corpus identity, size, sampling procedure and retention rights in the run manifest; then run exact-hash and near-duplicate matching between calibration items and every evaluation slice, reporting the overlap rate per slice rather than as a single aggregate. Where overlap is non-zero, re-certify on the disjoint remainder and report both numbers. Two secondary effects follow from the same data dependence. Distribution mismatch: a calibration sample drawn from generic web text will under-represent the structured-output, tool-calling and long-context shapes the service actually serves, and weight-only damage concentrates precisely where the calibration distribution is thin, so the artefact can look healthy in aggregate and be materially worse on the slices that carry the SLO. Analytical stance under test: kernel-dispatch-and-shape-coverage-first - a quantized kernel is fast only on the shapes it has a fast path for.

Quantized matrix-multiply kernels are not uniformly fast; they are collections of specialised implementations with shape constraints on batch dimension, hidden dimension alignment, group size and sometimes tile-friendly token counts, plus a generic fallback that can be slower than the unquantized baseline. Mechanism. Weight-only quantization (WOQ) reduces the BYTES OF WEIGHTS READ PER FORWARD PASS. It therefore helps only where the kernel is memory-bandwidth bound, which in LLM serving means small-batch autoregressive decode. Before any cross-arm comparison is meaningful, each arm must be shown to reproduce itself, and in a continuous-batching serving engine that is not automatic. Batch composition varies with arrival timing, and many reduction kernels are not deterministic with respect to batch composition, so the same prompt can produce different logits and occasionally different sampled tokens across runs even at fixed seed. Analytical stance under test: request-cancellation-and-client-disconnect-first - work abandoned mid-stream is charged to capacity but not to any benchmark metric.

Falsifiable hypothesis H198e: the share of production requests cancelled or disconnected before completion is small enough that ignoring them does not change the arm ranking, testable by replaying a trace that includes real cancellation timing on both arms and comparing goodput with and without cancellations. If cancellations are material, benchmark throughput measured on run-to-completion requests overstates both arms and can reorder them.

Streaming serving deployments routinely see clients disconnect mid-generation, whether from user navigation, upstream timeouts or agent loops that stop early once enough tokens have arrived. That work still consumed prefill and decode capacity, still held KV blocks until the engine noticed the cancellation, and still contributed nothing to any completed response, yet almost every quantization benchmark drives run-to-completion requests and therefore never measures it. Include cancellation in the trace. Replay production arrival and cancellation timing, and report goodput, defined as tokens delivered to clients that consumed them, alongside raw throughput; report also the KV block-hours consumed by cancelled requests and the engine's cancellation detection latency, since a slow detection path holds memory that the capacity argument assumed was available. The interaction with quantization is not neutral. If the quantized arm is faster per token, more requests complete before their client gives up, so the cancellation rate itself is arm-dependent and goodput can improve by more than raw throughput; conversely if the quantized arm shifts load toward larger batches with longer queue waits, more requests are abandoned in the queue and goodput can improve by less than throughput, or degrade while throughput improves. Neither direction is knowable without measuring it. Boundary condition: batch and offline inference workloads have no cancellation channel, so this consideration is specific to interactive streaming deployments and should be dropped explicitly rather than silently for offline use cases. ESTIMATE: capacity wasted on abandoned work is approximately the cancelled-request count times the mean tokens generated before cancellation times the per-token decode cost, plus the KV block-hours held until detection; derivation is multiplying observed cancellation statistics by measured per-token cost, and it is an ESTIMATE, not MEASURED. Rollback gate: no throughput-based adoption claim for an interactive service without a goodput number measured under a trace containing real cancellations.

A quantization verdict is only as trustworthy as the telemetry that produced it, and telemetry is a system with its own failure modes that are rarely audited in benchmark work. Clock skew between load generator and server corrupts any latency computed across the boundary. Falsifiable hypothesis H198g: the measured device-hour savings from the quantized arm repay the full conversion, validation and re-certification cost within the artefact's expected service life, testable by measuring conversion compute time, engineer time and validation compute, and dividing by the measured hourly saving. If the payback period exceeds the interval between base-model refreshes, the programme loses money even when every technical claim holds.

Quantization is often justified on steady-state serving cost while its production cost is left out of the ledger, which is an accounting error rather than a technical one. Build the full ledger. On the cost side: conversion or calibration compute time and the device class it required, storage and transfer for the additional artefact, validation compute for the quality and performance certification, engineer time for the study and the rollout, and the recurring repeat of all of the above on every base-model refresh, since a quantized checkpoint is derived from a specific base and does not survive its replacement. On the savings side: the measured device-hour reduction at the actual fleet packing outcome, not the percentage speedup, since savings materialise only when the packing changes. Then compute payback period and compare it against the empirical interval between model refreshes at this organisation. The decisive interaction is that refresh cadence sets the artefact's service life, so a fast-moving model roadmap can make an otherwise sound quantization programme permanently unprofitable, and that is a scheduling fact rather than a numerical one. Two secondary costs belong in the ledger and are usually missed. Operational complexity: two artefact classes in the fleet doubles the certification surface, the rollback matrix and the incident triage space, and that cost is recurring and human. Risk cost: a quality regression discovered in production carries an expected cost equal to its probability times its blast radius, which should be priced rather than assumed zero. Boundary condition: where the fleet is large and the model stable for long periods, amortisation is easy and the technical analysis dominates; where the fleet is small or the model churns, the ledger dominates and the technical result may be irrelevant. ESTIMATE: payback period equals total one-time cost divided by measured hourly saving, and the programme is viable only if that period is shorter than the observed mean interval between base-model refreshes; derivation is simple division over measured inputs, and it is an ESTIMATE, not MEASURED. Rollback gate: no programme approval without a payback period computed from measured conversion and validation cost and compared against the organisation's actual refresh cadence.

Mechanism. Weight-only quantization (WOQ) reduces the BYTES OF WEIGHTS READ PER FORWARD PASS. It therefore helps only where the kernel is memory-bandwidth bound, which in LLM serving means small-batch autoregressive decode. Prefill is compute bound; dequantization adds arithmetic there, so TTFT is flat or slightly worse. As batch size rises, decode GEMMs become compute bound too and the advantage decays monotonically toward 1.0x. Any claim of a uniform speedup across the concurrency range is mechanically wrong and should be treated as an instrumentation bug until explained.

Byte-count ceiling (ESTIMATE, derivation inline, not a throughput result). A 9B-parameter model in BF16 is 9e9 x 2 B = 18 GB of weights. INT4 with group-128 FP16 scale and zero point costs about 0.5 + ~0.06 B/param, i.e. ~5.0-5.3 GB. Ratio ~3.2-3.6x. This is pure byte counting with no kernel-efficiency model and no attention or KV traffic included; it is an upper bound on batch-1 decode speedup ONLY. Applying Amdahl with a decode-weight-read fraction f: f=0.4 bounds end-to-end gain near 1.33x, f=0.8 near 2.1x (ESTIMATE).

Mandatory two-arm-plus-one design. Run the quantized configuration TWICE: (a) with KV cache block count clamped to the BF16 baseline's block count, which isolates the kernel/bandwidth effect; (b) at native capacity, which shows the deployable benefit. Freed HBM becomes additional KV blocks and raises throughput by batching alone. If the clamped arm is flat, the honest conclusion is "we bought KV headroom", and tuning KV settings on the BF16 arm must be priced as the cheaper alternative before shipping a second numeric path.

Arm identity is frozen and hashed. Checkpoint hash, bit width, group size, symmetric/asymmetric, outlier or mixed-precision policy, calibration dataset hash, library and engine build, TP/PP layout, activation precision, KV precision, block size, max_num_seqs, max_model_len, chunked-prefill state, speculative-decoding state. The configuration symmetric difference between arms must be exactly the bit-width fields; anything else invalidates the comparison. Weight-only means weight-only: "INT4 plus FP8 KV" is two experiments, and the KV change usually explains most of the throughput delta while none of the quality delta gets attributed correctly.

Comparison point. Compare arms at the intersection of each arm's own latency-throughput frontier with the p95 SLO, never at a fixed batch size; the two arms have different optimal batch sizes, and fixed-batch comparison is the single most common way these studies mislead. Cost unit is GPU-seconds per 1,000 output tokens at that fixed p95 SLO, converted to currency last.

Measurement protocol. At least five concurrency points, at least three repeats per point, steady state with a fixed warmup-exclusion rule, greedy decoding and fixed seed for quality, bootstrap 95% CIs on ABSOLUTE quality deltas. Quality is sliced: long context, structured/JSON output, code, math, safety and refusal behaviour; aggregate scores can stay flat while repetition or truncation degrades, so sampled side-by-side output diffs are part of the evidence, not a nicety. A BF16-vs-BF16 A/A control across seeds and physical GPUs establishes the noise floor that any claimed delta must clear.

Confounders to control and report. Autotune cache warmth; clock and thermal drift over long runs; asymmetric telemetry overhead; prefill/decode mix drift between arms; silent kernel fallback to a dequantize-then-GEMM path (dump per-layer kernel names and timings and diff the arms - a null result with a fallback in the logs is a tooling defect, not a verdict on the method); calibration-set leakage into the eval set, disproved by hash comparison; library defaults silently changing group size across versions.

Evidence required before any decision. Per-request raw records (arrival, TTFT, per-token timestamps, output length, status); per-layer kernel name and achieved-bandwidth traces for both arms; the arm configuration manifest with hashes; per-slice quality scores with CIs plus raw generations; the HBM ledger with KV blocks as the residual and a measured high-water mark; the A/A noise-floor numbers; and matched-window fleet GPU-hour and token accounting, because benchmarks propose and production billing disposes.

Rollback gates, pre-committed. Revert if p95 TTFT or TPOT exceeds SLO at target concurrency; if any eval slice falls more than 1.0 point absolute with a 95% CI excluding zero; if structured-output compliance falls more than 2 points; if measured cost improvement is under 25%; if preemption or recompute rates rise without explanation; or if kernel-fallback evidence appears, in which case fix the tooling and re-run rather than concluding anything. Keep the BF16 arm warm and routable throughout so rollback is a routing flip rather than a redeploy, and rehearse the revert once before the canary.

Kernel efficiency on the specific shapes and TP degree in use, per-layer sensitivity of the specific checkpoint, and the production decode-token fraction are all MEASURED quantities in this design; none of them are asserted here. Every number above is labelled ESTIMATE and carries its derivation.
