Analytical stance under test: cold-start-and-autoscaling-behaviour-first - the artefact changes how fast capacity can appear, which is a separate SLO.

Falsifiable hypothesis H198h: the time from scale-out decision to a replica serving traffic at steady-state performance is no worse on the quantized arm, testable by measuring artefact pull time, load time, any on-the-fly conversion time, warmup steps to steady state and readiness-probe pass time on both arms from a cold node. If cold start is materially slower, the arm degrades burst response even when its steady-state numbers are better.

Serving cost is driven as much by how quickly capacity can be added as by how efficient a warm replica is, because autoscaled fleets must provision for the peak that arrives before new capacity is ready. Weight-only quantization touches this path in both directions and the net effect must be measured, not assumed. On the favourable side, a smaller artefact pulls from registry or object storage faster and occupies less page cache, which shortens the network-bound portion of cold start. On the unfavourable side, some pipelines perform conversion, repacking or kernel autotuning at load time, which adds a compute-bound phase that the baseline does not have; some quantized loaders are single-threaded where the baseline loader is parallel; and kernel autotune caches are cold on a fresh node, so the first requests run on untuned implementations. Measure the whole path from a genuinely cold node: artefact pull, load and any conversion, CUDA context and graph capture, warmup iterations until step time stabilises, and readiness-probe pass, reporting each phase separately so the regression can be attributed. Then translate into the operational quantity that matters: the headroom the fleet must hold to absorb a burst is proportional to cold-start time times the burst arrival rate, so a slower cold start forces more idle capacity and can cancel the steady-state saving. Boundary condition: fleets that run fixed capacity with no autoscaling are indifferent to this path, so the check should be scoped to elastic deployments and explicitly dropped otherwise. ESTIMATE: required standing headroom scales approximately linearly with cold-start time for a given burst ramp rate, so a doubling of cold start roughly doubles the idle replicas needed to hold the SLO during a ramp; derivation is capacity-deficit integration over the ramp interval, and it is an ESTIMATE, not MEASURED. Rollback gate: no adoption for an elastic fleet without phase-resolved cold-start measurements from a cold node on both arms.

Fairness in a cost-reduction comparison is as much a governance property as a measurement property, because the party proposing the saving usually also designs, runs and interprets the study, and every ambiguous methodological choice then has a direction that favours the proposal. Fix this structurally rather than by asking for care. A team wants lower serving cost through weight-only quantization. Define a fair comparison. Scenario variant 288: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.

Analytical stance under test: speculative-decoding-and-draft-model-interaction-first - the acceptance rate of a draft model is a function of the target model's precision.

Falsifiable hypothesis H199a: the draft-token acceptance rate of the speculative decoding path is statistically indistinguishable between the baseline and quantized target models on production prompts, testable by logging proposed and accepted token counts per request on both arms under identical draft model, draft length and acceptance rule. If acceptance drops on the quantized arm, the end-to-end speedup is smaller than the per-kernel speedup and can be negative.

Speculative decoding makes the comparison non-separable, because the quantized target model is not just faster per verification step, it is also a different acceptance oracle. Acceptance depends on agreement between the draft distribution and the target distribution, and weight-only quantization perturbs the target's logits, so the same draft model can see a different acceptance rate against the quantized target than against the baseline. If the study benchmarks the two targets without the speculative path and then enables it in production, the measured speedup does not transfer. Instrument the path directly: log proposed tokens, accepted tokens, acceptance rate per position in the draft window, and effective tokens per verification step, per arm, under an identical draft model, identical draft length and identical acceptance rule. Report the end-to-end tokens-per-second decomposed into verification-step cost times steps, rather than as a single number, so a per-step speedup that is cancelled by acceptance loss is visible rather than hidden. Two mechanisms drive the interaction. Quantization error is largest where the target distribution is flat or near-tied, which is exactly the regime where draft and target most often disagree, so acceptance loss concentrates in the uncertain positions that the draft was most useful for. Conversely, if the draft model is itself derived from the same base as the target, quantizing only the target breaks whatever distributional alignment made the draft effective, and re-tuning the draft length becomes part of the comparison rather than a fixed factor. Boundary condition: with speculative decoding disabled the two arms are directly comparable and this consideration drops out entirely, so the arm definition must state whether the speculative path is in scope, and if it is, the draft model and draft length must be treated as controlled factors and reported. ESTIMATE: end-to-end speedup is approximately the per-verification-step speedup times the ratio of accepted tokens per step across arms, so a per-step gain can be fully erased by a proportional acceptance loss; derivation is decomposing wall time into steps times per-step cost under a fixed token budget, and it is an ESTIMATE, not MEASURED.

Analytical stance under test: prefix-cache-hit-rate-and-block-reuse-first - the memory freed by quantization changes how much prompt work is avoided entirely.

Falsifiable hypothesis H199b: the prefix-cache hit rate measured under a replayed production trace is equal across arms after normalising for cache capacity, testable by logging cached-block hits, misses and evictions per request on both arms with the same trace and the same declared cache capacity. If hit rate differs, the throughput delta partly measures cache capacity rather than weight precision, and the two effects must be reported separately.

Modern serving stacks avoid recomputing shared prompt prefixes by caching key-value blocks and reusing them across requests, and the hit rate of that cache is a strong driver of prefill cost in workloads with system prompts, few-shot templates or multi-turn conversations. Weight-only quantization frees device memory, and if that memory is handed to the cache the quantized arm enjoys a larger cache and a higher hit rate, which improves throughput through a mechanism that has nothing to do with kernel speed. Mechanism. Weight-only quantization (WOQ) reduces the BYTES OF WEIGHTS READ PER FORWARD PASS. It therefore helps only where the kernel is memory-bandwidth bound, which in LLM serving means small-batch autoregressive decode. Prefill is compute bound; dequantization adds arithmetic there, so TTFT is flat or slightly worse. As batch size rises, decode GEMMs become compute bound too and the advantage decays monotonically toward 1.0x. Any claim of a uniform speedup across the concurrency range is mechanically wrong and should be treated as an instrumentation bug until explained.

Byte-count ceiling (ESTIMATE, derivation inline, not a throughput result). A 9B-parameter model in BF16 is 9e9 x 2 B = 18 GB of weights. INT4 with group-128 FP16 scale and zero point costs about 0.5 + ~0.06 B/param, i.e. ~5.0-5.3 GB. Ratio ~3.2-3.6x. This is pure byte counting with no kernel-efficiency model and no attention or KV traffic included; it is an upper bound on batch-1 decode speedup ONLY. Applying Amdahl with a decode-weight-read fraction f: f=0.4 bounds end-to-end gain near 1.33x, f=0.8 near 2.1x (ESTIMATE).

Mandatory two-arm-plus-one design. Run the quantized configuration TWICE: (a) with KV cache block count clamped to the BF16 baseline's block count, which isolates the kernel/bandwidth effect; (b) at native capacity, which shows the deployable benefit. Freed HBM becomes additional KV blocks and raises throughput by batching alone. If the clamped arm is flat, the honest conclusion is "we bought KV headroom", and tuning KV settings on the BF16 arm must be priced as the cheaper alternative before shipping a second numeric path.

Compare arms at the intersection of each arm's own latency-throughput frontier with the p95 SLO, never at a fixed batch size; the two arms have different optimal batch sizes, and fixed-batch comparison is the single most common way these studies mislead. Quantization recipes almost never quantize everything. Embedding tables and the output projection are commonly left in higher precision because they are quality-sensitive and, in tied-weight architectures, shared; normalisation parameters and biases are tiny but always excluded; and mixed-precision schemes deliberately retain sensitive layers or outlier channels at higher width. The nominal ratio implied by the bit width is therefore an upper bound on the saving, and the gap between nominal and realised can be large in models where vocabulary-related parameters are a substantial share of the total. Build the ledger from the loaded artefact rather than from the recipe description: enumerate every parameter tensor with dtype, element count and bytes, sum by quantized and unquantized groups, and add the metadata overhead that quantization introduces, namely per-group scales and any zero points, whose size depends on group granularity and can be non-trivial at fine granularity. Report realised bytes and the implied saving, and use that number, not the bit-width ratio, in every downstream capacity and cost calculation. The same ledger answers the memory-pressure question, because what matters for concurrency headroom is bytes actually freed on the device at steady state, after allocator rounding and any retained intermediate buffers. Boundary condition: models with large vocabularies relative to their depth have proportionally more unquantized parameter mass, so the realised saving is architecture-dependent and cannot be transferred between model families. Freed HBM becomes additional KV blocks and raises throughput by batching alone. If the clamped arm is flat, the honest conclusion is "we bought KV headroom", and tuning KV settings on the BF16 arm must be priced as the cheaper alternative before shipping a second numeric path.

Arm identity is frozen and hashed. Checkpoint hash, bit width, group size, symmetric/asymmetric, outlier or mixed-precision policy, calibration dataset hash, library and engine build, TP/PP layout, activation precision, KV precision, block size, max_num_seqs, max_model_len, chunked-prefill state, speculative-decoding state. The configuration symmetric difference between arms must be exactly the bit-width fields; anything else invalidates the comparison. Weight-only means weight-only: "INT4 plus FP8 KV" is two experiments, and the KV change usually explains most of the throughput delta while none of the quality delta gets attributed correctly.

Comparison point. Compare arms at the intersection of each arm's own latency-throughput frontier with the p95 SLO, never at a fixed batch size; the two arms have different optimal batch sizes, and fixed-batch comparison is the single most common way these studies mislead. Cost unit is GPU-seconds per 1,000 output tokens at that fixed p95 SLO, converted to currency last.

Measurement protocol. At least five concurrency points, at least three repeats per point, steady state with a fixed warmup-exclusion rule, greedy decoding and fixed seed for quality, bootstrap 95% CIs on ABSOLUTE quality deltas. Quality is sliced: long context, structured/JSON output, code, math, safety and refusal behaviour; aggregate scores can stay flat while repetition or truncation degrades, so sampled side-by-side output diffs are part of the evidence, not a nicety. A BF16-vs-BF16 A/A control across seeds and physical GPUs establishes the noise floor that any claimed delta must clear.

Analytical stance under test: queueing-nonlinearity-and-utilisation-operating-point-first - a capacity gain converts into latency at a rate that depends on where the system sits on its queueing curve.

If the curves have different knees, a benefit measured at low load does not predict behaviour at production load and may invert near saturation.

Serving latency is not a linear function of service rate. As offered load approaches capacity, waiting time grows sharply, so the same proportional improvement in service rate produces a small latency benefit at low utilisation and a very large one near the knee, and conversely a small capacity regression near the knee produces a disproportionate latency blowup. Benchmarks are typically run at a comfortable load where the system is far from saturation, which is precisely where the curve is flattest and least informative about the production operating point. Sweep the load instead of sampling it. Drive both arms across a range of offered loads spanning the production level and beyond it toward saturation, and report full latency-versus-load curves with the saturation point identified for each arm; the comparison is then between curves, and the decision-relevant quantity is the latency at the production offered load plus the headroom to the knee. Two effects specific to this workload class complicate the curve. Continuous batching means service rate itself depends on queue occupancy, so the system has a feedback loop that can produce a sharper knee than a simple queueing model predicts. Falsifiable hypothesis H199i: the per-step collective communication time and its overlap with compute are unchanged between arms in the tensor-parallel deployment, testable by profiling per-step timelines on both arms and extracting collective duration, exposed non-overlapped communication time and any synchronisation stalls. If communication becomes a larger share of the step on the quantized arm, the end-to-end speedup is bounded by the unchanged communication term rather than by the kernel gain.

In a sharded deployment the step time is a mixture of local compute and collective communication, and weight-only quantization shrinks only the first term. The communication term is determined by activation sizes and the parallelism topology, and activations are untouched by weight-only quantization, so the collective volume per step is unchanged. The immediate consequence is that the achievable end-to-end speedup is bounded by the compute share of the step: if communication is already a large fraction, a large kernel speedup produces a small step-time improvement, and the study must report the decomposition rather than the kernel number. Faster local compute reduces the window available to overlap communication with computation, so a scheduler that previously hid most of the collective behind compute may now expose it, and the exposed fraction rises faster than the compute time falls. Profile per-step timelines on both arms and extract collective duration, exposed non-overlapped time and synchronisation stalls, rather than inferring from step time alone. Faster compute can also change arrival timing at synchronisation points and expose or reduce load imbalance across ranks, so per-rank step times and the straggler distribution belong in the report. Boundary condition: a single-device deployment has no collective term and this axis drops out entirely, so the parallelism topology, including tensor-parallel degree and interconnect class, must be recorded as a fixed factor and held identical across arms. If agreement is at or near chance, the human instrument is not measuring anything and cannot license the adoption decision.

Many quantization studies end with automatic metrics that are statistically indistinguishable and then declare parity, but on open-ended generation those metrics often lack the resolution to detect the failure modes operators actually care about, such as subtle loss of instruction adherence, degraded reasoning chains or increased hedging. Escalating to human judgement is legitimate, but the human panel is an instrument and must be validated like one. Blind it: raters must not know which output came from which arm, and arm order must be randomised per item, because knowledge of the treatment reliably biases preference. Pre-declare the criteria and the rubric before any output is seen, and duplicate a fraction of items within and across raters to estimate intra-rater and inter-rater agreement; report those agreement statistics alongside the preference result, and treat a preference result with near-chance agreement as uninformative rather than as parity. Sample items from the production slice distribution rather than from a convenience set, since the failure modes concentrate on the hard slices and a uniform sample will dilute them. Finally, state the decision rule in advance, including how many items and what preference margin would be required to declare a regression, so the panel size is not chosen after inspecting an interim result. Boundary condition: where an automatic metric has been validated against human judgement on this task and shown adequate resolution, the human panel is unnecessary and the automatic result stands; that validation must be cited rather than presumed. ESTIMATE: the number of paired items needed to resolve a small preference margin grows roughly as the inverse square of the margin, so detecting a subtle regression requires a panel effort far larger than the pilot studies typically run; derivation is standard sample-size scaling for proportion comparisons, and it is an ESTIMATE, not MEASURED.

Production serving decisions are made under support obligations, not only under performance numbers. Analytical stance under test: latency-metric-decomposition-first - TTFT and TPOT are governed by different bottlenecks and the two parallelism axes move them in opposite directions.

Collapsing serving latency into a single number is the fastest way to a wrong parallelism decision, because prefill and decode are governed by different bottlenecks. TTFT is dominated by prefill, which is compute-bound and parallelises well across tensor shards, so tensor parallelism reduces TTFT roughly in proportion to the added devices minus the per-layer collective overhead. Pipeline parallelism does not help TTFT for a single request at all: the request must traverse every stage sequentially, and the stage transfers add to the path, so PP's TTFT is at best equal to the single-device case and typically slightly worse. TPOT behaves differently. Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound on weight reads, and tensor parallelism divides the weight bytes each device must read per step, so TPOT also improves under TP, but the per-layer collective is now a larger fraction of a much shorter step, so the improvement saturates and can invert past a TP degree where collective latency exceeds the compute it hid. Mechanism. Tensor parallelism (TP) splits every layer's weight matrices across devices, so each token's forward pass requires a collective (all-reduce or reduce-scatter/all-gather) at every TP-sharded block. TP therefore reduces per-device weight bytes and per-device FLOPs for a single request, and it lowers single-request latency, but it pays a collective on the critical path of every layer of every step. Pipeline parallelism (PP) splits the model by layer depth across devices, so a single request traverses stages sequentially and its latency is the sum of stage times plus point-to-point transfers; PP's inter-stage traffic is small (one activation tensor per boundary) but a single in-flight request leaves all but one stage idle. The mechanical consequence for a latency-sensitive service is asymmetric: TP reduces the latency of one request; PP does not, and only recovers device utilisation by keeping multiple microbatches in flight, which is a throughput mechanism, not a latency mechanism.

Boundary conditions that decide the answer. (1) Interconnect class within a TP group. TP is viable only when the devices in a TP group share a high-bandwidth, low-latency link; across a slower fabric the per-layer collective dominates and TP latency degrades rather than improves. (2) Whether the model fits. If per-device memory cannot hold weights plus KV cache plus activation workspace at the target context length and concurrency, some sharding is mandatory and the question becomes which axis, not whether. (3) Offered concurrency. At concurrency 1 PP is nearly pure loss; at high sustained concurrency PP's bubbles fill and its throughput per device can exceed TP's because it pays no per-layer collective. (4) Whether the latency target is on TTFT, TPOT, or end-to-end, since prefill is compute-bound and decode is bandwidth-bound and the two axes affect them differently.

If utilisation is low at production load, the pipeline is paying latency for throughput it is not actually delivering, and the layout is dominated by alternatives.

Pipeline parallelism converts a depth-partitioned model into a assembly line, and an assembly line is only efficient when it is full. With S stages and M microbatches in flight, the classic bubble fraction is approximately (S-1)/(M+S-1): the pipeline spends the first S-1 slots filling and the last S-1 draining, and only the steady middle is fully utilised. The decisive consequence for a latency-sensitive service is that M is not a free parameter, it is set by offered concurrency. At concurrency 1 there is one request in flight, M is effectively 1, the bubble fraction approaches (S-1)/S, and an S-stage pipeline leaves roughly a fraction (S-1)/S of its devices idle while delivering latency no better than a single device. That is why PP is a throughput mechanism and TP is a latency mechanism, and why the parallelism choice cannot be made without the concurrency distribution. Two complications specific to LLM decode make the arithmetic worse than the textbook formula. Stage times are not equal unless the layer partition is balanced against actual per-layer cost, including the embedding and output projection which sit at the ends and are often much heavier than a transformer block, so the slowest stage sets the rate and the imbalance adds to the bubble. And continuous batching means requests arrive and complete asynchronously, so the in-flight set churns and the pipeline never reaches the clean steady state the formula assumes. Profile the bubble rather than computing it: per-stage busy and idle time across the load sweep, with the partition's per-stage parameter and FLOP counts reported alongside. Boundary condition: at sustained high concurrency with a balanced partition the bubble fraction becomes small and PP's freedom from per-layer collectives can make it the better throughput-per-device layout; the crossover load must be measured, not assumed. ESTIMATE: bubble fraction is approximately (S-1)/(M+S-1), so a 4-stage pipeline at M=1 idles about 75 percent of its devices while at M=16 it idles about 16 percent; derivation is the fill-and-drain slot count over total slots, and it is an ESTIMATE, not MEASURED, since it ignores stage imbalance and scheduler churn which both make it worse.

Analytical stance under test: collective-topology-and-node-boundary-first - a TP group that crosses a slower fabric is a different system from one that does not.

Tensor parallelism pays a collective at every sharded block, which means the collective is on the critical path of every layer of every decoding step, and its cost is set by the slowest link in the group. Pipeline parallelism has the inverse property, since it transfers one activation tensor per stage boundary per microbatch rather than per layer, so its traffic is orders of magnitude smaller and it tolerates slower links, which is exactly why the conventional layout places TP within a node and PP across nodes. Do not infer the topology from the device count or from convention; enumerate it, recording device-to-device link types, bandwidths and any switch hierarchy as reported by the platform, and map the intended rank assignment onto physical devices before running anything, because rank-to-device assignment is frequently left to defaults and defaults do not always respect the topology. Then verify empirically with a collective microbenchmark at the message sizes the model actually produces, since achieved bandwidth at small message sizes is latency-dominated and can be far below the link's nominal figure, and decode-step collectives are small messages. Boundary condition: on a single-node deployment where all devices share one fabric, the boundary question does not arise and the TP degree is limited by collective overhead and memory rather than topology; on multi-node deployments the topology constraint usually decides the layout before any performance measurement is taken. Analytical stance under test: kv-cache-capacity-and-concurrency-ceiling-first - the layout that leaves the least KV headroom caps concurrency regardless of its per-request speed.

Falsifiable hypothesis H200f: the two layouts provide equal usable KV cache capacity in blocks at the target context length, testable by reading the engine's reported block count and measuring peak device memory for weights, activations and cache separately under each layout. If capacity differs, part of any throughput difference is a memory-budget effect rather than a parallelism effect and must be reported separately.

A parallelism layout is also a memory layout, and memory determines how many sequences can be resident, which determines the concurrency ceiling and therefore the throughput at any latency target. The two axes distribute memory differently. Tensor parallelism shards weights across all devices in the group, so per-device weight residency falls by the TP degree, and it also shards the KV cache along the head dimension, so per-device cache bytes per sequence fall too, but activation workspace and any replicated buffers do not shrink proportionally and the collective buffers add overhead. Pipeline parallelism gives each stage only its own layers' weights, so per-device weight residency falls by the stage count, but each stage must hold KV cache for its own layers for every sequence in flight, and the number in flight is inflated by the microbatching needed to fill the pipeline, so the cache demand per device is not simply divided. The net effect on usable blocks is layout-specific and allocator-specific and cannot be derived from parameter counts alone. Build the ledger empirically per arm: weights, per-stage or per-shard KV cache, activation workspace, collective and communication buffers, allocator fragmentation and a measured high-water mark, with the engine's reported block count as the observable that matters. Then check the consequence rather than the cause, by measuring preemption and KV recompute rates under the production trace, since a layout that runs out of blocks manifests as preemption and recompute long before it manifests as an out-of-memory error, and recompute silently inflates latency in a way that per-step profiling attributes to compute. Boundary condition: at short context lengths and low concurrency the cache is not the binding constraint and this axis drops out; at long context it typically dominates the layout decision. Falsifiable hypothesis H200g: recovery time from a single device failure is within the availability budget under both layouts, testable by injecting a device failure in a staging replica under each layout and measuring detection time, requests lost or degraded, and time to restore full serving capacity. If recovery exceeds the budget, the layout's availability cost must be priced against its latency benefit rather than assumed negligible.

Sharding a model couples devices into a single failure unit, and a latency-sensitive service usually also carries an availability commitment, so the failure behaviour is part of the comparison rather than an operational footnote. Under tensor parallelism the group fails as a unit: losing one device in a TP group takes down every request in that group, and the replica cannot serve until a full group is reconstituted, so the blast radius equals the TP degree and the recovery requires reloading sharded weights across the whole group. Under pipeline parallelism the failure is also fatal to in-flight requests but the blast radius is the stage, and depending on the engine a stage can sometimes be replaced without reloading the entire model, though many implementations restart the whole pipeline anyway and the difference must be verified rather than assumed. Both layouts also affect how gracefully the fleet degrades: with fewer, larger replicas the loss of one replica removes a larger fraction of capacity, so the layout choice interacts with replica count and headroom planning. Measure it by injection rather than by argument, in a staging replica under each layout, recording detection latency, the number of requests dropped or degraded, whether in-flight requests can be retried transparently by the router, time to restore full capacity, and whether any manual intervention was needed. Then check the fleet-level consequence, since a layout requiring more devices per replica reduces the number of independent replicas at fixed fleet size and concentrates risk. Boundary condition: a deployment with generous replica headroom and fast automated replacement can absorb a larger blast radius, so the availability cost is a function of fleet design, not of the layout alone. ESTIMATE: capacity lost per device failure scales with the number of devices per replica, so a layout that doubles devices per replica doubles the capacity removed by one failure at fixed fleet size; derivation is dividing fleet capacity by replica count under each layout, and it is an ESTIMATE, not MEASURED.

Mechanism. Tensor parallelism (TP) splits every layer's weight matrices across devices, so each token's forward pass requires a collective (all-reduce or reduce-scatter/all-gather) at every TP-sharded block. TP therefore reduces per-device weight bytes and per-device FLOPs for a single request, and it lowers single-request latency, but it pays a collective on the critical path of every layer of every step. Pipeline parallelism (PP) splits the model by layer depth across devices, so a single request traverses stages sequentially and its latency is the sum of stage times plus point-to-point transfers; PP's inter-stage traffic is small (one activation tensor per boundary) but a single in-flight request leaves all but one stage idle. The mechanical consequence for a latency-sensitive service is asymmetric: TP reduces the latency of one request; PP does not, and only recovers device utilisation by keeping multiple microbatches in flight, which is a throughput mechanism, not a latency mechanism.

Boundary conditions that decide the answer. (1) Interconnect class within a TP group. TP is viable only when the devices in a TP group share a high-bandwidth, low-latency link; across a slower fabric the per-layer collective dominates and TP latency degrades rather than improves. (2) Whether the model fits. If per-device memory cannot hold weights plus KV cache plus activation workspace at the target context length and concurrency, some sharding is mandatory and the question becomes which axis, not whether. (3) Offered concurrency. At concurrency 1 PP is nearly pure loss; at high sustained concurrency PP's bubbles fill and its throughput per device can exceed TP's because it pays no per-layer collective. (4) Whether the latency target is on TTFT, TPOT, or end-to-end, since prefill is compute-bound and decode is bandwidth-bound and the two axes affect them differently.

Assumptions that must be stated before any recommendation. Model parameter count and dtype; per-device memory capacity; target context length and output length distribution; the p95 or p99 latency target and which metric it is denominated in; offered load in requests per second and its burstiness; intra-node interconnect type and topology, and whether any parallel group would cross a node boundary; the serving engine and its scheduler mode (continuous batching, chunked prefill); and whether the deployment must tolerate device failure without full restart. A recommendation issued without these is not an engineering answer.

Falsifiability and controlled experiment. The comparison must fix the model checkpoint hash, the request trace, the tokenizer, the sampling policy (greedy, fixed seed, for quality) and the total device count, and vary only the parallelism layout. Sweep offered load across at least five points spanning the production level through saturation, at least three repeats per point, steady state with a declared warmup-exclusion rule, and report full latency-versus-load curves with per-arm knees rather than single-point numbers. Run an A/A control (identical layout, different seeds and different physical devices) first to establish the noise floor that any claimed delta must clear.

Evidence required before any decision. Per-request raw records with arrival timestamp, TTFT, per-token timestamps, output length and terminal status; per-step timeline profiles giving collective duration, exposed non-overlapped communication time, point-to-point stage transfer time, and per-rank straggler distribution; the memory ledger per device with weights, KV blocks and activation workspace itemised plus a measured high-water mark; the achieved KV block count and preemption or recompute rate per arm, since a layout that leaves less KV headroom silently caps concurrency; the interconnect topology as enumerated by the platform rather than assumed; and a reconfiguration drill measuring time to recover from a single device failure under each layout.

Confounders to control and report. Autotune and kernel-cache warmth, which favours whichever arm ran second; clock and thermal drift over long sweeps; asymmetric telemetry overhead between arms; NUMA placement and whether any parallel group crosses a socket or node boundary; scheduler differences such as chunked prefill being enabled by default at one layout and not the other; and PP microbatch or TP group size being left at engine defaults rather than tuned per arm, which compares a tuned configuration against an untuned one.

Rollback gates, pre-committed. Revert if p95 TTFT or TPOT exceeds the SLO at target concurrency; if achieved throughput per device at the SLO-constrained operating point is worse than the incumbent; if preemption or KV recompute rates rise without an explanation traced to a named mechanism; if any quality slice regresses with a 95% CI excluding zero, which would indicate a numerics or sharding-correctness defect rather than a performance trade; or if the failure-recovery drill exceeds the availability budget. Keep the incumbent layout warm and routable so rollback is a routing flip, and rehearse the revert once before the canary.

Analytical stance under test: layer-partition-balance-and-heterogeneous-block-cost-first - PP assumes equal stages, and transformer stacks are not equal at their ends.

Falsifiable hypothesis H200h: the proposed pipeline partition yields per-stage step times within a stated tolerance of each other, testable by profiling per-stage busy time under a fixed microbatch and comparing the maximum against the mean. If the slowest stage exceeds the mean beyond tolerance, pipeline throughput is set by that stage and the nominal stage count overstates the achievable speedup.

Pipeline throughput is governed by the slowest stage, not by the average, so a partition that divides layers evenly by count but not by cost wastes capacity on every stage that finishes early. Transformer stacks are heterogeneous precisely at the boundaries where naive partitions place cuts: the embedding table and the output projection are large and, in tied-weight architectures, shared, so a first or last stage that carries one of them can be substantially more expensive than an interior stage holding the same number of transformer blocks. Interior blocks are not always uniform either, since some architectures interleave attention variants, vary expert routing, or apply different context-window handling at different depths. Partition by measured cost rather than by layer count: profile per-layer forward time and per-layer parameter bytes at the target shapes first, then cut to equalise stage time, and re-profile after the cut because the cut itself changes memory pressure and kernel selection per device. Report the per-stage step-time distribution and the ratio of maximum to mean as the partition's quality metric. Two further effects deserve measurement rather than assumption: memory imbalance across stages can force a different maximum batch per stage, which the scheduler must respect globally and which therefore propagates the constraint from the tightest stage to the whole pipeline; and imbalance compounds with the bubble, since a slow stage both sets the rate and lengthens the fill and drain phases. Boundary condition: with a well-balanced partition and high in-flight microbatch count, PP's per-device efficiency approaches its ideal and its freedom from per-layer collectives becomes an advantage; with an unbalanced partition the same layout can be worse than no pipelining at all. ESTIMATE: pipeline throughput is approximately the reciprocal of the slowest stage time, so a partition whose slowest stage is 40 percent above the mean delivers roughly 70 percent of the balanced-partition throughput; derivation is taking the maximum rather than the mean of stage times as the rate-limiting term, and it is an ESTIMATE, not MEASURED.

Analytical stance under test: hybrid-layout-search-space-first - the question as posed is a false binary, and the decision variable is a factorisation of the device count.

Falsifiable hypothesis H200i: the best layout at the stated latency target lies at one of the two extremes of the parallelism factorisation rather than at an interior hybrid point, testable by sweeping the full set of valid (TP degree, PP degree) factorisations of the fixed device count under an identical trace and comparing SLO-constrained throughput per device. If an interior hybrid point wins, the binary framing of the original question would have selected a dominated configuration.

Framing the decision as tensor versus pipeline discards most of the search space. With a fixed device count N, any factorisation into TP degree times PP degree times data-parallel replica count is a candidate, and the extremes the question names are just two of them. The interior points are often better because the two axes have complementary constraints: TP is limited by collective overhead, which grows with degree and eventually dominates the shortening step, and by topology, which caps the degree at the size of the high-bandwidth domain; PP is limited by the bubble, which shrinks with in-flight microbatches but grows with stage count. A hybrid that sets TP to the largest degree the topology and collective overhead support, then uses PP only to the extent additional memory capacity is required, then spends the remainder on data-parallel replicas, frequently dominates both extremes. Data parallelism deserves explicit consideration rather than silent omission: if the model fits with a modest TP degree, additional devices buy more independent replicas, which improves throughput linearly and improves availability, and neither TP nor PP does that. Enumerate the valid factorisations of N, exclude those violating memory or topology constraints, and measure the survivors under an identical trace, reporting SLO-constrained throughput per device rather than raw latency so the comparison is decision-relevant. Boundary condition: when the model does not fit on one device, the minimum sharding degree is forced and the search space shrinks accordingly; when it fits comfortably, pure data parallelism is often the correct answer and both sharded layouts are dominated. ESTIMATE: the candidate set is the set of factorisations of the device count, which is small enough to sweep exhaustively for typical node sizes, so exhaustive measurement is cheaper than the modelling effort needed to prune it; derivation is counting divisors of N under the memory and topology constraints, and it is an ESTIMATE, not MEASURED.

Analytical stance under test: numerical-equivalence-and-sharding-correctness-first - a parallelism change is supposed to be quality-neutral, and that neutrality is a testable claim rather than a guarantee.

Falsifiable hypothesis H200j: outputs are numerically equivalent within a stated tolerance across the two layouts under greedy decoding with a fixed seed and identical inputs, testable by running a fixed prompt set through both layouts and comparing generated token sequences and logits. If outputs diverge beyond floating-point reassociation tolerance, there is a sharding or collective-correctness defect and no performance number from either arm is trustworthy until it is resolved.

Unlike quantization, changing the parallelism layout is not supposed to change what the model computes, which makes numerical comparison a correctness test rather than a quality trade-off. That test is worth running because the layouts differ in real ways that can break equivalence. Collective reductions change the order of floating-point accumulation, and floating-point addition is not associative, so bitwise identity is not expected; small logit differences are normal and can flip a token at a near-tie, which then diverges the whole continuation. Distinguish that benign mechanism from genuine defects by comparing logit distributions on the first generated position rather than only the final text, since a reassociation difference shows as a tiny logit perturbation while a sharding bug, a wrong rank mapping, a mis-partitioned attention head group or an incorrectly replicated normalisation parameter shows as a large one. Run a fixed prompt set under greedy decoding with a fixed seed through both layouts, report first-position logit differences and the position at which text first diverges, and treat large early divergence as a blocking defect. Long-context and structured-output slices deserve extra weight because attention-head sharding and position-handling bugs frequently only manifest past a certain sequence length or with particular masking patterns. Boundary condition: with sampling enabled, seeds do not guarantee identical streams across layouts because the number and order of random draws can differ, so the equivalence test must be run under greedy decoding and the sampling path validated separately by distributional comparison. ESTIMATE: benign reassociation differences are on the order of floating-point epsilon accumulated over the reduction tree depth, which is far smaller than the logit gaps that separate confident predictions, so a large early logit difference indicates a defect rather than reassociation; derivation is comparing accumulated rounding magnitude against typical logit separation, and it is an ESTIMATE, not MEASURED.

Analytical stance under test: scheduler-interaction-and-chunked-prefill-first - the parallelism layout is evaluated through a scheduler whose policy can dominate the effect being measured.

Falsifiable hypothesis H201a: the two layouts are compared under equivalent scheduler policy, testable by dumping the engine's effective scheduler configuration per arm - chunked prefill on or off, chunk size, max running sequences, max batched tokens, preemption policy - and diffing them. If the configurations differ, part of any measured latency delta is a scheduler effect rather than a parallelism effect and the comparison is confounded.

Serving latency is produced jointly by the parallelism layout and the request scheduler, and modern engines set scheduler defaults as a function of the layout, so a naive A/B silently varies two things at once. Chunked prefill is the clearest case: it splits long prefills into token-budgeted chunks interleaved with decode steps, which lowers decode-step jitter and TPOT tail at the cost of TTFT, and whether it is enabled by default can differ between a tensor-parallel and a pipeline-parallel configuration. Max-batched-tokens and max-running-sequences are similarly derived from available KV blocks, which the layout changes, so the two arms can end up running different admission policies without anyone choosing that. The discipline is to dump the effective, runtime-resolved scheduler state per arm rather than the requested configuration, diff it field by field, and either equalise the policy or report the difference as a named, quantified confounder. Where equalising is impossible because a policy is not supported under one layout, that limitation is itself a finding and belongs in the comparison rather than in a footnote. Boundary condition: at low offered load the scheduler rarely queues and its policy is nearly inert, so this axis matters mainly at or above the knee of the load curve, which is exactly where the SLO-constrained operating point sits. ESTIMATE: chunked prefill trades TTFT for TPOT tail, so enabling it on one arm only can move the two metrics in opposite directions and produce a verdict that reverses when the policy is equalised; derivation is the reallocation of step time between prefill and decode work, and it is an ESTIMATE, not MEASURED.

Performance comparisons are usually framed as one-shot decisions, but serving layouts are revisited as models, traffic and hardware change, so the cost of changing one's mind is a real term. --- Shared substrate (identical across this study, stated once so the stance above is the only variable) ---

Mechanism. Tensor parallelism (TP) splits every layer's weight matrices across devices, so each token's forward pass requires a collective (all-reduce or reduce-scatter/all-gather) at every TP-sharded block. TP therefore reduces per-device weight bytes and per-device FLOPs for a single request, and it lowers single-request latency, but it pays a collective on the critical path of every layer of every step. Pipeline parallelism (PP) splits the model by layer depth across devices, so a single request traverses stages sequentially and its latency is the sum of stage times plus point-to-point transfers; PP's inter-stage traffic is small (one activation tensor per boundary) but a single in-flight request leaves all but one stage idle. The mechanical consequence for a latency-sensitive service is asymmetric: TP reduces the latency of one request; PP does not, and only recovers device utilisation by keeping multiple microbatches in flight, which is a throughput mechanism, not a latency mechanism.

Boundary conditions that decide the answer. (1) Interconnect class within a TP group. TP is viable only when the devices in a TP group share a high-bandwidth, low-latency link; across a slower fabric the per-layer collective dominates and TP latency degrades rather than improves. (2) Whether the model fits. If per-device memory cannot hold weights plus KV cache plus activation workspace at the target context length and concurrency, some sharding is mandatory and the question becomes which axis, not whether. (3) Offered concurrency. At concurrency 1 PP is nearly pure loss; at high sustained concurrency PP's bubbles fill and its throughput per device can exceed TP's because it pays no per-layer collective. (4) Whether the latency target is on TTFT, TPOT, or end-to-end, since prefill is compute-bound and decode is bandwidth-bound and the two axes affect them differently.

Assumptions that must be stated before any recommendation. Model parameter count and dtype; per-device memory capacity; target context length and output length distribution; the p95 or p99 latency target and which metric it is denominated in; offered load in requests per second and its burstiness; intra-node interconnect type and topology, and whether any parallel group would cross a node boundary; the serving engine and its scheduler mode (continuous batching, chunked prefill); and whether the deployment must tolerate device failure without full restart. The comparison must fix the model checkpoint hash, the request trace, the tokenizer, the sampling policy (greedy, fixed seed, for quality) and the total device count, and vary only the parallelism layout. Sweep offered load across at least five points spanning the production level through saturation, at least three repeats per point, steady state with a declared warmup-exclusion rule, and report full latency-versus-load curves with per-arm knees rather than single-point numbers. Analytical stance under test: Stance 20 - Roofline decomposition of decode latency.

Common frame (applies to every stance below).
Assumptions (must be restated by the answering engineer, not inherited silently):
A1. Single node, 8 GPUs, NVLink/NVSwitch intra-node; inter-node only if TP is stretched across nodes (which we forbid).
A2. Decode-dominant, latency-sensitive serving: SLO expressed as TTFT p95 and TPOT (inter-token latency) p95, not mean.
A3. Model weights fit in aggregate HBM with KV-cache headroom >= 20% at target concurrency.
A4. No speculative decoding, no quantization change, no batching-policy change during the comparison; exactly one variable moves.
Mechanism, stated plainly:
- Tensor parallelism (TP) splits every layer's GEMMs across GPUs. Each transformer layer needs 2 collectives per block (all-reduce after attention out-proj and after MLP down-proj). Per-token decode latency therefore carries L * 2 * allreduce_latency of added synchronous cost, where L = number of layers. TP is latency-additive but capacity-multiplying: it cuts per-GPU weight bytes and per-GPU KV bytes by TP degree, and it raises the effective HBM bandwidth applied to a single token.
- Pipeline parallelism (PP) splits layers into stages. Per-token cost adds only (PP-1) point-to-point sends of one hidden-state vector, which is tiny, but decode serializes through stages: a single request's token must traverse all stages, and with micro-batching the pipeline bubble is (PP-1)/(micro_batches + PP-1). At low concurrency there are not enough in-flight micro-batches to fill the pipeline, so PP bubbles dominate and PP is the worse latency choice.
Boundary conditions that flip the answer:
- B1. If interconnect is NVLink-class (hundreds of GB/s, single-digit microsecond small-message all-reduce), TP up to 8 is normally latency-viable. If interconnect is PCIe-only or crosses nodes over RoCE/IB, TP all-reduce latency grows by roughly an order of magnitude and TP stops paying for itself past TP=2 (ESTIMATE; derivation: decode all-reduce messages are small, hidden_size * dtype_bytes per token per layer, so they are latency-bound not bandwidth-bound, and the latency floor of a fabric hop is what matters).
- B2. If the model does not fit on one GPU, some sharding is mandatory; then the question is only which axis, not whether.
- B3. If concurrency is high and steady, PP's bubble amortizes and PP becomes competitive on throughput per GPU while still losing on single-request latency.
Default recommendation: TP within the node up to the point where the collective cost stops being amortized by the reduced per-GPU memory traffic; use PP only to cross node boundaries or to fit a model that TP alone cannot fit. Do not use PP as a latency optimization.

Decompose TPOT into three additive terms and attack the largest. Evidence required: profiler traces separating GEMM time from collective time. Rollback gate: if p95 TPOT regresses more than 5% versus the incumbent config, revert to incumbent within one deploy cycle.

Common frame (applies to every stance below).
Assumptions (must be restated by the answering engineer, not inherited silently):
A1. Single node, 8 GPUs, NVLink/NVSwitch intra-node; inter-node only if TP is stretched across nodes (which we forbid).
A2. Decode-dominant, latency-sensitive serving: SLO expressed as TTFT p95 and TPOT (inter-token latency) p95, not mean.
A3. Model weights fit in aggregate HBM with KV-cache headroom >= 20% at target concurrency.
A4. No speculative decoding, no quantization change, no batching-policy change during the comparison; exactly one variable moves.
Mechanism, stated plainly:
- Tensor parallelism (TP) splits every layer's GEMMs across GPUs. Each transformer layer needs 2 collectives per block (all-reduce after attention out-proj and after MLP down-proj). Per-token decode latency therefore carries L * 2 * allreduce_latency of added synchronous cost, where L = number of layers. TP is latency-additive but capacity-multiplying: it cuts per-GPU weight bytes and per-GPU KV bytes by TP degree, and it raises the effective HBM bandwidth applied to a single token.
- Pipeline parallelism (PP) splits layers into stages. Per-token cost adds only (PP-1) point-to-point sends of one hidden-state vector, which is tiny, but decode serializes through stages: a single request's token must traverse all stages, and with micro-batching the pipeline bubble is (PP-1)/(micro_batches + PP-1). At low concurrency there are not enough in-flight micro-batches to fill the pipeline, so PP bubbles dominate and PP is the worse latency choice.
Boundary conditions that flip the answer:
- B1. If interconnect is NVLink-class (hundreds of GB/s, single-digit microsecond small-message all-reduce), TP up to 8 is normally latency-viable. If interconnect is PCIe-only or crosses nodes over RoCE/IB, TP all-reduce latency grows by roughly an order of magnitude and TP stops paying for itself past TP=2 (ESTIMATE; derivation: decode all-reduce messages are small, hidden_size * dtype_bytes per token per layer, so they are latency-bound not bandwidth-bound, and the latency floor of a fabric hop is what matters).
- B2. If the model does not fit on one GPU, some sharding is mandatory; then the question is only which axis, not whether.
- B3. If concurrency is high and steady, PP's bubble amortizes and PP becomes competitive on throughput per GPU while still losing on single-request latency.
Default recommendation: TP within the node up to the point where the collective cost stops being amortized by the reduced per-GPU memory traffic; use PP only to cross node boundaries or to fit a model that TP alone cannot fit. Do not use PP as a latency optimization.

If the deployment is or may become multi-node, treat fabric correctness as a gate that precedes any latency comparison. RDMA over converged Ethernet depends on a lossless or near-lossless configuration; misconfigured flow control or ECN produces intermittent pause storms and retransmissions that appear as unexplained latency spikes and are frequently misattributed to the parallelism strategy. GPUDirect RDMA must be verified as actually engaged rather than assumed, since a silent fallback to a staged host-memory copy adds latency and CPU cost without any error. Falsifiable hypothesis H35: with GPUDirect RDMA disabled, inter-node collective latency for small messages increases materially and p99 TPOT for any node-spanning TP group degrades far more than p50 (ESTIMATE; derivation: the staged copy adds a host round trip on the critical path of every collective). Controlled experiment: run the same topology with the direct path enabled and disabled, capturing transport selection and per-collective timing. Evidence required: NIC and switch counters for pause frames, ECN marks, discards and retransmits; explicit confirmation of which transport and which memory path the collective library selected. Rollback gate: any node-spanning configuration whose fabric counters show nonzero discards under load is rejected before latency is even considered.

Evaluate the choice by what happens on a bad day. A TP group is a gang-scheduled unit: it must be co-scheduled, it restarts together, and its startup cost includes loading shards and re-establishing collective communicators. Evidence required: timeline of pod/process restarts, communicator re-initialization duration, and error budget consumed during recovery. Rollback gate: do not adopt a parallel degree whose single-fault recovery consumes more than a pre-agreed fraction of the monthly error budget.

Mechanism, stated plainly:
- Tensor parallelism (TP) shards every layer's GEMMs. Each transformer block needs two all-reduces (after attention out-projection and after the MLP down-projection), so decode carries L * 2 * allreduce_latency of synchronous cost, where L is the layer count. The decidable difference between the layouts is often not latency but recovery behaviour under partial failure. A TP group is a tightly coupled unit: losing one rank aborts every in-flight request in that group and requires a full group restart with weight reload. A PP deployment loses one stage and still loses the whole pipeline, but its stages are smaller and can sometimes be rescheduled independently, and its weight reload per stage is smaller. The operator-visible quantity is therefore mean time to restore capacity, not mean token latency. Falsifiable hypothesis H53: time-to-first-healthy-request after a single-rank kill is lower for the layout with the smaller per-process weight footprint, because restore time is dominated by weight load from storage rather than by process startup (ESTIMATE; derivation: weight bytes per process divided by effective storage or host-to-device bandwidth is the dominant term when weights are large relative to any fixed initialisation cost). Controlled experiment: in a non-production replica, kill one rank in each arm under identical load and measure time to first healthy request, capacity restored over time, and requests failed. Evidence required: per-process weight footprint, weight-load throughput from the actual storage path, orchestrator restart policy, and the failure blast radius definition for each arm. Rollback gate: a layout whose measured restore time exceeds the availability budget is rejected even if it wins on p95 latency.

A single-replica benchmark answers a question nobody operates. Nominal free HBM is not usable HBM. Paged KV allocators, activation workspaces, communication buffers and autotuning scratch all interact, and the two layouts request memory in different shapes: TP asks for many smaller weight shards plus per-rank collective buffers, PP asks for fewer, larger contiguous stage weights plus inter-stage staging buffers. Controlled experiment: ramp concurrency to first allocation failure in each arm, recording reserved-versus-allocated memory over time and the allocator's own fragmentation statistics. Evidence required: allocator reserved and allocated timeseries, KV block pool configuration, and the exact failure mode and stack at first out-of-memory event. Rollback gate: size production concurrency from the measured first-failure point with margin, never from the arithmetic capacity estimate.

KV cache grows linearly with sequence length while weights do not, so at long context the memory picture is dominated by KV rather than by parameters. TP shards KV across ranks and therefore raises the concurrency ceiling at a given context length; PP does not shard KV within a stage, it only reduces the number of layers whose KV a given device holds, which is a different and often weaker lever. Evidence required: per-sequence KV byte accounting versus context length, TPOT curves per layout across the sweep, and the measured maximum concurrency at each context point. Rollback gate: never extrapolate a short-context layout verdict to a long-context deployment without re-running the sweep.

A2. Decode-dominant, latency-sensitive serving: the SLO is TTFT p95 and TPOT (inter-token latency) p95, never a mean.
A3. Model weights fit in aggregate HBM with at least 20% KV-cache headroom at target concurrency.
A4. Exactly one variable moves per arm: no simultaneous change of quantization, batching policy, or speculative decoding.
Mechanism, stated plainly:
- Tensor parallelism (TP) shards every layer's GEMMs. Each transformer block needs two all-reduces (after attention out-projection and after the MLP down-projection), so decode carries L * 2 * allreduce_latency of synchronous cost, where L is the layer count. TP is latency-additive in collectives but capacity- and bandwidth-multiplying: per-GPU weight bytes and per-GPU KV bytes both fall by the TP degree.
- Pipeline parallelism (PP) shards layers into stages. Per token it adds only (PP-1) small point-to-point hidden-state sends, which are cheap, but a single request serializes through all stages and the bubble fraction is (PP-1)/(micro_batches + PP-1). At low concurrency there are too few in-flight micro-batches to fill the pipeline, so PP loses badly on single-request latency.
Boundary conditions that flip the answer:
- B1. On NVLink-class fabric, small-message all-reduce latency is in the single-digit microseconds and TP up to 8 is normally latency-viable. Over PCIe-only or across nodes on RoCE/IB the same collective's latency floor rises roughly an order of magnitude and TP stops paying past TP=2 (ESTIMATE; derivation: decode all-reduce payload is hidden_size * dtype_bytes per token per layer, which is small, so the collective is latency-bound rather than bandwidth-bound and the per-hop latency floor dominates).
- B2. If the model cannot fit on one GPU, sharding is mandatory and the question reduces to which axis, not whether.
- B3. Under high, steady concurrency the PP bubble amortizes and PP becomes competitive on throughput per GPU while still losing on single-request latency.
Default recommendation: use TP inside the node up to the point where collective cost stops being repaid by reduced per-GPU memory traffic; use PP only to cross a node boundary or to fit a model TP alone cannot fit. PP is not a latency optimization.

Devices boost opportunistically and drop clocks under sustained power or thermal load. A TP arm keeps all ranks busy simultaneously with correlated compute and interconnect activity, raising aggregate board and chassis power, while a PP arm staggers activity across stages. If one arm hits a power cap and the other does not, the measured latency difference is partly a clock difference, and it will not reproduce in a differently cooled rack. Falsifiable hypothesis H84: sustained-run clocks in the arm with correlated activity fall below its short-run clocks by more than in the staggered arm, and pinning both arms to a common locked clock reduces the measured gap (ESTIMATE; derivation: achieved throughput scales with achieved clock, so an arm-dependent clock reduction propagates directly into an arm-dependent latency penalty). Controlled experiment: log per-device clock, power draw, temperature and throttle reason at high rate during every run, then repeat both arms with clocks locked to a common sustainable frequency and compare gaps. Evidence required: high-rate clock, power, temperature and throttle-reason telemetry per device per arm; ambient and rack cooling conditions; and paired free-clock versus locked-clock results. Rollback gate: treat any layout conclusion drawn from a run showing throttling events as invalid until repeated under locked clocks.

During migration both layouts serve traffic simultaneously, so the fleet's latency distribution is a mixture and any SLO alarm thresholds tuned on the old layout will misfire. Evidence required: checkpoint resharding procedure and its verification, replica-count and capacity arithmetic for both layouts, canary mixed-state percentile measurements split by layout, and the alarm thresholds in force. Rollback gate: abort the migration and restore the previous layout if canary fleet-level p95 breaches the SLO at any point, and require a tested checkpoint reshard path before the first production replica is switched.

Presenting the choice as TP versus PP is a false dichotomy. The deployable space is the product of tensor degree, pipeline degree, data-parallel replica count and, for MoE models, expert parallel degree, subject to the constraint that their product equals the device budget. For a latency-sensitive service, the usual answer is the smallest tensor degree that fits the model and KV working set within the fastest interconnect domain, pipeline only when memory forces crossing that domain, and spend everything remaining on replicas, because replicas add throughput without adding synchronous per-step overhead. Falsifiable hypothesis H86: at fixed device budget and fixed SLO, the configuration maximising replica count subject to fitting within the fast interconnect domain achieves higher SLO-sustaining throughput than any configuration that raises tensor or pipeline degree beyond that fit (ESTIMATE; derivation: replication adds no per-step collective or bubble cost, whereas both other axes add synchronous overhead to every step). Controlled experiment: enumerate all factorisations of the device budget, discard those that do not fit memory, and measure SLO-sustaining throughput for each survivor rather than comparing two hand-picked points. Evidence required: the enumerated configuration grid with its memory-feasibility calculation, the interconnect domain boundary and its measured bandwidth, and SLO-sustaining throughput per surviving configuration. Rollback gate: reject any decision memo that compares only two configurations without showing the feasible grid it selected them from.

Detokenisation, stop-sequence matching, structured-output constraint masks and logit processors run per token, often on the host and sometimes single-threaded. A constrained-decoding mask over a large vocabulary can cost more per token than the collective the layout argument is about, and this cost is layout-invariant, so it compresses the relative difference between arms and inflates absolute latency. Rollback gate: do not spend engineering effort on a layout change until host-side per-token cost has been measured and shown to be smaller than the gap being chased.

A layout that wins a benchmark but exposes no per-rank or per-stage signal is operationally worse than a slightly slower one that does. TP failures surface as a whole replica dying with a collective timeout whose root cause is on some other rank; PP failures surface as one stage stalling while the rest idle. Each demands different dashboards, different timeouts and different runbook entry points, and those must exist before the layout carries traffic. Controlled experiment: inject the same fault classes into both layouts, have an on-call engineer who did not design the experiment diagnose from dashboards alone, and time to correct root cause. Evidence required: the signal inventory per layout including per-rank and per-stage coverage, collective timeout settings, fault-injection drill transcripts with timings, and the runbook entries for each failure shape. Rollback gate: do not route production traffic to a layout whose failure shapes lack a dashboard signal and a runbook entry, regardless of its benchmark result.

If prefill and decode run on separate device pools connected by a KV transfer path, the layout no longer has to be a single compromise: the compute-bound prefill pool can take a layout that maximises arithmetic throughput while the memory-bandwidth-bound decode pool takes one that maximises KV capacity and minimises per-step overhead. Rollback gate: collapse back to a colocated layout if measured transfer time or pool imbalance pushes TTFT past the SLO at target load.

In a synchronous group, one failed device takes the whole group out. A4. Exactly one variable moves per arm: no simultaneous change of quantization, batching policy, or speculative decoding.
Mechanism, stated plainly:
- Tensor parallelism (TP) shards every layer's GEMMs. Each transformer block needs two all-reduces (after attention out-projection and after the MLP down-projection), so decode carries L * 2 * allreduce_latency of synchronous cost, where L is the layer count. TP is latency-additive in collectives but capacity- and bandwidth-multiplying: per-GPU weight bytes and per-GPU KV bytes both fall by the TP degree.
- Pipeline parallelism (PP) shards layers into stages. Per token it adds only (PP-1) small point-to-point hidden-state sends, which are cheap, but a single request serializes through all stages and the bubble fraction is (PP-1)/(micro_batches + PP-1). At low concurrency there are too few in-flight micro-batches to fill the pipeline, so PP loses badly on single-request latency.
Boundary conditions that flip the answer:
- B1. On NVLink-class fabric, small-message all-reduce latency is in the single-digit microseconds and TP up to 8 is normally latency-viable. Over PCIe-only or across nodes on RoCE/IB the same collective's latency floor rises roughly an order of magnitude and TP stops paying past TP=2 (ESTIMATE; derivation: decode all-reduce payload is hidden_size * dtype_bytes per token per layer, which is small, so the collective is latency-bound rather than bandwidth-bound and the per-hop latency floor dominates).

Speculative decoding replaces one-token-at-a-time decode with a draft-then-verify loop in which the target model scores several candidate tokens in a single forward pass. That converts a chain of tiny, latency-bound steps into fewer, wider steps, which raises arithmetic intensity and amortises each layer's collectives over more accepted tokens. Tensor parallelism, whose cost is a fixed per-layer synchronous all-reduce, is repaid better under speculation than under plain decode. Pipeline parallelism sees the opposite pressure: the verify step is still one logical request walking every stage, so the bubble is unchanged while the per-step work grows. Controlled experiment: Run four arms: TP-only and PP-only, each with speculation off and on, holding draft model, acceptance threshold, batching policy and quantisation fixed. In decode the dominant device cost is streaming weights out of HBM, and weight-only quantisation reduces those bytes roughly in proportion to the bit-width ratio. Collectives, however, operate on activations, which are usually kept at higher precision and are unaffected. So quantisation shrinks the numerator of the compute term while leaving the tensor-parallel synchronisation term intact, raising the fraction of step time spent in all-reduce. A tensor-parallel degree that looked free at full precision can become the visible bottleneck once weights are compressed. Controlled experiment: Sweep tensor degree over at least two values, crossed with quantised and unquantised weights, four cells total, holding batching policy, speculation setting and sequence-length distribution fixed. Capture a collective-level profile in every cell. Mechanism, stated plainly:
- Tensor parallelism (TP) shards every layer's GEMMs. Each transformer block needs two all-reduces (after attention out-projection and after the MLP down-projection), so decode carries L * 2 * allreduce_latency of synchronous cost, where L is the layer count. TP is latency-additive in collectives but capacity- and bandwidth-multiplying: per-GPU weight bytes and per-GPU KV bytes both fall by the TP degree.
- Pipeline parallelism (PP) shards layers into stages. Per token it adds only (PP-1) small point-to-point hidden-state sends, which are cheap, but a single request serializes through all stages and the bubble fraction is (PP-1)/(micro_batches + PP-1). At low concurrency there are too few in-flight micro-batches to fill the pipeline, so PP loses badly on single-request latency.

The two layouts have different blast radii. Under tensor parallelism every rank participates in every collective, so the loss of one GPU stalls the whole replica and the collective communicator must be torn down and rebuilt; under pipeline parallelism the loss of one stage breaks the chain equally but the surviving stages hold distinct weight shards, which changes what must be reloaded. Rollback gate: a layout whose measured recovery exceeds the error budget for the expected fault rate is rejected even if it wins every latency benchmark.

Tensor parallelism shards attention heads and therefore divides per-GPU KV bytes by the tensor degree, raising the number of concurrent sequences the replica can hold; pipeline parallelism gives each stage the full KV for its own layers only, which also reduces per-GPU KV but leaves per-stage capacity coupled to the layer split. Controlled experiment: sweep closed-loop concurrency upward in fixed steps on both arms until the SLO breaks, and at each step record free cache blocks, preemption count, recomputed tokens and step time, rather than reporting a single throughput number. Rollback gate: a layout is not promoted if it meets the SLO only at a concurrency that leaves less than the declared cache headroom, because normal traffic drift would then push it into preemption.

Controlled experiment: profile both arms with a device timeline plus host-side sampling profiler at concurrency 1, 4 and 16, report the host and device split of each step, then repeat with graph capture enabled and disabled. Rollback gate: if the layout advantage disappears once host overhead is equalised, the layout change is not adopted and the work is redirected to the host path, which is the cheaper fix.

A2. Decode-dominant, latency-sensitive serving: the SLO is TTFT p95 and TPOT (inter-token latency) p95, never a mean.
A3. Model weights fit in aggregate HBM with at least 20% KV-cache headroom at target concurrency.
A4. Exactly one variable moves per arm: no simultaneous change of quantization, batching policy, or speculative decoding.
Mechanism, stated plainly:
- Tensor parallelism (TP) shards every layer's GEMMs. Each transformer block needs two all-reduces (after attention out-projection and after the MLP down-projection), so decode carries L * 2 * allreduce_latency of synchronous cost, where L is the layer count. TP is latency-additive in collectives but capacity- and bandwidth-multiplying: per-GPU weight bytes and per-GPU KV bytes both fall by the TP degree.
- Pipeline parallelism (PP) shards layers into stages. Per token it adds only (PP-1) small point-to-point hidden-state sends, which are cheap, but a single request serializes through all stages and the bubble fraction is (PP-1)/(micro_batches + PP-1). At low concurrency there are too few in-flight micro-batches to fill the pipeline, so PP loses badly on single-request latency.
Boundary conditions that flip the answer:
- B1. On NVLink-class fabric, small-message all-reduce latency is in the single-digit microseconds and TP up to 8 is normally latency-viable. Over PCIe-only or across nodes on RoCE/IB the same collective's latency floor rises roughly an order of magnitude and TP stops paying past TP=2 (ESTIMATE; derivation: decode all-reduce payload is hidden_size * dtype_bytes per token per layer, which is small, so the collective is latency-bound rather than bandwidth-bound and the per-hop latency floor dominates).
- B2. If the model cannot fit on one GPU, sharding is mandatory and the question reduces to which axis, not whether.
- B3. Under high, steady concurrency the PP bubble amortizes and PP becomes competitive on throughput per GPU while still losing on single-request latency.
Default recommendation: use TP inside the node up to the point where collective cost stops being repaid by reduced per-GPU memory traffic; use PP only to cross a node boundary or to fit a model TP alone cannot fit. PP is not a latency optimization.

Rollback gate: if measured KV transfer latency exceeds the declared fraction of the TTFT budget, disaggregation is reverted to co-located serving rather than absorbed as an unowned regression.

Once KV blocks are pooled, transferred between nodes or tiered into host memory or SSD, the decode path acquires a dependency on a storage and network system with its own queueing, hit rate and tail behaviour. A layout benchmark that keeps all KV resident in device memory measures a system without that dependency and therefore cannot bound production tail latency. Controlled experiment: instrument block-fetch hit rate, fetch latency distribution and per-step stall time, run both layouts with the tiered layer enabled and disabled, and report p50 and p99 separately for each of the four cells. Rollback gate: if measured stall time exceeds the declared share of the TPOT budget, the tiering tier is disabled or capacity is added before any layout conclusion is drawn from that configuration.

A tensor-parallel group is a synchronous unit; one dead rank stalls the collective and takes the whole replica down until the group is rebuilt. A pipeline arrangement is also synchronous within a replica, but its stage boundaries give a coarser, more restartable unit and a smaller blast radius when replicas are packed per node. Availability, not just latency, is therefore a function of the layout. Falsifiable hypothesis H184: injecting a single-rank fault produces a longer measured time-to-recovered-serving in the tensor arm than an equivalent single-stage fault in the pipeline arm, at equal replica count, because group reconstruction spans more coupled processes (ESTIMATE; derivation: recovery time scales with the number of processes that must be restarted and re-synchronised before the first token can be served, which is larger for a tightly coupled collective group). Controlled experiment: run identical fault-injection drills against both arms, killing one process per drill, and measure time from fault to first successfully served token plus the number of requests failed, repeated enough times to report a distribution. Rollback gate: a layout whose measured recovery time exceeds the availability budget is not promoted regardless of its latency advantage, and the drill is re-run after any topology change.

A draft-and-verify loop replaces the per-token decode step with a draft phase of k tokens plus one batched verification forward pass. Prefill processes many positions at once and is dominated by dense GEMM throughput, so TP's added collectives are amortized over a large amount of compute. Mechanism, stated plainly:

- Pipeline parallelism (PP) shards layers into stages. Per token it adds only (PP-1) small point-to-point hidden-state sends, which are cheap, but a single request serializes through all stages and the bubble fraction is (PP-1)/(micro_batches + PP-1). At low concurrency there are too few in-flight micro-batches to fill the pipeline, so PP loses badly on single-request latency.

- B1. On NVLink-class fabric, small-message all-reduce latency is in the single-digit microseconds and TP up to 8 is normally latency-viable. TP splits attention along the head axis. With multi-head attention there are as many KV heads as query heads and sharding is uniform. With grouped-query or multi-query attention the KV head count is much smaller, so at TP degrees above the KV head count the framework must replicate KV heads across ranks.
